research.topic: Google Gemma 4 model family (Hugging Face + ai.google.dev, as of 2026-10-04): variants, repo ids/gating, architecture of the 31B dense and 26B-A4B MoE, license, memory requirements
research.summary: The discussion's two headline numbers are CORRECT: Gemma 4 31B is a 30.7B dense model and Gemma 4 26B A4B is a 25.2B-total / 3.8B-active MoE (official model card at ai.google.dev; reproduced to within rounding from config.json: 30.70B and 25.23B/3.82B). The family (launched 2026-04-02, 12B added 2026-06-03) is: E2B (2.3B effective / 5.1B w/ embeddings, 35 layers, 128K, text+image+audio), E4B (4.5B eff / 8B, 42 layers, 128K, text+image+audio), 12B Unified (11.95B, 48 layers, 256K, encoder-free text+image+audio), 26B A4B MoE (25.2B/3.8B, 30 layers, 256K, text+image), 31B dense (30.7B, 60 layers, 256K, text+image). Official HF repos: google/gemma-4-31B, google/gemma-4-31B-it, google/gemma-4-26B-A4B, google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it; the HF API reports gated:false for all four and the raw config.json files are fetchable anonymously (no license click-through), unlike Gemma 1-3. Architecture (config.json, verified): 31B = 60 layers, hidden 5376, intermediate 21504, 32 heads, 16 KV heads on sliding layers / 4 KV heads on global layers, head_dim 256 (sliding) / 512 (global), vocab 262144, gelu_pytorch_tanh in a gated (GeGLU-style) MLP, sliding window 1024, layer pattern 5 sliding : 1 full repeated (50 sliding + 10 full, last layer full), 256K context, tied embeddings, final logit softcap 30. 26B A4B = 30 layers, hidden 2816, dense MLP intermediate 2112, 16 heads, 8/2 KV heads (sliding/global), head_dim 256/512, same vocab/activation/window, 25 sliding + 5 full layers; MoE in EVERY layer: 128 routed experts, top-8 per token, expert intermediate 704, plus the always-on dense MLP (intermediate 2112 = 3x expert) which Google's model card counts as "1 shared" expert; router = scale-less RMSNorm -> learned scale -> linear (no bias) -> fp32 softmax -> top-k -> renormalize to sum 1 -> per-expert learned scale; outputs of dense MLP and experts are post-normed separately and added (transformers modeling_gemma4.py and llama.cpp gemma4.cpp agree; llama.cpp uses LLAMA_EXPERT_GATING_FUNC_TYPE_SOFTMAX + LLM_FFN_GELU). Global layers reuse K as V (attention_k_eq_v) and use p-RoPE (partial_rotary_factor 0.25, theta 1M) vs standard RoPE theta 10k on sliding layers. License: Apache 2.0 (HF license field, ai.google.dev/gemma/apache_2, tech report, launch blog); the Gemma Terms of Use page explicitly excludes Gemma 4; the HF repos have no LICENSE file (404), the license is declared in README front matter. A Prohibited Use Policy (last modified 2024-02-21) is still linked from the Gemma 4 docs but is not incorporated into the Apache text - whether it binds is an open question. Official memory numbers (ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core, weights-only incl. 20% overhead): 31B 69.9 GB BF16 / 34.9 GB SFP8 / 17.5 GB Q4_0; 26B A4B 57.7 / 28.8 / 14.4 GB; tech report Table 3 (text-only, 32k ctx): 31B 64.0 GB bf16, 19.2 GB Q4_0, +1.10 GB int8 KV; 26B-A4B 52.0 GB bf16 (7.6 GB active), 16.2 GB Q4_0 (2.8 active), +0.28 GB KV. Launch blog: both large models' bf16 weights "fit efficiently on a single 80GB NVIDIA H100". Google also ships QAT Q4_0 GGUFs (google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf, google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf) and MTP speculative-decoding drafters (google/gemma-4-31B-it-assistant 0.5B, google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-assistant 0.4B). llama.cpp has native support (arch "gemma4", PR #21309, vision + MoE, no audio).

26B_A4B.router: linear -> fp32 softmax -> top-8 -> renormalize -> per_expert_scale
26B_A4B.modalities: text, image (vision encoder ~550M, 27-layer ViT); audio_config null

findings.claim: Gemma 4 family = five models: E2B (2.3B effective, 5.1B with embeddings, dense), E4B (4.5B effective, 8B with embeddings, dense), 12B Unified (11.95B dense), 26B A4B (25.2B total / 3.8B active, MoE), 31B Dense (30.7B). This confirms the discussion's ~30.7B dense and ~25.2B/3.8B-active '26B A4B' figures.
findings.note: Official Google model card. Same table is reproduced in the HF README of google/gemma-4-31B-it (Total Parameters row: 25.2B and 30.7B; Active Parameters: 3.8B for 26B A4B).

findings.claim: Layer counts and sliding windows per variant: E2B 35 layers / 512-token window; E4B 42 / 512; 12B 48 / 1024; 26B A4B 30 / 1024; 31B 60 / 1024. Context: 128K for E2B/E4B, 256K for 12B, 26B A4B and 31B. Modalities: text+image+audio for E2B/E4B/12B; text+image only for 26B A4B and 31B. Vocabulary 262K for all.
findings.note: Model card quotes: '8 active / 128 total and 1 shared' experts for 26B A4B; 'hybrid attention mechanism that interleaves local sliding window attention with full global attention, ensuring the final layer is always global'. Vision encoder ~550M on 26B A4B and 31B.

findings.claim: Tech report Table 1 parameter breakdown: 26B-A4B = 550M vision encoder + 740M embedder + 24,500M einsums (2,800M active) + 430M drafter; 31B = 550M vision + 1,410M embedder + 29,290M einsums + 500M drafter. Text: 'an MoE model with 3.8B activated parameters for 26B total parameters (26B-A4B)'; dense models 'effective 2.3B (E2B), effective 4.5B (E4B), 12B and 31B'.
findings.note: Gemma 4 Technical Report, Gemma Team / Google DeepMind, report dated 2026-06-19; arXiv 2607.02770 v1 2026-07-02, v2 2026-07-24 (abstract page https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02770). Read from the downloaded PDF.

findings.claim: Parameter counts recomputed from config.json match the official numbers: 31B -> 29.287B non-embedding + 1.409B embedding (262144x5376) = 30.70B (Table 1: 29,290M + 1,410M). 26B-A4B -> attention 1.110B + dense MLP 0.535B + routers 0.011B + 128 experts 22.838B = 24.494B non-embedding (Table 1: 24,500M) + 0.738B embedding (Table 1: 740M) = 25.23B total; active (8 of 128 experts) = 3.084B non-embedding, 3.82B including embeddings (headline 3.8B).
findings.note: Computed with k_eq_v (no v_proj) on global layers and tied embeddings. Table 1's '2,800M (active)' einsum figure does not match my 3.084B non-embedding active; the counting convention for that cell is unclear (see open questions). Headline totals match.

findings.claim: Official HF repo ids for the two large variants: base google/gemma-4-31B and google/gemma-4-26B-A4B; instruction-tuned google/gemma-4-31B-it and google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. All four report gated:false and private:false in the HF API with license apache-2.0, pipeline_tag image-text-to-text, library transformers; each ships 2 safetensors shards (model-00001-of-00002 / 00002-of-00002) plus config.json, generation_config.json, processor_config.json, tokenizer.json, tokenizer_config.json (the -it repos also have chat_template.jinja).
findings.note: Also checked https://huggingface.co/api/models/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it , https://huggingface.co/api/models/google/gemma-4-31B , https://huggingface.co/api/models/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B . lastModified 2026-07-20 (it) / 2026-07-15 (base). Not gated: raw config.json was fetchable anonymously, which fails for gated repos.

findings.claim: The google/gemma-4 HF collection also lists: google/gemma-4-12B and -12B-it, google/gemma-4-E2B(-it), google/gemma-4-E4B(-it), five '-it-assistant' repos (E2B 78M, E4B 78.8M, 12B 0.4B, 26B-A4B 0.4B, 31B 0.5B), and google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it.
findings.note: The '-assistant' repos are the Multi-Token-Prediction speculative-decoding draft models ('smaller, faster draft model ... up to 3x' speedup) per https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-31B-it-assistant ; tech report §2.6 describes a 4-layer drafter with model dim 1024 for 26B-A4B and 31B.

findings.claim: Google also publishes official QAT Q4_0 GGUFs: google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf (files gemma-4-31B_q4_0-it.gguf + gemma-4-31B-it-mmproj.gguf) and google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf (gemma-4-26B_q4_0-it.gguf + gemma-4-26B-it-mmproj.gguf); both gated:false, Apache 2.0, lastModified 2026-07-17.
findings.note: Second repo: https://huggingface.co/api/models/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf

findings.claim: 31B config.json (text_config): num_hidden_layers 60, hidden_size 5376, intermediate_size 21504, num_attention_heads 32, num_key_value_heads 16, num_global_key_value_heads 4, head_dim 256, global_head_dim 512, vocab_size 262144, hidden_activation 'gelu_pytorch_tanh', sliding_window 1024, max_position_embeddings 262144, attention_k_eq_v true, enable_moe_block false (num_experts/top_k_experts null), tie_word_embeddings true, final_logit_softcapping 30.0, rms_norm_eps 1e-6, dtype bfloat16, architectures ['Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration'], model_type gemma4 / gemma4_text, transformers_version 5.5.0.dev0.
findings.note: Base repo config (https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-31B/raw/main/config.json) has identical text_config values.

findings.claim: 31B layer_types array is 60 entries in the repeating pattern [sliding x5, full_attention] -> 50 sliding-window layers and 10 full (global) attention layers; layers 6,12,...,60 are full, so the final layer is global. 26B A4B uses the same pattern over 30 layers -> 25 sliding + 5 full.
findings.note: Matches tech report: 'We conserve a 5:1 ratio of local sliding window to global self-attention (4:1 for the 2.3B model)'. transformers default: sliding_window_pattern = 6  # by default 5:1, and 'Last layer must use full_attention' is enforced in configuration_gemma4.py.

findings.claim: 26B A4B config.json (text_config): num_hidden_layers 30, hidden_size 2816, intermediate_size 2112 (dense MLP), num_attention_heads 16, num_key_value_heads 8, num_global_key_value_heads 2, head_dim 256, global_head_dim 512, vocab_size 262144, hidden_activation 'gelu_pytorch_tanh', sliding_window 1024, max_position_embeddings 262144, attention_k_eq_v true, enable_moe_block true, num_experts 128, top_k_experts 8, moe_intermediate_size 704, tie_word_embeddings true, final_logit_softcapping 30.0, dtype bfloat16.
findings.note: Base repo config (https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-26B-A4B/raw/main/config.json) identical. Vision config on both large models: gemma4_vision, 27 layers, hidden 1152, intermediate 4304, 16 heads, head_dim 72, patch_size 16, 280 soft tokens per image; audio_config null.

findings.claim: In transformers, head_dim 256 and num_key_value_heads apply to sliding-attention layers; full-attention layers are overridden via per_layer_config to head_dim = global_head_dim (512) and num_key_value_heads = num_global_key_value_heads when attention_k_eq_v is set. So: 31B = 32 heads x 256 (16 KV heads) on sliding layers, 32 x 512 (4 KV heads) on global layers; 26B A4B = 16 x 256 (8 KV) sliding, 16 x 512 (2 KV) global.
findings.note: Code: layer_overrides = {'head_dim': global_head_dim}; num_key_value_heads = num_global_key_value_heads if getattr(self,'attention_k_eq_v',True) else None; per_layer_config built for every layer whose type == 'full_attention'. llama.cpp converter writes key_length/value_length = head_dim_full and key_length_swa/value_length_swa = head_dim (conversion/gemma.py).

findings.claim: attention_k_eq_v: on global (full-attention) layers the value projection is dropped and V = K ('use_alternative_attention = config.attention_k_eq_v and not self.is_sliding'; 'self.v_proj = ... if not self.use_alternative_attention else None'; 'value_states = self.v_proj(hidden_states)... if self.v_proj is not None else key_states'). QK-norm (Gemma4RMSNorm on q and k, scale-less v_norm on v) is applied; attention scaling is 1.0 in the text attention.
findings.note: Tech report: 'We improve memory efficiency by re-using keys as values in the global attention layers (except in E2B and E4B), i.e., values = keys', with p-RoPE p=0.25 on global layers 'effectively reducing the global KV cache by 37.5%'. llama.cpp PR #21309 describes 'K=V on global layers (attention_k_eq_v)' and '256 SWA / 512 global' head dims.

findings.claim: RoPE: sliding layers use default RoPE with rope_theta 10000; full-attention layers use rope_type 'proportional' (p-RoPE) with partial_rotary_factor 0.25 and rope_theta 1000000.
findings.note: Same in 31B config. Tech report: 'The RoPE frequencies are set to 1M and 10k on global and local attention layers, respectively.'

findings.claim: Activation: hidden_activation is 'gelu_pytorch_tanh' (tanh-approximated GELU) used in a gated MLP: down_proj(act_fn(gate_proj(x)) * up_proj(x)) for the dense MLP, and act_fn(gate) * up for experts (GeGLU-style). llama.cpp builds both with LLM_FFN_GELU (dense MLP as LLM_FFN_PAR).
findings.note: Gemma4TextMLP.forward and Gemma4TextExperts.forward; llama.cpp src/models/gemma4.cpp lines ~300-331.

findings.claim: 26B A4B MoE structure (every one of the 30 layers has a MoE block since enable_moe_block applies to all decoder layers): 128 routed experts stored as fused 3D tensors (gate_up_proj [128, 2*704, 2816], down_proj [128, 2816, 704]), top-8 per token, each expert intermediate 704. The dense MLP (intermediate 2112) runs on every token in parallel and acts as the always-on 'shared expert' (2112 = 3 x 704). Outputs: hidden_states_1 = post_feedforward_layernorm_1(mlp(pre_ffn_norm(x))); hidden_states_2 = post_feedforward_layernorm_2(experts(pre_feedforward_layernorm_2(residual))); combined = hidden_states_1 + hidden_states_2, then post_feedforward_layernorm and residual add.
findings.note: Gemma4TextDecoderLayer.__init__/forward. The 'shared expert = dense MLP' identification is Google's own framing ('8 active / 128 total and 1 shared' in the model card) plus llama.cpp's comment '// MLP (shared exp)' and 'cur = ggml_add(ctx0, cur_mlp, cur_moe)'. The 3x size ratio is computed from config (2112/704 = 3.0) and is also stated in Maarten Grootendorst's visual guide (secondary).

findings.claim: Router (Gemma4TextRouter): input = scale-less RMSNorm of the pre-MLP residual, multiplied by a learned per-dim 'scale' vector and hidden_size**-0.5; expert_scores = Linear(hidden_size -> 128, bias=False); router_probabilities = softmax(scores, fp32); top_k = torch.topk(probs, k=8); weights renormalized to sum to 1 per token; then multiplied by a learned per_expert_scale[expert]. No bias / sigmoid / expert-choice routing; no auxiliary-loss code in the inference path.
findings.note: llama.cpp mirrors it: router logits computed from attn_out via ggml_rms_norm -> scale 1/sqrt(n_embd) -> mul ffn_gate_inp_s -> matmul ffn_gate_inp; build_moe_ffn(..., LLAMA_EXPERT_GATING_FUNC_TYPE_SOFTMAX, norm_w=true, scale 1.0); per_expert_scale is converted to an FFN_DOWN_EXP '.scale' tensor (conversion/gemma.py modify_tensors).

findings.claim: llama.cpp has native Gemma 4 support: GGUF arch 'gemma4' (LLM_ARCH_GEMMA4), src/models/gemma4.cpp, converter class Gemma4Model registered for 'Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration' / 'Gemma4ForCausalLM' in conversion/gemma.py (examples: google/gemma-4-31B-it, google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, google/gemma-4-E2B-it), plus Gemma4UnifiedModel (12B) and Gemma4AssistantModel (MTP drafters). It writes sliding_window_pattern from layer_types, key/value_length (global) vs key/value_length_swa, expert_feed_forward_length from moe_intermediate_size, per-layer head_count_kv array, and a ROPE_FREQS tensor emulating proportional RoPE with partial_rotary_factor 0.25 on full layers. The main PR (#21309, 'support gemma 4 (vision + moe, no audio)') is reported merged 2026-04-02.
findings.note: Graph: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/src/models/gemma4.cpp ; PR: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/21309 (merge date taken from a summarized fetch of the PR page). Note the converter now lives in conversion/gemma.py, not inside convert_hf_to_gguf.py.

findings.claim: 12B Unified config.json: 48 layers, hidden 3840, intermediate 15360, 16 heads, 8 KV heads (sliding) / 1 global KV head, head_dim 256 / global 512, vocab 262144, gelu_pytorch_tanh, sliding_window 1024, 262144 positions, attention_k_eq_v true, dense (enable_moe_block false); vision_config and audio_config both present (encoder-free unified design feeds raw patches/audio chunks).
findings.note: Announced 2026-06-03: 'Novel unified architecture: No multimodal encoders' (https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/introducing-gemma-4-12b/).

findings.claim: License: Gemma 4 is released under Apache License 2.0. HF README front matter: 'license: apache-2.0' and 'license_link: https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/gemma_4_license' (which serves the Apache 2.0 text). Tech report: 'We release the Gemma 4 models under an Apache 2.0 license'. Launch blog: 'released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license'. Google Open Source blog calls it 'the first in the Gemmaverse to be released under the OSI-approved Apache 2.0 license'.
findings.note: Also https://ai.google.dev/gemma/apache_2 (page title 'Apache License 2.0'), https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemma-4/ (2026-04-02), https://opensource.googleblog.com/2026/03/gemma-4-expanding-the-gemmaverse-with-apache-20.html . There is NO LICENSE file in the HF repo (https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-31B-it/raw/main/LICENSE returns 404); the license is declared via README metadata.

findings.claim: The Gemma Terms of Use (which govern Gemma 1-3/3n and derivatives, with redistribution notice and use-restriction pass-through obligations) explicitly do NOT apply to Gemma 4: 'For Gemma 4 terms, see the Gemma 4 license' (linking /gemma/apache_2). Consequence for local use: download/run/fine-tune/redistribute under standard Apache 2.0 terms (keep LICENSE/NOTICE, mark modified files, no trademark grant, patent grant with termination clause); no HF license click-through is required.
findings.note: Apache 2.0 Section 4 (copy of license, prominent notices on modified files) and Section 6 (no trademark rights) quoted on https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/gemma_4_license .

findings.claim: Google's Gemma 4 docs still reference a 'Prohibited use' policy (ai.google.dev/gemma/prohibited_use_policy, 'Last modified: February 21, 2024', wording 'You may not use nor allow others to use Gemma or Model Derivatives to: ...') and an 'Intended use statement'; the docs/core page says models 'permit responsible commercial use'. The Apache 2.0 text itself contains no use restrictions and does not incorporate the policy.
findings.note: Whether this policy is contractually binding on Apache-2.0 licensees is not stated anywhere I could find - flagged as an open question, not a conclusion.

findings.claim: Official memory table (ai.google.dev, 'Table 1. Approximate GPU or TPU memory required to load Gemma 4 models based on parameter count, quantization level and 20% overhead of loading additional things'): E2B 11.4/5.7/2.9 GB (BF16/SFP8/Q4_0), Mobile 1.1, Mobile text-only 0.84; E4B 17.9/8.9/4.5, Mobile 2.5 / 2.2; 12B 26.7/13.4/6.7; 26B A4B 57.7/28.8/14.4; 31B 69.9/34.9/17.5 GB. Caveat: 'The estimates ... only account for the memory required to load the static model weights. They don't include the additional VRAM needed for supporting software or the context window.'
findings.note: Mobile versions use LiteRT-LM. The 69.9 GB BF16 figure does not reproduce exactly from 30.7B x 2 bytes x 1.2 (=73.7 GB); basis unclear.

findings.claim: Tech report Table 3 ('Text only, Gb memory footprint ... for weights and int8 KV caching (+KV) at 32k context size'): E2B 4.6 bf16 / 0.8 mobile-quant / +0.05 KV; E4B 9.0 / 2.3 / +0.14; 12B 24.0 / 7.65 Q4_0 / +0.28; 26B-A4B 52.0 total (7.6 active) bf16 / 16.2 (2.8) Q4_0 / +0.28; 31B 64.0 bf16 / 19.2 Q4_0 / +1.10 KV.
findings.note: Q4_0 is described as blockwise 4-bit (as in llama.cpp); QAT checkpoints are provided for it. The int8 KV cost at 32k is small because of the 5:1 local/global ratio, K=V reuse and p-RoPE.

findings.claim: Launch blog hardware statement: the 26B MoE and 31B dense models' 'unquantized bfloat16 weights fit efficiently on a single 80GB NVIDIA H100 GPU'; edge models 'run completely offline ... across edge devices like phones, Raspberry Pi, and NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano'. Blog also states: 'The edge models feature a 128K context window, while the larger models offer up to 256K' and that the 26B MoE activates 'only 3.8 billion of its total parameters during inference'.
findings.note: Published 2026-04-02; four sizes at launch (E2B, E4B, 26B MoE, 31B); 12B followed 2026-06-03. No official memory statement exists for the 12B beyond the docs/core table.

findings.claim: Transformers requirement: HF README says 'You can use all Gemma 4 models with the latest version of Transformers' and the shipped config was written by transformers 5.5.0.dev0 (model_type gemma4 / Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration), i.e. a transformers 5.x release with the gemma4 model class is needed.
findings.note: The README (as fetched) contains no memory/hardware table and no llama.cpp/vLLM/Ollama section.

findings.claim: Modality nuance: the launch blog says 'All models natively process video and images', while the model card lists only 'Text, Image' for 26B A4B and 31B (audio only on E2B/E4B/12B). Video therefore appears to be handled as sampled image frames (config has a video_token_id) rather than a separate encoder.
findings.note: video_token_id 258884 present in both large-model configs; no video encoder config exists. Not independently verified how frames are sampled.

open_questions: Tech report Table 1 lists '2,800M (active)' einsum parameters for 26B-A4B, but recomputing from config.json (attention + dense MLP + routers + 8 of 128 experts, excluding embeddings) gives ~3.08B; the counting convention behind the 2.8B cell is unclear. The headline 3.8B active (incl. 0.74B embeddings -> 3.82B computed) and 25.2B total do match.

Does Google's Gemma Prohibited Use Policy (last modified 2024-02-21) legally bind users of the Apache-2.0-licensed Gemma 4 weights? The docs link it and speak of 'responsible commercial use', but the Apache 2.0 text does not incorporate it and the Gemma Terms of Use page excludes Gemma 4. No official statement found either way.

The ai.google.dev memory table's 31B BF16 figure (69.9 GB) does not reproduce exactly from 30.7B params x 2 bytes x 1.2 overhead (73.7 GB), nor does the 26B A4B 57.7 GB from 25.2B (60.5 GB); the exact basis (maybe excluding embeddings or vision encoder) is unstated.
E2B and E4B config.json files were not fetched; their layer counts/windows/context (35/42 layers, 512 window, 128K) are taken from the official model card only.

The llama.cpp PR #21309 merge date (2026-04-02) comes from a summarized fetch of the PR page rather than the raw GitHub timeline; the code itself (src/models/gemma4.cpp, conversion/gemma.py) was read directly.
Whether vLLM / Ollama / MLX ship first-party Gemma 4 support was not researched (out of scope of the primary sources requested).

checked.claim: Gemma 4 family = five models: E2B (2.3B effective, 5.1B with embeddings), E4B (4.5B effective, 8B), 12B Unified (11.95B), 26B A4B (25.2B total / 3.8B active, MoE), 31B Dense (30.7B).
checked.correction: Verified on the official model card and in the HF README of google/gemma-4-31B-it (rows 'Total Parameters' 25.2B / 30.7B, 'Active Parameters' 3.8B). Independent cross-check: the safetensors headers give 30,697,345,340 text params for 31B-it and 25,233,141,790 for 26B-A4B-it (see claim 4). Caveat for scripts: the HF repo badge / model.safetensors.index.json metadata reports total_parameters 32,682,372,656 for 31B (double-counts the tied lm_head), so the base repo shows '33B' and 26B-A4B base shows '27B' in the collection UI.

checked.claim: Layers/sliding windows per variant: E2B 35/512; E4B 42/512; 12B 48/1024; 26B A4B 30/1024; 31B 60/1024. Context 128K (E2B/E4B), 256K (12B, 26B A4B, 31B). Modalities text+image+audio for E2B/E4B/12B, text+image for 26B A4B and 31B. Vocab 262K.
checked.correction: All values verified on the model card and the HF README table. Minor precision on the note: the ~550M vision encoder is listed for 31B and 26B A4B only; 12B has no encoder ('–', encoder-free; tech report: 'larger models use a 550M encoder (except for the unified 12B)'). Audio encoder is '~300M' on the model card vs 305M in tech report Table 1. '8 active / 128 total and 1 shared' and 'ensuring the final layer is always global' quotes verified verbatim. 12B config.json confirms 48 layers (8 full), sliding_window 1024, max_position_embeddings 262144.

findings.claim: Feature request issue #21314 "Feature Request: gemma4 model architecture support" (error: unknown model architecture: 'gemma4') was opened and closed the same day, 2026-04-02.

The GGUF architecture string is "gemma4" (LLM_ARCH_GEMMA4 -> "gemma4" in src/llama-arch.cpp line 60); a second arch "gemma4-assistant" (LLM_ARCH_GEMMA4_ASSISTANT) exists for the MTP drafter. gguf-py mirrors this: MODEL_ARCH.GEMMA4: "gemma4", MODEL_ARCH.GEMMA4_ASSISTANT: "gemma4-assistant" (constants.py lines 1338-1339). Both community GGUFs inspected carry general.architecture = 'gemma4'.

The model implementation now lives in src/models/gemma4.cpp (class llama_model_gemma4; dispatched from llama-model.cpp `case LLM_ARCH_GEMMA4: return new llama_model_gemma4(params);`). The converter now lives in conversion/gemma.py (`@ModelBase.register("Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration", "Gemma4ForCausalLM") class Gemma4Model(Gemma3Model)`, with `@ModelBase.example("google/gemma-4-31B-it", "google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it", "google/gemma-4-E2B-it")`); convert_hf_to_gguf.py is now a thin wrapper that imports the `conversion` package.
findings.note: Both 31B dense and 26B-A4B MoE are explicitly listed as converter examples; GGUFs of both exist on HF (see repo findings).

findings.claim: Gemma 4 MTP (multi-token prediction) speculative decoding was added by PR #23398 "llama : add Gemma4 MTP" (am17an), merged 2026-06-07T12:50:55Z. PR text: ">2x speedup" for the dense model, "For the MoE model I don't observe a speed-up on my system"; "works for the 31B and 26B-4B but not the E4B E2B variants for now"; multi-GPU may need `--spec-draft-device` with `-sm layer`.

Vision handling was fixed later by PR #28335 "model, mtmd: fix gemma4 vision handling" (merged 2026-09-04): always causal attn for E2B/E4B, keep global layer causal, fix vision token budget. Its table states gemma-4-26B-A4B-it = "MoE, 128 experts / top-8", hidden 2816; gemma-4-31B-it = "dense, 60 layers", hidden 5376.

findings.note: From `gh api search/issues q='repo:ggml-org/llama.cpp is:issue is:open gemma4 OR "gemma 4" OR "gemma-4"'`; many are backend-specific (Vulkan/HIP) rather than core MoE routing bugs. No open issue claiming a MoE routing/quality bug on the CPU backend was found.

findings.claim: MoE expert tensors in Gemma 4 GGUFs are stored as ONE 3-D tensor per layer, with gate and up MERGED: `blk.N.ffn_gate_up_exps.weight` dims [2816, 1408, 128] (= n_embd, 2*n_ff_exp, n_expert) and `blk.N.ffn_down_exps.weight` dims [704, 2816, 128] (= n_ff_exp, n_embd, n_expert). Router: `blk.N.ffn_gate_inp.weight` dims [2816, 128] type F32 plus `blk.N.ffn_gate_inp.scale` dims [2816] F32. Per-expert output scale: `blk.N.ffn_down_exps.scale` dims [128] F32. No `*_shexp` tensors exist (shexp present? -> False). 658 tensors total; expert_count=128, expert_used_count=8, expert_feed_forward_length=704.
findings.note: Verified by downloading the first 32 MiB of unsloth gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf and bartowski google_gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf via HTTP range and parsing the GGUF v3 header; identical tensor names/dims in both.

findings.claim: llama.cpp loader (src/models/gemma4.cpp lines 111-130) reads: router `LLM_TENSOR_FFN_GATE_INP "weight" {n_embd, n_expert}` (TENSOR_NOT_REQUIRED; its presence marks a MoE layer) and `LLM_TENSOR_FFN_GATE_INP "scale" {n_embd}`; experts `LLM_TENSOR_FFN_GATE_UP_EXPS "weight" {n_embd, n_ff_exp*2, n_expert}` (TENSOR_NOT_REQUIRED) with fallback to separate `LLM_TENSOR_FFN_GATE_EXPS` {n_embd,n_ff_exp,n_expert} + `LLM_TENSOR_FFN_UP_EXPS` {n_embd,n_ff_exp,n_expert} if the merged tensor is absent; `LLM_TENSOR_FFN_DOWN_EXPS "weight" {n_ff_exp, n_embd, n_expert}`. Comment: "for expert layers, we use normal FFN as shared expert (same as python code)" — the dense blk.N.ffn_gate/ffn_up/ffn_down act as the shared expert; there are no ffn_*_shexp tensors for gemma4. Per-expert `*_exps.scale` {n_expert} tensors are loaded generically in llama-model.cpp lines 1682-1690 (ffn_gate_exps_s / ffn_down_exps_s / ffn_up_exps_s).

Generic GGUF tensor name templates (src/llama-arch.cpp LLM_TENSOR_NAMES): LLM_TENSOR_FFN_GATE_INP "blk.%d.ffn_gate_inp"; LLM_TENSOR_FFN_GATE_EXPS "blk.%d.ffn_gate_exps"; LLM_TENSOR_FFN_GATE_UP_EXPS "blk.%d.ffn_gate_up_exps"; LLM_TENSOR_FFN_DOWN_EXPS "blk.%d.ffn_down_exps"; LLM_TENSOR_FFN_UP_EXPS "blk.%d.ffn_up_exps"; LLM_TENSOR_FFN_GATE_SHEXP "blk.%d.ffn_gate_shexp"; FFN_UP_SHEXP "blk.%d.ffn_up_shexp"; FFN_DOWN_SHEXP "blk.%d.ffn_down_shexp"; FFN_GATE_INP_SHEXP "blk.%d.ffn_gate_inp_shexp"; FFN_EXP_PROBS_B "blk.%d.exp_probs_b". LLM_TENSOR_INFOS: FFN_GATE_INP -> GGML_OP_MUL_MAT; FFN_{DOWN,GATE,UP,GATE_UP}_EXPS -> GGML_OP_MUL_MAT_ID (lines 853, 947-950).

gguf-py MODEL_ARCH.GEMMA4 tensor list (constants.py line 3398) includes FFN_GATE_UP_EXP, FFN_GATE_EXP, FFN_UP_EXP, FFN_DOWN_EXP, FFN_GATE_INP, FFN_PRE_NORM_2, FFN_POST_NORM_1, FFN_POST_NORM_2, LAYER_OUT_SCALE, PER_LAYER_* — and no SHEXP entries. HF->GGUF name mapping (tensor_mapping.py): `model.layers.{bid}.experts.gate_up_proj` -> FFN_GATE_UP_EXP (line 626, # gemma4); `model.layers.{bid}.experts.down_proj` -> FFN_DOWN_EXP (line 687); `model.layers.{bid}.router.proj` -> FFN_GATE_INP (line 480); `model.layers.{bid}.layer_scalar` -> LAYER_OUT_SCALE (line 755).

On the HF side, Google stores experts already fused per layer: model.safetensors.index.json of google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it lists `model.language_model.layers.N.experts.gate_up_proj`, `...experts.down_proj`, `...router.proj.weight`, `...router.scale`, `...router.per_expert_scale` (60 'experts.' entries = 2 per layer x 30 layers; 90 'router' entries). The converter (conversion/gemma.py Gemma4Model.modify_tensors) maps `router.scale` -> FFN_GATE_INP ".scale" (blk.N.ffn_gate_inp.scale) and `router.per_expert_scale` -> FFN_DOWN_EXP ".scale" (blk.N.ffn_down_exps.scale), with the comment that per_expert_scale "is mathematically equivalent to a per-expert scalar on the down_proj output, which is exactly where ffn_down_exps_s is applied at inference"; filter_tensors appends ".weight" to `.experts.` names lacking a suffix. set_gguf_parameters writes expert_feed_forward_length from `expert_intermediate_size`/`moe_intermediate_size`.

Google config.json (google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it): model_type gemma4, text_config: hidden_size 2816, intermediate_size 2112 (dense/shared MLP), moe_intermediate_size 704, num_experts 128, top_k_experts 8, enable_moe_block true, num_hidden_layers 30, num_attention_heads 16, num_key_value_heads 8 (SWA) / num_global_key_value_heads 2, head_dim 256 / global_head_dim 512, sliding_window 1024, max_position_embeddings 262144, hidden_activation gelu_pytorch_tanh, final_logit_softcapping 30, vocab_size 262144, use_bidirectional_attention "vision", attention_k_eq_v true, hidden_size_per_layer_input 0. google/gemma-4-31B-it: hidden_size 5376, intermediate_size 21504, num_hidden_layers 60, heads 32, kv heads 16 / global 4, enable_moe_block false, num_experts null. Both: architectures Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration, audio_config null (no audio), vision_config gemma4_vision (27 layers, hidden 1152, 280 soft tokens/image).

findings.claim: mmap/mlock in current llama.cpp master: the legacy `--mmap/--no-mmap/--mlock` flags and `use_mmap/use_mlock` params no longer exist. They are replaced by `enum llama_load_mode load_mode` in llama_model_params (llama.h: LLAMA_LOAD_MODE_AUTO=-1 "auto-detect based on device capabilities", NONE=0, MMAP=1, MLOCK=2, MMAP_MLOCK=3, DIRECT_IO=4) and the CLI flag `-lm, --load-mode MODE` (env LLAMA_ARG_LOAD_MODE) with help text: "auto: mmap, unless a device does not support it; none: no special loading mode; mmap: memory-map model (if mmap disabled, slower load but may reduce pageouts if not using mlock); mlock: force system to keep model in RAM rather than swapping or compressing; mmap+mlock: ...; dio: use DirectIO if available". Default is auto (llama_model_default_params sets LLAMA_LOAD_MODE_AUTO).
findings.note: grep of common/arg.cpp for '"--mlock"' / '"--no-mmap"' returns nothing; only the --load-mode help text mentions mlock. llama.h lines 206-213, 328; llama-model.cpp:2931.

findings.claim: How AUTO resolves: llama-model-loader.cpp:559 `use_mmap = load_mode == MMAP || load_mode == MMAP_MLOCK || load_mode == AUTO`; llama-model.cpp:1514-1520 then turns mmap off under AUTO if any device reports `!props.caps.mmap_support`; `use_mlock = load_mode == MLOCK || load_mode == MMAP_MLOCK` (llama-model.cpp:1504). So on a plain CPU build the default is memory-mapped loading, which lets a model larger than RAM run with page-faulting from disk, and `--load-mode mmap+mlock` pins it (which cannot work if the model exceeds RAM).
findings.note: The last clause (mlock cannot pin more than physical RAM) is an inference from mlock semantics, not a llama.cpp statement.

findings.claim: `-lzm, --lazy-mode <on|auto|off>` (default auto; env LLAMA_ARG_LAZY_MODE) enables "on-demand reading of certain tensors, for example per-layer embeddings ... (requires mmap)"; auto = only for such tensors larger than 4 GiB (LLAMA_LAZY_MODE_AUTO). Only tensors created with the TENSOR_READ_LAZY flag qualify; in gemma4.cpp that is only `per_layer_tok_embd` (line 59), which 26B-A4B/31B do not have (hidden_size_per_layer_input = 0). Expert tensors are NOT lazy-readable; code search shows TENSOR_READ_LAZY used only in gemma4.cpp and qwen4exp.cpp.

`-ot, --override-tensor <tensor name pattern>=<buffer type>,...` (env LLAMA_ARG_OVERRIDE_TENSOR): comma-separated `<regex>=<buffer type name>` pairs; the buffer type must match a name from `ggml_backend_buft_name` of a loaded device (e.g. CPU, CUDA0); an unknown name prints "Available buffer types:" and throws. Patterns are std::regex applied to GGUF tensor names (llama_model_tensor_buft_override {pattern, buft} in llama.h; `llama_max_tensor_buft_overrides()` caps the count). llama-bench spells it `-ot --override-tensor <tensor name pattern>=<buffer type>;...` with `;` as separator (because `,` is llama-bench's multi-value separator). Draft-model equivalent: `-otd, --override-tensor-draft / --spec-draft-override-tensor`.

`-cmoe, --cpu-moe` (env LLAMA_ARG_CPU_MOE) = "keep all Mixture of Experts (MoE) weights in the CPU" and `-ncmoe, --n-cpu-moe N` (env LLAMA_ARG_N_CPU_MOE) = "keep the MoE weights of the first N layers in the CPU". They push buffer-type overrides using `LLM_FFN_EXPS_REGEX = "\\.ffn_(up|down|gate|gate_up)_(ch|)exps"` (common/common.h:1219) and `llm_ffn_block_regex(i) = "blk\\.%d" + regex`; the regex includes `gate_up`, so Gemma 4's merged `ffn_gate_up_exps` tensors are covered. A dense-model sibling exists: `-ncffn, --n-cpu-ffn N` using `LLM_FFN_DENSE_REGEX = "\\.ffn_(up|down|gate)\\."`. Draft equivalents: `-cmoed/--cpu-moe-draft`, `-ncmoed/--n-cpu-moe-draft`. llama-bench also accepts `-ncmoe, --n-cpu-moe <n>` (default 0).

KV-cache quantization: `-ctk, --cache-type-k TYPE` and `-ctv, --cache-type-v TYPE` (env LLAMA_ARG_CACHE_TYPE_K / _V), allowed values f32, f16, bf16, q8_0, q4_0, q4_1, iq4_nl, q5_0, q5_1 (kv_cache_types in common/arg.cpp:304-314), default f16; stored in llama_context_params.type_k/type_v ("data type for K cache [EXPERIMENTAL]"). Draft-model variants `-ctkd/-ctvd` (--cache-type-k-draft / --spec-draft-type-k). llama-bench exposes `-ctk/-ctv <t>` (default f16). `-fa, --flash-attn <on|off|auto>` (llama_context_params.flash_attn_type) is listed alongside in llama-bench.

Speculative decoding flags (common args, enabled for LLAMA_EXAMPLE_SERVER, CLI, SPECULATIVE): `-md, --model-draft, --spec-draft-model FNAME` (env LLAMA_ARG_SPEC_DRAFT_MODEL); `-hfd, --hf-repo-draft, --spec-draft-hf <user>/<model>[:quant]`; `--spec-type <list>` (comma-separated; names: none, draft-simple, draft-eagle3, draft-mtp, draft-dflash, draft-dspark, ngram-simple, ngram-map-k, ngram-map-k4v, ngram-mod, ngram-cache); `--spec-draft-n-max N` ("number of tokens to draft"), `--spec-draft-n-min N`; `--spec-draft-p-min / --draft-p-min P`; `--spec-draft-p-split / --draft-p-split P`; `--spec-draft-sampling {greedy,probabilistic}`; `--spec-draft-backend-sampling`; `-ngld, --gpu-layers-draft, --n-gpu-layers-draft, --spec-draft-ngl N`; `-devd, --device-draft, --spec-draft-device`; `-td/--threads-draft`, `-tbd/--threads-batch-draft`; `-ctkd/-ctvd`; `-otd`; `-cmoed`; `-ncmoed`; `--mtp` ("also download the multi-token prediction (MTP) head, if available" — pushes COMMON_SPECULATIVE_TYPE_DRAFT_MTP); ngram tuning `--spec-ngram-mod-n-min/-n-max/-n-match`, `--spec-ngram-simple-size-n/-m`. No `--draft-max`/`--draft-min` aliases were found in current arg.cpp (only the p-min / p-split legacy aliases remain).
findings.note: Flag definitions: common/arg.cpp lines ~3084 and 3982-4330. For Gemma 4 the natural pairing is the `mtp-gemma-4-*.gguf` head (type draft-mtp) or `dflash-gemma-4-*.gguf` (type draft-dflash) shipped in the ggml-org/unsloth/bartowski repos.

findings.claim: llama-bench usage (tools/llama-bench/README.md): `llama-bench [options]`; test params `-m/--model <file>` (repeatable), `-hf/--hf-repo`, `-p/--n-prompt <n>` (default 512), `-n/--n-gen <n>` (default 128), `-pg <pp,tg>`, `-d/--n-depth <n>` (prefill KV to depth), `-b/--batch-size` (2048), `-ub/--ubatch-size` (512), `-ctk/-ctv` (f16), `-t/--threads`, `-C/--cpu-mask`, `-ngl/--n-gpu-layers` (-1), `-ncmoe/--n-cpu-moe` (0), `-sm/--split-mode`, `-nkvo/--no-kv-offload`, `-fa/--flash-attn <on|off|auto>`, `-lm/--load-mode <auto|none|mmap|mlock|mmap+mlock|dio>` (auto), `-lzm/--lazy-mode`, `-ot/--override-tensor <pattern>=<buft>;...`, `--repack <0|1>` (1); general `-r/--repetitions` (5), `-o/--output <csv|json|jsonl|md|sql>`, `--progress`, `--no-warmup`, `-fitt/--fit-target <MiB>`. Multiple values per param via commas or ranges `first-last[+step|*mult]`; every combination is run; results are mean t/s ± sd; tokenization/sampling time excluded. Example: `./llama-bench -m models/7B/ggml-model-q4_0.gguf -p 0 -n 128,256,512`.

Eval callback API: `struct llama_context_params` has `ggml_backend_sched_eval_callback cb_eval; void * cb_eval_user_data;` (include/llama.h lines 392-393, right after defrag_thold and before type_k/type_v). llama_context copies them into cparams (llama-context.cpp:141-142) and installs them with `ggml_backend_sched_set_eval_callback(sched.get(), cparams.cb_eval, cparams.cb_eval_user_data)` (llama-context.cpp:1428). Default params set both to nullptr.

ggml/include/ggml-backend.h line 318: `typedef bool (*ggml_backend_sched_eval_callback)(struct ggml_tensor * t, bool ask, void * user_data);` with the doc comment: "Evaluation callback for each node in the graph (set with ggml_backend_sched_set_eval_callback) / when ask == true, the scheduler wants to know if the user wants to observe this node / this allows the scheduler to batch nodes together in order to evaluate them in a single call / when ask == false, the scheduler is passing the node tensor to the user for observation / if the user returns false, the scheduler will cancel the graph compute". Setter: `GGML_API void ggml_backend_sched_set_eval_callback(ggml_backend_sched_t sched, ggml_backend_sched_eval_callback callback, void * user_data);` (line 356).

The example lives at examples/eval-callback (binary `llama-eval-callback`; README usage: `llama-eval-callback --hf-repo ggml-org/models --hf-file phi-2/ggml-model-q4_0.gguf --model phi-2-q4_0.gguf --prompt hello --seed 42 -ngl 33`, printing lines like `ggml_debug: norm-0 = (f32) NORM(...) = {2560, 1, 1, 1}` with values). eval-callback.cpp sets `params.cb_eval = common_debug_cb_eval; params.cb_eval_user_data = &cb_data; params.warmup = false;` where cb_data is `common_debug_cb_user_data` from common/debug.{h,cpp}. common_debug_cb_eval returns true on ask ("Always retrieve data"), applies optional regex filters (`std::regex_search(t->name, filter)`), copies non-host tensors via `ggml_backend_tensor_get`, and prints non-quantized tensors; a `--tensor-filter REGEX` CLI arg (repeatable, common/arg.cpp:4572) fills params.tensor_filter, and the struct has an `abort_on_nan` option.
findings.note: common/debug.cpp doc: "@param ask when ask is true, the scheduler wants to know if we are interested in data from this tensor; if we return true, a follow-up call will be made with ask=false in which we can do the actual collection."

findings.claim: Per-layer tensor naming: llama_context::graph_get_cb() (llama-context.cpp:2636-2641) returns a lambda `cb(ubatch, cur, name, il)` doing `if (il >= 0) ggml_format_name(cur, "%s-%d", name, il); else ggml_set_name(cur, name);` — so every `cb(x, "ffn_moe_topk", il)` yields a ggml tensor named exactly `ffn_moe_topk-<layer>` (e.g. `ffn_moe_topk-17`), which is what the eval callback sees in `t->name`.

MoE router tensor names assigned in llm_graph_context::build_moe_ffn (src/llama-graph.cpp, starts line 2011; wrapper overload at 1967): `ffn_moe_logits` (only when probs_in==nullptr), `ffn_moe_logits_biased`, `ffn_moe_probs` (after softmax/sigmoid per gating_op), `ffn_moe_probs_biased` (exp_probs_b / grovemoe), `ffn_moe_group_topk` + `ffn_moe_probs_masked` (only if n_expert_groups > 1), `ffn_moe_argsort` (set on selected_experts->src[0]), `ffn_moe_topk` (= ggml_argsort_top_k(selection_probs, n_expert_used), I32 [n_expert_used, n_tokens]), `ffn_moe_weights` (= ggml_get_rows(probs, selected_experts), [1, n_expert_used, n_tokens]), `ffn_moe_weights_softmax` (SOFTMAX_WEIGHT gating), `ffn_moe_weights_sum`, `ffn_moe_weights_sum_clamped`, `ffn_moe_weights_norm` (when norm_w), `ffn_moe_weights_scaled` (w_scale != 1), `ffn_moe_weighted` (llama4 pre-FFN weighting or post-down weighting), `ffn_moe_gate_up` / `ffn_moe_gate_up_scaled` / `ffn_moe_gate_up_biased` (merged path) then views `ffn_moe_gate` and `ffn_moe_up`; separate path `ffn_moe_up`, `ffn_moe_up_scaled/_biased`, `ffn_moe_gate`, `ffn_moe_gate_scaled/_biased`; activations `ffn_moe_silu`, `ffn_moe_swiglu`, `ffn_moe_swiglu_limited`, `ffn_moe_up_clamped`, `ffn_moe_silu_clamped`, `ffn_moe_swiglu_oai`, `ffn_moe_geglu`, `ffn_moe_gelu`, `ffn_moe_reglu`, `ffn_moe_relu`, `ffn_moe_relu_sqr`, `ffn_moe_situ`; `ffn_moe_down`, `ffn_moe_down_scaled`, `ffn_moe_down_biased`, and final `ffn_moe_out`.
findings.note: The current build_moe_ffn signature also takes gate_inp_b, up/gate/down bias tensors, probs_in, gate_up_exps(+_b), up/gate/down `_s` scale tensors and selected_experts_in.

findings.claim: For Gemma 4 specifically (src/models/gemma4.cpp lines 292-345): the router logits are computed in the model file, not in build_moe_ffn — `tmp = rms_norm(attn_out) * 1/sqrt(n_embd) * ffn_gate_inp_s; logits = build_lora_mm(ffn_gate_inp, tmp); cb(logits, "ffn_moe_logits", il)` — then passed as `probs_in` with gate_inp=nullptr, exp_probs_b=nullptr, type_op LLM_FFN_GELU, norm_w=true, w_scale=1.0f, gating LLAMA_EXPERT_GATING_FUNC_TYPE_SOFTMAX, plus ffn_gate_up_exps and the *_exps_s scales. Hence the per-layer names a callback will see on a 26B-A4B run are: ffn_moe_logits-N, ffn_moe_probs-N, ffn_moe_argsort-N, ffn_moe_topk-N, ffn_moe_weights-N, ffn_moe_weights_sum-N, ffn_moe_weights_sum_clamped-N, ffn_moe_weights_norm-N, ffn_moe_gate_up-N, ffn_moe_gate-N, ffn_moe_up-N, ffn_moe_down-N, ffn_moe_down_scaled-N (because blk.N.ffn_down_exps.scale exists), ffn_moe_weighted-N, ffn_moe_out-N, followed by gemma4-specific `ffn_moe-N` (post-norm) and `ffn_moe_combined-N` (= dense `ffn_mlp-N` + MoE). The dense/shared MLP path is named `ffn_mlp-N` and its input norm `ffn_norm_2-N`.
findings.note: Exact list derived by combining the gemma4.cpp call arguments with the build_moe_ffn branches; the GELU-with-gate activation name is expected to be `ffn_moe_geglu-N` (see separate inferred finding).

findings.claim: The activation tensor name for Gemma 4's MoE experts is `ffn_moe_geglu-N` (LLM_FFN_GELU with a gate present), as opposed to `ffn_moe_gelu-N` for gate-less GELU.
findings.note: Both strings `ffn_moe_geglu` and `ffn_moe_gelu` are present in build_moe_ffn (cb calls at relative lines 322/325), and the SILU branch follows the same has_gate->swiglu / else silu pattern; the exact GELU if/else lines were not printed, so treat the geglu/gelu choice as inferred.

findings.claim: Gemma 4's MoE has NO shared-expert (`ffn_*_shexp`) tensors in GGUF; instead every MoE layer also has a full dense MLP (blk.N.ffn_gate/ffn_up/ffn_down, 2816x2112) that is always executed and summed with the routed-expert output (`ffn_moe_combined`). The HF index likewise has `mlp.gate_proj/up_proj/down_proj` alongside `experts.*` in every layer, and the 26B-A4B GGUF has both in all 30 blocks.

Verified GGUF hyperparameters for 26B-A4B (from both inspected files): gemma4.block_count 30, embedding_length 2816, feed_forward_length 2112, expert_feed_forward_length 704, expert_count 128, expert_used_count 8, context_length 262144, attention.head_count 16, head_count_kv per-layer array (8 for SWA layers, 2 for global), key/value_length 512 (global) and 256 (SWA), sliding_window 1024, final_logit_softcapping 30, rope.freq_base 1e6 (global) / 10000 (SWA), rope.dimension_count 512 / 256 SWA, tokenizer.ggml.model 'gemma4', general.file_type 15 (Q4_K_M).

Expert tensor sizes implied by the shapes: per layer, gate_up_exps holds 2816*1408*128 = 507,576,320 weights and down_exps 704*2816*128 = 253,788,160 weights, i.e. 761,364,480 expert weights per MoE layer and ~22.84 B across 30 layers; at Q4_K (4.5 bits/weight) gate_up is ~285 MB/layer and at Q5_1 (6 bpw) down is ~190 MB/layer. The dense/shared MLP is 3 x 2816 x 2112 = 17.8 M weights per layer.
findings.note: Arithmetic from verified dims (2816, 704, 128, 30) and nominal GGML bits-per-weight; actual file sizes include scales/metadata.

findings.claim: Running a Gemma 4 GGUF larger than RAM on CPU: with the default `--load-mode auto` the file is mmap'd and the OS pages weights in on demand (no mlock); `--load-mode none` reads everything into anonymous memory (fails if > RAM); `--load-mode mlock` / `mmap+mlock` pins pages. `-ot`/`--cpu-moe` only choose the buffer type (CPU vs GPU) per tensor and do not stream experts from disk. The only on-demand (lazy) tensor mechanism (`--lazy-mode`) applies solely to TENSOR_READ_LAZY-flagged tensors (per-layer token embeddings), not to `ffn_*_exps`.
findings.note: Composite of verified facts (load_mode semantics; lazy flag scope; override semantics). No llama.cpp doc explicitly discusses MoE streaming; llama-bench README notes `mmap may report incorrect progress on some platforms; ... use --load-mode none` (server README line 2126).

findings.claim: The server README documents the same flags with env vars: `-lm, --load-mode` (LLAMA_ARG_LOAD_MODE; `LLAMA_ARG_LOAD_MODE=mlock` locks the model in RAM, `=mmap+mlock` maps and locks), `-ot, --override-tensor` (LLAMA_ARG_OVERRIDE_TENSOR), `-cmoe/--cpu-moe` (LLAMA_ARG_CPU_MOE), `-ncmoe/--n-cpu-moe N` (LLAMA_ARG_N_CPU_MOE), `-ncffn/--n-cpu-ffn N` (LLAMA_ARG_N_CPU_FFN), `-ctk/-ctv` with allowed values f32, f16, bf16, q8_0, q4_0, q4_1, iq4_nl, q5_0, q5_1 (default f16), `--spec-draft-model, -md, --model-draft FNAME` (LLAMA_ARG_SPEC_DRAFT_MODEL), `-otd`, `-cmoed`, `-ncmoed`.

The Gemma 4 vision tower is supported in llama.cpp via mtmd (`tools/mtmd/models/gemma4v.cpp`, mmproj-*.gguf files shipped by all quantizers; clip projector types gemma4v / gemma4a / gemma4uv / gemma4ua in gguf-py constants). Audio is not supported for the 26B-A4B/31B (PR title "no audio"; those configs have audio_config null). Several vision-path bugs were reported and fixed between April and October 2026 (#21402, #21497, #28954), and #29916 (quantizing mmproj with gemma4v audio 3D conv) is still open.

key_numbers.gated_repos: none (HF API gated=false for all 10 GGUF repos and both google/* source repos)

open_questions: No numeric per-quant perplexity or KL-divergence table for Gemma 4 GGUFs was found from any quantizer: Unsloth publishes only an image chart ('26B A4B - KLD benchmarks'), bartowski only qualitative labels, ggml-org and lmstudio-community nothing. If numbers matter, llama-perplexity --kl-divergence must be run locally.

PR #21309's squash-commit title ('fix gguf conversion for audio/vision mmproj') does not match its PR title ('model: support gemma 4 ...'); the diff confirms it added gemma4, but whether an earlier gemma4 implementation PR existed under another number was not established.
The exact GELU-branch tensor name for Gemma 4 experts (`ffn_moe_geglu-N` vs `ffn_moe_gelu-N`) is inferred from the has_gate pattern, not from a printed if/else line.

Whether the merged `ffn_gate_up_exps` layout was present from the very first release (b8637) or introduced later was not determined; both inspected community files (made at b8746 and April-2026 unsloth builds) already use it, and the loader keeps a fallback to separate gate/up tensors.
Open issue #28448 (ggml_gallocr stale allocation plan -> sparse MoE corruption) is generic to dynamic-topology MoE graphs; its practical impact on Gemma 4 26B-A4B CPU inference is unconfirmed.
Which llama.cpp build removed the legacy `--mmap/--no-mmap/--mlock` flags in favor of `--load-mode` was not researched; third-party guides may still show the old flags.

The lmstudio-community and ggml-org GGUFs were produced at different llama.cpp builds (b10069 vs automated) than bartowski (b8746); chat-template and eos_token_id metadata differ between quantizers (e.g. unsloth eos 106 vs bartowski eos 1), which may affect tool-calling behaviour independent of quant quality.
research.summary: llama.cpp supports both Gemma 4 large variants. Support landed in PR #21309 (merged 2026-04-02, commit 63f8fe0, release b8637) with GGUF architecture name "gemma4" (plus "gemma4-assistant" for the MTP drafter added in PR #23398, June 2026); the model code is now src/models/gemma4.cpp and the converter is conversion/gemma.py (Gemma4Model, registered for Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration/Gemma4ForCausalLM, examples google/gemma-4-31B-it and google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it). Vision is supported via mmproj (several vision bugs fixed through 2026-10-01); audio is not. Of 112 open issues mentioning Gemma 4, the notable ones are backend-specific crashes (Vulkan -np 4 MoE crash #29221, HIP/CUDA `<unused49>` infinite loops #26088/#26239), tool-call/thinking parser instability (#29655, #28827), MTP-related crashes (#25522, #29419, #24795) and a generic sparse-MoE allocator bug (#28448); no open CPU-backend MoE routing/quality bug was found. In GGUF the 26B-A4B experts are one 3-D tensor per layer with gate and up MERGED: blk.N.ffn_gate_up_exps.weight [2816,1408,128] and blk.N.ffn_down_exps.weight [704,2816,128]; the router is blk.N.ffn_gate_inp.weight [2816,128] (F32) plus blk.N.ffn_gate_inp.scale [2816]; a per-expert blk.N.ffn_down_exps.scale [128] exists; there are NO ffn_*_shexp tensors — the always-on dense MLP (blk.N.ffn_gate/up/down) plays the shared-expert role (verified by parsing the headers of unsloth and bartowski Q4_K_M files; expert_count 128, expert_used_count 8, n_ff_exp 704, 30 layers). Community GGUF repos (all ungated, Apache-2.0): bartowski has the full quant ladder for both models (26B-A4B: Q2_K 10.95 GB, IQ3_XXS 12.16, Q3_K_M 13.02, IQ3_M 13.28, IQ4_XS 14.21, Q4_K_M 17.04, Q5_K_M 19.32, Q6_K 22.86, Q8_0 26.86; 31B: Q2_K 12.63, IQ3_XXS 12.98, IQ3_M 15.13, Q3_K_M 15.92, IQ4_XS 17.16, Q4_K_M 19.60, Q5_K_M 22.61, Q6_K 26.73, Q8_0 32.64; built at b8746 with imatrix); unsloth has UD-* dynamic quants (26B-A4B UD-Q4_K_XL 17.01 GB, UD-IQ4_XS 13.60, UD-Q3_K_M 12.73, UD-IQ3_XXS 11.42, UD-Q2_K_XL 10.55, Q8_0 26.86; 31B Q4_K_M 18.32, UD-Q4_K_XL 18.82, IQ4_XS 16.37, Q3_K_M 14.74, Q6_K 25.20, Q8_0 32.64) plus QAT repos with a single UD-Q4_K_XL each; ggml-org ships only Q4_0/Q8_0/BF16 (+ mtp/dflash drafts); lmstudio-community only Q4_K_M/Q6_K/Q8_0 (b10069). Quality notes are qualitative (bartowski) or image-only KLD charts (Unsloth; it recommends UD-Q4_K_XL and temp 1.0 / top_p 0.95 / top_k 64). CPU-side features in current master: mmap/mlock are controlled by `-lm/--load-mode {auto|none|mmap|mlock|mmap+mlock|dio}` (default auto = mmap unless a device lacks mmap support; the old --no-mmap/--mlock flags are gone); `-ot/--override-tensor "<regex>=<buft>,..."`; `-cmoe/--cpu-moe` and `-ncmoe/--n-cpu-moe N` use regex `\.ffn_(up|down|gate|gate_up)_(ch|)exps` (covers Gemma 4's gate_up tensors); `-ctk/-ctv` accept f32,f16,bf16,q8_0,q4_0,q4_1,iq4_nl,q5_0,q5_1; speculative decoding uses `-md/--model-draft`, `--spec-type` (draft-simple, draft-mtp, draft-dflash, draft-dspark, ngram-*, ...), `--spec-draft-n-max/-n-min`, `--draft-p-min`, `-ngld`, `--mtp`; llama-bench takes -m/-p/-n/-pg/-d/-t/-ngl/-ncmoe/-ctk/-ctv/-fa/-lm/-ot(`;`-separated)/-r/-o. Eval callback: llama_context_params.cb_eval / cb_eval_user_data of type `bool (*ggml_backend_sched_eval_callback)(struct ggml_tensor * t, bool ask, void * user_data)` (ask==true: say whether to observe; ask==false: observe, return false to cancel), installed via ggml_backend_sched_set_eval_callback; examples/eval-callback (`llama-eval-callback`) uses common_debug_cb_eval with `--tensor-filter REGEX`. Tensor names are formatted "%s-%d" with the layer index; in build_moe_ffn the router outputs are ffn_moe_logits-N, ffn_moe_probs-N, ffn_moe_argsort-N, ffn_moe_topk-N (I32 [n_expert_used,n_tokens]), ffn_moe_weights-N, ffn_moe_weights_sum-N, ffn_moe_weights_sum_clamped-N, ffn_moe_weights_norm-N, then ffn_moe_gate_up-N, ffn_moe_gate-N, ffn_moe_up-N, (ffn_moe_geglu-N, inferred), ffn_moe_down-N, ffn_moe_down_scaled-N, ffn_moe_weighted-N, ffn_moe_out-N; Gemma 4 computes its logits in gemma4.cpp (softmax gating, top-8, norm_w=true, GELU) and adds ffn_moe-N / ffn_moe_combined-N / ffn_mlp-N.

verify.summary: Adversarial re-check of 16 claim groups (12 narrative claims + 4 key-number groups) against primary sources on 2026-10-04: GitHub API (PRs #21309/#23398/#28335, release b8637, 22 issues, issue search), raw llama.cpp master sources (llama-arch.cpp, llama-model.cpp, models/gemma4.cpp, conversion/gemma.py, convert_hf_to_gguf.py, gguf-py constants.py, common/arg.cpp, common.h, speculative.cpp), HF API (?blobs=true for 10 repos, gated flags for 12), google config.json for both models, five quantizer READMEs, and independent GGUF v3 header parses of unsloth UD-Q4_K_M and bartowski Q4_K_M. Result: NO claim refuted; all numbers, repo ids, flag names, tensor names/dims, line numbers (within ~1 line), dates, SHAs and file sizes reproduce exactly. Three caveats worth hard-coding around: (1) expert tensor dtypes differ between quantizers even at the same quant label (unsloth UD-Q4_K_M: gate_up Q4_K, down_exps Q5_1, dense Q8_0; bartowski Q4_K_M: gate_up Q4_K, down_exps Q8_0, dense Q4_K) so scripts must read per-tensor types, not assume uniform Q4_K; (2) ggml-org Q4_0 files are plausibly QAT conversions (their cards list the google qat-q4_0-unquantized checkpoints as sources; 14.62 GB vs bartowski's 14.76 GB plain Q4_0) — inferred, not explicit; (3) the sub-note "no open CPU-backend MoE routing bug" is an unverifiable negative (uncertain); also #28917 was reproduced on an Ollama harness. Line numbers are valid for master as of 2026-10-04 and will drift.

research.topic: Raspberry Pi 5 hardware numbers relevant to CPU LLM inference and streaming weights from storage (RAM/bandwidth, storage throughput, Cortex-A76 ISA + llama.cpp flags + 16K pages, published llama.cpp tok/s incl. MoE, thermal throttling and PCIe HAT constraints)

findings.claim: Pi 5 memory subsystem is a 32-bit LPDDR4X SDRAM subsystem running at 4267 MT/s (official launch post).
findings.note: Verbatim: "32-bit LPDDR4X SDRAM subsystem, running at 4267MT/s". Same post: 2.4GHz quad-core Cortex-A76, 512KB per-core L2, 2MB shared L3; "High-speed microSD card interface with SDR104 mode support"; "PCIe 2.0 x1 interface"; "2 × USB 3.0 ports, supporting simultaneous 5Gbps operation".

findings.claim: Official product page lists RAM variants "LPDDR4X-4267 SDRAM (1GB, 2GB, 4GB, 8GB, and 16GB)" and shows "Raspberry Pi 5 16GB is available now for $305".
findings.note: A 1GB SKU is now listed in addition to 2/4/8/16GB. The $305 figure is what the page rendered at fetch time (2026-10-04); it differs sharply from the Jan-2025 $120 launch price — treat the current price as unconfirmed/possibly regional.

findings.claim: 16GB Pi 5 launched 9 Jan 2025 at $120; requires the BCM2712 D0 stepping ("includes support for memories larger than 8GB"); uses a single Micron package with eight 16Gbit LPDDR4X die.
2GB Pi 5 launched 29 Aug 2024 at $50 on the D0 stepping; measured idle 2.4W (vs 3.2–3.3W C1 4/8GB), stress-ng load 8.9W (vs 9.8W).
Theoretical peak DRAM bandwidth = 4267e6 transfers/s × 4 bytes (32-bit bus) ≈ 17.07 GB/s, identical for all RAM capacities.
findings.note: Computed from the official 32-bit @ 4267 MT/s spec. Secondary sites quote "17.1 GB/s".

findings.claim: Measured tinymembench on a pre-production Pi 5 8GB: standard memcpy 4805.4 MB/s, standard memset 13676.9 MB/s; idle power 2.8 W, max stress 9.7 W.
findings.note: Same issue: SanDisk Extreme 128GB microSD 1M seq read 91.5 MB/s; Kioxia XG8 NVMe Gen2 seq read 454 MB/s / Gen3 894 MB/s; SanDisk Extreme PRO USB 3.1 flash drive 301 MB/s.

findings.claim: Measured sbc-bench/tinymembench on a production Pi 5 8GB (Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, kernel 6.1 rpi-2712): memcpy 5158.3 MB/s, memchr 13463.2 MB/s, memset 11671.4 MB/s; 7-zip 10930 avg (3136 single-thread).

Measured tinymembench on Raspberry Pi 500+ (16GB, same BCM2712 2.4GHz silicon as Pi 5 16GB): standard memcpy 5865.0 MB/s, standard memset 9738.5 MB/s; Geekbench 6 883/2111; idle 2.9W, max stress 9.4W.
findings.note: Closest available 16GB-DRAM measurement; no Pi 5 Model B 16GB tinymembench run was found. Same issue: Samsung 256GB NVMe seq read 797.70 MB/s / write 750.91 MB/s (PCIe gen not stated).

findings.claim: Measured tinymembench on Compute Module 5 (4GB): standard memcpy 6012.7 MB/s, memset 12646.0 MB/s; Pinedrive 256GB NVMe at PCIe Gen 3: 1M seq read 823.04 MB/s, write 758.51 MB/s.

Measured STREAM (GCC 13.2, -O3 -march=native, Apr-2024 EEPROM) on Pi 5 4GB: 1 thread Copy 10890.9 / Scale 12384.9 / Add 10915.6 / Triad 12388.4 MB/s; 4 threads Copy 7719.0 / Triad 7654.8 MB/s. Pi 5 8GB: 1 thread Copy 8741.2 / Triad 11740.0 MB/s; 4 threads Copy 5999.3 / Scale 6613.5 / Add 4832.1 / Triad 5618.6 MB/s.
findings.note: Poster lurk101, thread started 23 Apr 2024 (pre SDRAM-tuning firmware). Raspberry Pi engineer Dom: "Larger RAM size results in a larger percentage of the time being spent doing refresh." A devmem SDRAM-timing tweak raised 8GB single-thread Copy to 11167.7 MB/s but still ~10% below 4GB. Note multi-thread STREAM is LOWER than single-thread on this platform.

findings.claim: Dec 2024 firmware SDRAM tuning (plus SDRAM_BANKLOW=1 and NUMA emulation) raised Geekbench 6 on Pi 5 from 833/1805 to 899/2169 (+8% single, +32% multi) at stock 2.4GHz; Raspberry Pi claims 10–20% speedup from SDRAM tuning alone.
findings.note: Mechanism: lets 8GB parts use Micron timings validated for 4GB modules, reducing refresh overhead. No tinymembench/STREAM before/after published in that post.

findings.claim: llama.cpp effective decode bandwidth on Pi 5 (4 threads, commit d73c1d6) stayed 9.76–10.55 GB/s across Q2_K..Q8_0 of a small dense model: Q4_K_M 0.398 GB file → 25.77 tok/s (10.25 GB/s); Q8_0 0.531 GB → 19.87 tok/s (10.55 GB/s).
findings.note: Author did not run an independent STREAM baseline; RAM size/OS not stated. Implies ~60% of the 17.07 GB/s theoretical peak is achievable for weight streaming from DRAM.

findings.claim: Pi 5 microSD slot supports UHS-I SDR104 (104 MB/s bus maximum); measured large-block sequential read on a SanDisk Extreme 128GB was 91.5 MB/s (1M blocks), and ~89 MB/s read / 19 MB/s write on a SanDisk SL32G.
findings.note: 91.5 MB/s from github.com/geerlingguy/sbc-reviews/issues/21; 89 MB/s from the CNX Software review. bret.dk's 67–78 MB/s 'sequential' figures use fio 4KB blocks and are not comparable large-block numbers.

findings.claim: `sdram_freq` cannot be used to speed up Pi 5 memory: "SDRAM overclocking on Raspberry Pi 4 or newer is not supported"; `temp_limit` "Values over 85 are clamped to 85"; Pi 5 firmware defaults to kernel_2712.img "because this image contains optimisations specific to those models (for example, 16K page-size)".

Device-tree params: `sd_overclock` = "Clock (in MHz) to use when the MMC framework requests 50MHz" (a High-Speed-mode lever); `sd_cqe` (2712 only, default 1) = "Modify Command Queuing behaviour on the main SD interface... 1: allow CQ for known-good SD A2 cards"; `pciex1` default off; `pciex1_gen` = "Sets the PCIe 'GEN'/speed for the external PCIe link", default 2 (2712 only).
findings.note: Inference: because Pi 5 already negotiates SDR104 (208 MHz) by default, `sd_overclock` is not the Pi 5 microSD tweak; the Pi-5-specific gain comes from A2 command queueing (`sd_cqe`), which improves random IOPS, not sequential MB/s.

findings.claim: Measured effect of A2 command queueing on Pi 5 (dtparam=sd_cqe): SanDisk Extreme Pro 128GB A2 random 4K read 3,019 → 6,338 IOPS, random 4K write 1,133 → 4,739 IOPS, sequential write 61.4 → 64.4 MB/s; Raspberry Pi engineer jdb's Integral Ultima Pro 128GB with CQ: 65.2 MiB/s seq write, 24.7 MiB/s 4K random read, 22.7 MiB/s 4K random write.
findings.note: Posts dated 16–25 Mar 2024.

findings.claim: Official Raspberry Pi microSD card spec: A2, SDR104, command queueing; random 4KB read 5,000 IOPS and write 2,000 IOPS on Pi 5 (SDR104) vs 3,200/1,200 on Pi 4 (DDR50). No sequential MB/s is specified.

USB 3.0 storage measured on Pi 5: NVMe SSD in a USB 3 enclosure ~388 MB/s read / 411 MB/s write (CNX, iozone); Kioxia Exceria G2 in an RTL9210 USB3 enclosure hdparm 359.32 MB/s read / dd 254 MB/s write; Samsung EVO SATA via ASM1153E (UASP firmware) dd 1M read 416 MB/s / write 204 MB/s.
findings.note: CNX figure: cnx-software.com review (above). SATA figures: forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=359890 (392 MB/s read before the UASP firmware update).

findings.claim: Native NVMe over the Pi 5 FPC: Kioxia XG8 seq read 454 MB/s at Gen 2 and 894 MB/s at Gen 3 (dtparam=pciex1_gen=3); Kioxia Exceria G2 hdparm 416.98 MB/s (Gen 2) → 784.10 MB/s (Gen 3), dd write 261 → 377 MB/s.
findings.note: Geerling: "about 450 MB/sec" Gen 2, "very nearly 900 MB/sec" Gen 3; connection "certified for Gen 2.0 speed (5 GT/sec)". Exceria G2 numbers from forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=362903 (Pimoroni NVMe Base). Secondary reports (Tom's Hardware 837 MB/s for the official SSD, Pimoroni Base 876 MB/s) could not be fetched (pages truncated) and are unverified.

findings.claim: Official M.2 HAT+ docs: "Single-lane PCIe 2.0 interface (500 MB/s peak transfer rate)"; Gen 3 can be enabled but "The Raspberry Pi 5 is not certified for Gen 3.0 speeds. PCIe Gen 3.0 connections might be unstable."; up to 3 A to the M.2 device.

Official Raspberry Pi SSD measured with fio 4K on Pi 5 (4GB) + M.2 HAT+: read IOPS 106,246 (Gen 2) → 196,947 (Gen 3); write 90,264 → 151,692; product spec "Complies with PCIe Gen 3 standard", 256GB rated 40k read / 70k write 4kB IOPS.
findings.note: Spec from raspberrypi.com/products/ssd/. Shows Gen 3 roughly doubles small-block throughput, consistent with the ~2x sequential gain.

findings.claim: Pi 5 /proc/cpuinfo: CPU implementer 0x41, part 0xd0b (Cortex-A76); Features = "fp asimd evtstrm aes pmull sha1 sha2 crc32 atomics fphp asimdhp cpuid asimdrdm lrcpc dcpop asimddp".
findings.note: asimddp = ARMv8.2 DotProd; fphp/asimdhp = FP16 arithmetic (scalar + SIMD). No 'i8mm', 'bf16', 'sve' flags present.

findings.claim: GCC's core table defines cortex-a76 as Armv8.2-A with (F16, RCPC, DOTPROD) only — no I8MM, BF16 or SVE; by contrast cortex-a710 lists (SVE2_BITPERM, MEMTAG, I8MM, BF16).
findings.note: Verbatim: AARCH64_CORE("cortex-a76", cortexa76, cortexa57, V8_2A, (F16, RCPC, DOTPROD), neoversen1, 0x41, 0xd0b, -1). So on Pi 5: dotprod YES, FP16 arithmetic YES, i8mm NO, SVE NO, BF16 NO.

findings.claim: llama.cpp build defaults: GGML_NATIVE is ON unless cross-compiling (or SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH set); GGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH is an empty string option for explicit -march; GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI defaults OFF; GGML_CPU_REPACK defaults ON ("runtime weight conversion of Q4_0 to Q4_X_X").

llama.cpp ARM detection: with GGML_NATIVE it runs `${CMAKE_C_COMPILER} -mcpu=native -E -v -`, extracts the -mcpu/-march flag, then probes dotprod (vdotq_s32), i8mm (vmmlaq_s32), sve (svdot_s32), sme and fma via check_arm_feature, appending +feature/+nofeature fixes; with GGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH it appends -march=${GGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH}; GGML_CPU_ALL_VARIANTS maps dotprod→armv8.2-a, i8mm→armv8.6-a, sme→armv9.2-a.
findings.note: Inference: on a Pi 5 with GCC, -mcpu=native resolves to cortex-a76, i.e. armv8.2-a+fp16+dotprod+rcpc; the i8mm/sve/sme probes fail and are excluded. A manual equivalent is -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF -DGGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH=armv8.2-a+dotprod+fp16. Older flags like GGML_ARM_DOTPROD/GGML_ARM_SVE seen in blog posts are not in the current CMake.

findings.claim: llama.cpp KleidiAI backend selects kernels in order SME2 > SME > SVE+I8MM+DOTPROD > I8MM+DOTPROD > DOTPROD (baseline), for Q4_0, Q8_0, F16, F32 tensors; on Pi 5 only the DOTPROD-tier kernels apply.
findings.note: Build: cmake -S . -B build -DGGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON (docs/build.md). K-quants (Q4_K_M) are not KleidiAI paths; they use ggml's own NEON/dotprod kernels.

findings.claim: Native vs generic build matters enormously on Pi 5: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct Q4_K_M generation 1.10 tok/s (generic ARM64 prebuilt) → 17.80 tok/s (-DGGML_NATIVE=ON); Q8_0 0.85 → 15.40 tok/s; prompt eval 5.95 → 42.10 tok/s (Pi 5 8GB, Bookworm, kernel 6.6).
findings.note: llama.cpp commit not stated. Another report (note.com/ai_meg) saw 1.5 → 7 tok/s generation and 10 → 20 tok/s prompt-eval on a Q4_K_M model after native/dotprod build (model/version unstated).

findings.claim: Raspberry Pi OS on Pi 5 uses a 16 KB page-size kernel by default: "bcm2712_defconfig builds kernel_2712.img, which is optimised for BCM2712... uses a 16K page size"; the bcm2711 build (kernel8.img) "also runs on these devices but with a 4K page size".
findings.note: Raspberry Pi engineer PhilE: "The default kernel for a Pi 5 on RPiOS also uses 16KB pages, because it can give a 7+% performance increase in random memory accesses" (forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=361390). Switch to 4K with `kernel=kernel8.img` in config.txt.

findings.claim: Raspberry Pi OS based on Debian 13 'trixie' (Raspberry Pi OS 6.0) shipped 1 Oct 2025 on kernel 6.12; the Sept-2026 image reportedly runs kernel 6.18.
findings.note: Dates/kernel versions come from secondary sources in search results; the raspberrypi.com Trixie announcement itself was not fetched. The official docs still describe kernel_2712.img (16K) as the firmware's default load, so the 16K default persists on trixie; pi5-llm-arena ran Debian 13 on a Pi 5 16GB.

findings.claim: llama.cpp's mmap is 16K-page safe: it calls `mmap(NULL, file->size(), PROT_READ, flags, fd, 0)` (offset 0), uses `sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)` for alignment in unmap_fragment, sets MAP_POPULATE when prefetching, and uses POSIX_MADV_WILLNEED / POSIX_MADV_RANDOM.
findings.note: Inference for weight streaming: with 16 KB pages the minimum page-fault unit when streaming weights from NVMe is 16 KiB (4x fewer faults/TLB misses than 4K), which is why PhilE's 7%+ random-access gain exists; no llama.cpp mmap bug related to 16K pages was found. Software that IS broken by 16K pages (bookworm-feedback #107): jemalloc, hardened_malloc, Box64/Wine, Chromium <102, Geekbench <6.2.2, Zig, etc.

findings.claim: Pi 5 16GB (Debian 13, llama.cpp native build -mcpu=cortex-a76 -march=armv8.2-a+fp16+dotprod, no throttling 51–58°C): deepseek-r1:1.5b 12.02 tg / 60.66 pp tok/s; gemma4:e2b 7.04 / 45.44; qwen2.5:3b 6.01 / 28.89; llama3.2:3b 5.71 / 27.23; deepseek-r1:7b (opt) 2.78 tg / 13.22 pp. Ollama on same box: llama3.1:8b 2.46 tg, qwen2.5-coder:7b 2.77, gemma4:e4b 3.71.
findings.note: Ollama default tags are Q4_K_M (inferred); llama.cpp version not stated. The 'gemma4' entries are Ollama-tagged models whose exact quant was not shown.

findings.claim: Jeff Geerling ai-benchmarks (llama-bench methodology): Llama 3.2 3B on Pi 5 CPU = 4.88 tok/s at 11.9 W (16GB) and 4.61 tok/s at 13.9 W (8GB).
findings.note: Quantization not stated in the table (Ollama llama3.2:3b default = Q4_K_M, inferred).

findings.claim: Pi 5 8GB (Ollama, 64-bit RPi OS, Apr 2026): Gemma 3 270M ~22 tok/s; 1B ~10; 1B QAT ~11; 4B Q4_K_M ~3.5 (3.8 GB RAM); 4B QAT ~5; Gemma 3n E2B ~6; E4B ~2.5.
findings.note: Ollama (llama.cpp-based) rather than llama.cpp directly; version not stated.

findings.claim: arXiv 2511.07425 (Pi 5 8GB, Ollama/Llamafile, all models q4_k_m): models ≤1.5B sustain 5–15 tok/s, 3B models 2–5 tok/s, sub-360M >20 tok/s; peak power ~10 W.
Early (Apr 2024) llama.cpp vs llamafile on Pi 5 8GB: TinyLlama-1.1B Q8_0 4.77 tok/s (llama.cpp) vs 5.75 tok/s (llamafile).

No published Pi 5 token/s numbers were found for OLMoE-1B-7B or for Mixtral-8x7B Q4_K_M (which at ~26 GB would require streaming weights from storage on any Pi 5).

findings.claim: Throttling thresholds (Raspberry Pi engineer jdb): "There is a soft-throttle that starts at 80°C and a hard throttle at 85°C. The soft-throttle linearly decreases the maximum allowed ARM frequency by 100MHz per degree until 85°C, then the idle frequency is forced." Soft-throttle is reported in `vcgencmd get_throttled` bit 0x80000.

Official thermal tests (`stress --cpu 4`, sustained): bare board idle ~65°C and under load "remains stable just above the 85°C thermal limit" with the clock throttled from 2.4GHz to 1.5GHz; Active Cooler idle ~45°C, load max 62–63°C (fan holds ~60°C); Active Cooler + M.2 HAT stabilises ~64°C; official case with fan ~72–74°C; fan steps at 60°C (low), 67.5°C (medium), 75°C (full).
findings.note: The documentation page gives the firmware fan curve as 0% <50°C, 30% at 50°C, 50% at 60°C, 70% at 67.5°C, 100% at 75°C (raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html). Launch post: Pi 5 is "designed to handle typical client workloads, uncased, with no active cooling"; sustained 4-core load is the exception.

findings.claim: Independent thermal test (CNX, sbc-bench, 8GB): with Active Cooler idle 46–47°C, peak 66°C, no throttling; heatsink only (fan unplugged) hit 85°C with "CPU frequency dropping as low as 1,500 MHz"; official case without fan idle 67–68°C and rapidly exceeded 85°C with significant throttling; case with fan peak 75°C, no throttling.
Sustained 4-thread llama.cpp inference on a Pi 5 16GB with active cooling stayed at 51.0–57.6°C with zero throttling (vcgencmd 0x0) across the benchmark suite.

The Pi 5 exposes exactly one PCIe 2.0 x1 link on the FPC; the AI HAT+/AI HAT+ 2 and the AI Kit (M.2 HAT+ + Hailo-8L, 13 TOPS) all occupy it, so an official AI HAT and an official M.2 HAT+ with NVMe cannot be stacked: "There is only one PCIe interface".
findings.note: AI HAT+ docs: both AI HAT+ models "connect to a Raspberry Pi 5 using its PCIe port" (raspberrypi.com/documentation/accessories/ai-hat-plus.html); AI Kit docs: "bundles the Raspberry Pi M.2 HAT+ with a Hailo AI acceleration module" (raspberrypi.com/documentation/accessories/ai-kit.html).

findings.claim: Hailo + NVMe can coexist via PCIe-switch boards: Pimoroni NVMe Base Duo ("two PCIe Gen 2 M.2 slots behind a PCIe Gen2 Packet Switcher", ~450 MB/s total / 220+ MB/s per disk, NVMe boot needs firmware 2024-05-17+, "Can be paired with other PCIe devices, such as the Raspberry Pi AI Kit"); a forum moderator confirmed booting from NVMe with the Hailo recognised on a Base Duo.
findings.note: Moderator quote from forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=371991.

findings.claim: Pineboards Ai Bundle (Hailo 8L), announced 1 Aug 2024 at €90 ex-VAT: ASMedia ASM1182e "PCIe Gen2 x1 to 2x PCIe Gen2 x1" switch, Hailo-8L in an M.2 2230 A/E-key socket plus an M-key 2230/2242/2280 NVMe socket, both usable simultaneously and bootable.
findings.note: pineboards.io product/documentation URLs returned 404 at fetch time.

findings.claim: Seeed Studio sells a "PCIe3.0 Switch to dual M.2 hat for Raspberry Pi 5, Support NVMe SSD, Support Hailo8/8L" (Gen 3 switch), but the switch chip and concurrent-use details are not on the product page.
findings.note: Page confirms the product exists and claims Hailo + NVMe support; no chip, lane or throughput figures given, and Gen 3 remains uncertified on Pi 5.

findings.claim: Running the Hailo at Gen 3 vs Gen 2 roughly doubles vision throughput (YOLOv8s ~80.7 fps vs ~41.8 fps), and all devices behind a Gen 2 switch share the single lane's ~500 MB/s peak — so a Gen 2 switch board caps NVMe weight streaming at roughly the 400–450 MB/s Gen 2 NVMe figures above while the Hailo is active.
findings.note: fps figures are quoted in the forum thread; the bandwidth-sharing consequence follows from the Gen2 x1 upstream link (M.2 HAT+ docs: 500 MB/s peak) and the Pimoroni 450 MB/s total figure.

open_questions: No tinymembench/STREAM run on a Pi 5 Model B 16GB with the Dec-2024 SDRAM-tuning firmware was found; the closest is the Pi 500+ (16GB, same silicon) at 5865 MB/s memcpy. Whether 16GB parts carry the same refresh-overhead penalty engineer Dom described for 8GB (vs 4GB) is unmeasured.
The official product page rendered "Raspberry Pi 5 16GB ... $305" on 2026-10-04 versus the $120 launch price — needs confirmation (DRAM-price-driven increase vs regional/retailer artefact).

Exact Raspberry Pi OS trixie release date/kernel (reported 2025-10-01, kernel 6.12; Sept-2026 image on 6.18) comes from secondary sources; the raspberrypi.com announcement was not fetched. The docs still make kernel_2712.img (16K pages) the default load.

Almost no published Pi 5 LLM benchmark states the llama.cpp commit (exception: issue #26484, commit d73c1d6), so numbers from 2024 (e.g. TinyLlama 4.77 tok/s) likely predate repack/dotprod-path improvements and are not comparable to 2026 numbers.

No measured Pi 5 numbers exist for streaming MoE weights from NVMe via mmap (e.g. Mixtral-8x7B Q4_K_M ~26 GB, OLMoE). The only Mixtral-family data point is '<1 tok/s' for a 2-expert Q4 variant on 8GB (DFRobot). Geerling explicitly used --no-mmap for Qwen3-30B-A3B on 16GB.
Secondary NVMe figures (Tom's Hardware: official Pi SSD 837 MB/s dd; Pimoroni NVMe Base 876 MB/s at Gen 3) could not be verified because those pages were truncated on fetch.
Seeed's PCIe 3.0 dual-M.2 switch HAT: switch chip, per-slot lane config, and whether Hailo + NVMe run concurrently at Gen 3 are not documented on the product page; Gen 3 remains uncertified on Pi 5.

Whether sd_cqe (A2 command queueing) changes large-block sequential microSD read on Pi 5 is only lightly measured (sequential write 61.4 → 64.4 MB/s); the gain is in random IOPS, so weight streaming from microSD stays bounded near ~90 MB/s.
research.summary: Pi 5 memory is a 32-bit LPDDR4X-4267 bus (official) → 17.07 GB/s theoretical (inferred); measured tinymembench memcpy is 4.8–6.0 GB/s (8GB: 4805–5158; 16GB Pi 500+: 5865; CM5 4GB: 6013) and single-thread STREAM Triad ~11.5–12.4 GB/s, dropping to 5.6–7.7 GB/s at 4 threads (8GB lower than 4GB due to refresh overhead per RPi engineer Dom); llama.cpp decode achieves ~10 GB/s effective across quantizations (issue #26484). RAM SKUs now listed: 1/2/4/8/16 GB; 16GB launched Jan 2025 at $120 on the D0 stepping. Storage: microSD is SDR104 (104 MB/s bus) with ~89–92 MB/s measured large-block read; sd_overclock only affects the 50 MHz mode and sdram_freq is unsupported on Pi 4+, while the Pi-5-specific tweak is dtparam=sd_cqe (A2 command queueing) which roughly doubles-to-quadruples random 4K IOPS but barely moves sequential MB/s. USB 3.0 SSD/NVMe-in-enclosure reads 360–416 MB/s. Native NVMe over the FPC reads ~417–454 MB/s at Gen 2 and ~784–894 MB/s with dtparam=pciex1_gen=3 (officially 'not certified', 'might be unstable'). Cortex-A76 (0xd0b) is Armv8.2-A with dotprod (asimddp) and FP16 arithmetic (fphp/asimdhp) but no i8mm, SVE or BF16 (GCC core def: V8_2A (F16, RCPC, DOTPROD)); llama.cpp's GGML_NATIVE (default ON) probes -mcpu=native and auto-enables dotprod/fp16 while i8mm/sve/sme probes fail; the manual equivalent is GGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH=armv8.2-a+dotprod+fp16; KleidiAI (OFF by default) falls to its DOTPROD-tier kernels. A native build matters enormously: Llama-3.2-1B Q4_K_M goes from 1.1 to 17.8 tok/s versus a generic ARM64 binary. Raspberry Pi OS loads kernel_2712.img with 16 KiB pages by default on Pi 5 (PhilE: 7+% random-access gain; kernel=kernel8.img reverts to 4K); llama.cpp's mmap uses offset 0 and sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE), so 16K pages are handled and simply make 16 KiB the minimum fault unit when streaming weights. Published Q4_K_M-class tok/s on Pi 5: ~1–1.5B 10–18 tok/s, 3B 4.6–6.0, 7–8B 2.3–2.8; MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B at Q3_K_S-2.70bpw on a 16GB board does 7.99 tok/s tg128 with 8–10 pp (Geerling, --no-mmap -c 4096) and 5.3 tok/s at Q4_K_S-3.92bpw (byteshape); a 2-expert Mixtral Q4 on 8GB ran <1 tok/s; 4× Pi 5 via distributed-llama hit 13–15 tok/s. No OLMoE or Mixtral-8x7B Pi 5 numbers exist. Thermals: soft throttle from 80°C at −100 MHz/°C, hard throttle at 85°C to 1.5 GHz; a bare board under 4-core stress sits just above 85°C (throttled) while the $5 Active Cooler holds 62–66°C with no throttling, and sustained 4-thread LLM runs on a cooled 16GB board stayed at 51–58°C. The Pi 5 has a single PCIe 2.0 x1 link, so an AI HAT+/AI Kit and an M.2 HAT+ NVMe cannot be stacked; coexistence requires a PCIe-switch board (Pimoroni NVMe Base Duo or Pineboards Ai Bundle with the ASM1182e Gen2 switch, ~450–500 MB/s shared; Seeed sells a Gen 3 switch variant with undocumented details), which caps NVMe weight streaming at Gen 2 rates while sharing the lane with the Hailo.
