verify.summary: All 12 claims CONFIRMED against their primary sources; every quoted number (MT/s, MB/s, tok/s, GB, W, Geekbench, dates) matched verbatim. One substantive correction: the $305 price for the Pi 5 16GB is real and official, not a regional/unconfirmed artefact - raspberrypi.com documents three memory-driven rises ($120 -> $145 on 2025-12-01, +$60 on 2026-02-02, +$100 on 2026-04-01), so any script hard-coding $120 is stale. Nuances worth carrying: (a) the llama.cpp issue never names the model and its author explicitly refuses to read ~10 GB/s as a % of peak, so '60% of 17.07 GB/s' is the researcher's inference only; (b) the 899/2169 Geekbench gain includes NUMA emulation, not SDRAM tuning alone; (c) GGML_NATIVE also defaults OFF when SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is set; (d) the '100 MHz/C throttle slope' and '1500 MHz at 85C' are not in official docs (uncertain); (e) 'Apr-2024 EEPROM' qualifier on the STREAM thread not explicitly confirmed. Bonus spot-checks of script-critical items (GGML CMake defaults, GCC cortex-a76 def, dtparam=pciex1_gen=3, fan curve, 16K page-size default) all confirmed from source.

research.topic: Prior art and reported results for Mixture-of-Experts LLM inference with experts offloaded to storage/host memory on consumer or edge hardware (CPU-only or low-RAM); measured expert-activation locality; realistic hit rate / bytes-per-token for a ~25B-total / ~3.8B-active MoE (Gemma 4 26B-A4B) with a 2-4 GB expert cache streaming from microSD (90 MB/s), USB3 SSD (350 MB/s) or NVMe Gen3 x1 (800 MB/s)

findings.claim: LLM in a Flash (Apple) targets DENSE models with ReLU-induced FFN neuron sparsity (OPT 6.7B, Falcon 7B sparsified, Persimmon 8B, Phi-2, Llama-2 7B sparsified), not MoE experts. Mechanisms: windowing (DRAM cache of neuron rows used by the last k=4-5 tokens), row-column bundling (doubles chunk size for flash reads), sparsity prediction. Hardware: Apple M1 Max 1TB SSD / M2 Ultra 2TB SSD for the CPU runs (flash >6 GiB/s linear, 2.25 GiB/s random at 32 KiB chunks with 32 threads) and an RTX 4090 for the GPU runs; roughly half the model in DRAM (52.1% for OPT 6.7B).
findings.note: Reported per-token latency for OPT 6.7B (Table 3): CPU naive 2196 ms I/O + 986 ms compute = 3182 ms vs optimized 105 ms I/O + 506 ms compute = 669 ms (~4-5x); GPU naive 2218 ms vs optimized 84 ms (~20-25x). Data loaded per token cut from 13.4 GB to ~0.2 GB (~98%) for OPT 6.7B. Experiments were run both CPU-only (Apple SoC) and GPU.

findings.claim: PowerInfer-2 runs TurboSparse-Mixtral-47B on a OnePlus 12 (24 GB DRAM, UFS 4.0, Snapdragon 8 Gen 3) at 11.68 tokens/s with ~50% of FFN weights offloaded to flash, and 2.13 tokens/s when only 7 GB is available; 24.6x (up to 27.8x) faster than llama.cpp and 3.84x (up to 4.63x) faster than an LLM-in-a-Flash port. Mechanisms: neuron clusters, hot/cold neuron split (hot on NPU, cold on CPU), segmented neuron cache, next-layer prefetch, I/O-compute pipelining. UFS 4.0 measured 4 GB/s sequential (512 KB blocks) and ~1 GB/s random 4 KB.
findings.note: Compute is hybrid CPU+NPU (phone GPU deliberately avoided). Not CPU-only. Second device: OnePlus Ace 2 (16 GB, UFS 3.1). Requires the TurboSparse (ReLU-fied) variant of Mixtral, not stock Mixtral.

findings.claim: MoE-Infinity (RTX A5000, PCIe 4.0, 32 GB-1 TB host DRAM) uses request-level Expert Activation Matrix tracing with cosine-matched history (EAMC of ~120 entries suffices) to drive prefetch and eviction with layer-proximity decay; reports 3.1-16.7x per-token latency improvement vs vLLM/Ollama/DeepSpeed/BrainStorm. Key locality observation: at batch size 1, for ~100-expert models fewer than 5% of experts are repeatedly activated while decoding a request; Mixtral shows ~25% expert activation per request; reuse is skewed within a request but uniform across requests.
findings.note: GPU + host DRAM offload (no SSD streaming). DeepSeek-V2-Lite avg TPOT 155 ms vs vLLM 485 ms vs DeepSpeed 737 ms. No explicit hit-rate-vs-cache-size table extracted.

findings.claim: Fiddler keeps experts in host DRAM and, for small batches, computes them on the CPU instead of transferring weights (rule: run on CPU when cpu_lat(s) < gpu_lat(s) + trans_lat). Measured that weight transfer takes ~2-5x longer than the GPU compute it enables. Hardware: Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB + Xeon Gold 6126 (PCIe 3 x16) and RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB + Xeon 8480+ (PCIe 4). Mixtral-8x7B fp16 (56/256 or 125/256 experts fit on GPU). Speedups: 1.26x single-batch, 1.30x long prefill, 11.57x beam search; 1.65x vs Mixtral-offloading on long prefill.
findings.note: Requires a GPU; no CPU-only or SSD mode. Later version also validates Phi-3.5-MoE.

findings.claim: KTransformers (Tsinghua) places MLA attention/KV/shared expert on one GPU and all routed experts in CPU DRAM with AMX kernels + 'expert deferral'. DeepSeek-V3/R1 671B Q4_K_M on dual Xeon Gold 6454S (64 cores) + RTX 4090D: prefill 82.94 tok/s (8 experts) / 97.32 tok/s (6 experts), decode 12.2 / 13.69 tok/s vs llama.cpp 10.31 prefill / 4.51 decode (up to 3.03x decode, 9.44x prefill). Needs 382 GB (single socket) to 1 TB DRAM and >=14 GB VRAM; experts live in DRAM, not SSD.
findings.note: Not an edge/low-RAM system. The SOSP'25 PDF could not be parsed by the fetch tool (madsys.cs.tsinghua.edu.cn/.../SOSP25-chen.pdf), so paper-specific numbers beyond the tutorial are unverified.

findings.claim: Eliseev & Mazur ('Mixtral offloading', dvmazur) combine an LRU expert cache (k=2 experts/layer for 12 GB GPUs, k=4 for 16 GB), speculative expert loading (apply layer N+1's gate to layer N's hidden state; Fig. 2 shows ~60-90% recall when preloading 1-2 experts 1-10 layers ahead), and HQQ mixed quantization (4-bit attention + 2-bit experts = 17.54 GB; 3-bit experts 21.37 GB; 4-bit 23.99 GB). Table 2 tokens/s (2-bit experts): T4 2.092 / RTX 3060 2.278 / RTX 3080 Mobile 2.655 / A100 3.061 for the full algorithm vs naive offloading 0.661 / 0.919 / 1.059 / 1.392 (~3x). Without cache & pre-loading: 1.168 / 1.547 / 1.758 / 2.265.
findings.note: GPU + host RAM only; no CPU-only or SSD results. The paper states 'some experts are reused between adjacent tokens' and plots LRU hit ratio vs k (Fig. 2 left) but the numeric hit-rate values were not extractable from the page. The GitHub README (https://github.com/dvmazur/mixtral-offloading) lists speculative prefetching as NOT yet implemented in the released code.

findings.claim: Pre-gated MoE (ISCA 2024) trains a pre-gate at MoE block N that emits the expert mask for block N+1, so experts can be prefetched from CPU DRAM over PCIe before they are needed. Hardware: A100 80 GB + EPYC 7V12 (1.8 TB DDR4), PCIe Gen4 32 GB/s. Models: Switch Transformer Base/Large (8-128 experts). Results: 1.7x avg speedup vs on-demand MoE offload, 81% of oracle GPU-only throughput, 4.2x lower peak GPU memory (23% of GPU-only), small accuracy degradation on some tasks.
findings.note: GPU required; experts in host DRAM; requires fine-tuning the model.

findings.claim: SwapMoE (ACL 2024) keeps a dynamically updated compact set of 'Virtual Experts' in main memory (importance = sum ||x||·||G(x)_i||·||E_i||), swapping experts from storage asynchronously and amortized across samples. Edge hardware: Jetson Nano (4 GB) and Jetson AGX Orin. Switch Transformer summarization: memory 14.2 GiB -> 4.7 GiB (-67%), 50% lower latency, Rouge-2 -0.041; another setting -37% memory / -18% latency at -0.012 Rouge-2.
findings.note: Jetson GPUs (unified memory), not CPU-only. Accepts accuracy loss by routing only within the in-memory expert subset.

findings.claim: AdapMoE combines sensitivity-based adaptive gating (skips ~25% of expert activations vs top-2 with no accuracy loss), next-layer prefetching (~90% prediction accuracy on most layers) and layer-aware cache allocation (more cache to early layers, which are harder to prefetch). Mixtral-8x7B/8x22B at 4-bit and 4+2-bit on RTX 4090 and A6000; 1.35x average latency reduction vs Mixtral-Offloading.
findings.note: GPU + CPU/SSD offload for storage of inactive experts; not CPU-only.

findings.claim: HOBBIT (built on llama.cpp) replaces cache-miss experts with low-precision substitutes at token level, does layer-level adaptive prefetch (96% next-layer prediction accuracy), and a sequence-level multidimensional cache (LRU/LFU/LHU/FLD, precision-aware). Hardware: Jetson AGX Orin (32 GB unified, 12 CPU cores) and RTX 4090 (24 GB) + 256 GB DRAM, Samsung 980 PRO NVMe (7 GB/s). Results: on Orin int8, 13.0x (Mixtral-8x7B) and 18.9x (Phi-3.5-MoE) decode speedup vs llama.cpp baseline; on 4090 fp16, 3.21x vs Mixtral-Offloading; accuracy drop <=1%.
findings.note: GPU-centric (Orin GPU / 4090) with optional CPU-GPU cooperation; not CPU-only.

findings.claim: ExpertFlow (DAC'26) uses a transformer routing-path predictor (up to ~95% in-domain expert prediction accuracy, 5-10 pt drop cross-domain), token scheduling, and a Predictive Locality-aware Expert Cache; reports 91.96% expert cache hit ratio (up to 61.15 pts better than LRU on Switch-32), up to 93.72% GPU-memory reduction, 2.01x/3.19x/5.86x speedups on Switch-32/64/128 and ~2x on Mixtral-8x7B and Qwen1.5-MoE. Hardware: one A40 48 GB + Xeon Gold 6338.
findings.note: GPU + CPU DRAM; not CPU-only. Cache sizes for the 91.96% figure not extracted.

findings.claim: ProMoE uses a learned predictor on intermediate hidden states to predict experts several layers ahead ('stride' prefetch; 84.7% average accuracy, -5 pts with stride) so loads leave the critical path. Hardware: RTX 4090 24 GB + i9-14900K + 128 GB DRAM, PCIe 4.0 32 GB/s. Models: DeepSeek-MoE 16.4B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite 15.7B, Qwen1.5-MoE 14.3B, Qwen2-MoE 57.4B, Mixtral-8x7B. Speedups 2.20x (up to 3.21x) prefill and 2.07x (up to 5.02x) decode vs open-source offloading; 1.78x/1.34x vs hand-crafted caches.
findings.note: GPU + host DRAM; predictor runs on CPU; not CPU-only.

findings.claim: MoE-Lightning is a throughput-oriented batch system (CGOPipe CPU-GPU-I/O pipelining, paged weights, Hierarchical Roofline Model) for Mixtral 8x7B/8x22B and DBRX on 1-4 T4s or an L4 with 192-416 GB host DRAM; up to 10.3x higher throughput than FlexGen on a single T4; experts offloaded to CPU DRAM, not SSD.
findings.note: Not a latency/single-stream or edge design; GPU required.

findings.claim: Hermes (ICCD 2024, arXiv 2409.04249) is a memory-efficient PipeLoad pipeline-execution mechanism for BERT/ViT/GPT-style models on edge devices (4.24x speedup, 86.7% less memory for BERT/ViT; 2.58x and 90.3% for GPT-style). It does not address Mixture-of-Experts models or expert caching at all.
findings.note: Included because the task listed it; it is prior art for layer-streaming on edge, not for MoE expert offload.

findings.claim: eMoE uses an XLNet-based expert-sequence predictor (~71% accuracy on OpenMoE and Mixtral), periodic re-prediction (every ~40 prompts), task-aware expert loading and SLO-aware request scheduling; reports up to 80% memory reduction, up to 17% latency reduction, 1.5x throughput, 93.7-99.8% accuracy retained when loading 60-80% of experts. Hardware: 4x A100 40 GB + Xeon with 128 GB host memory (experts on CPU, loaded to GPU).
findings.note: Datacenter GPU serving system, not edge/CPU-only.

findings.claim: EdgeMoE (2023) is the earliest CPU-capable edge MoE system: expert-wise bitwidth adaptation (INT2/4/8 by sensitivity) plus in-memory expert management that preloads experts predicted from prior-layer activation statistics. Hardware: Jetson TX2 (8 GB, SSD 550/520 MB/s and HDD 50/20 MB/s), Raspberry Pi 4B (8 GB, SD card, CPU-only) and a Xiaomi 14 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3). Observations: experts are 86.5% of memory but 26.4% of compute in Switch-base-16; expert activation paths are power-law ('the 20% most frequently activated paths contribute to more than 99% of the activation cases'). Results: 1.19x-2.77x speedup vs STI/dynamic-loading baselines, 1.05-1.18x memory reduction, <=2% accuracy loss.
findings.note: Models are Switch Transformer and GPTSAN (encoder-decoder / small decoder), not modern top-8-of-128 LLMs; the 20%->99% path statistic is for Switch-style top-1 routing.

findings.claim: HybriMoE (DAC'25, built on kTransformers + llama.cpp kernels, Marlin 4-bit) adds dynamic intra-layer CPU/GPU scheduling, impact-driven inter-layer prefetch (3 layers ahead) and a Minus-Recent-Score cache policy. Hardware: RTX A6000 + Xeon Gold 5220R limited to 10 cores. Cache hit rate at 25% capacity, LRU -> MRS: Mixtral-8x7B 30.2% -> 36.2%; DeepSeek-V2-Lite 47.7% -> 52.7%; Qwen2-57B-A14B 45.0% -> 52.8%. Speedup vs kTransformers: 1.33x prefill, 1.70x decode.
findings.note: GPU + CPU DRAM hybrid; useful as a direct LRU-hit-rate datapoint at 25% expert capacity.

findings.claim: DALI (Feb 2026, extends KTransformers) observes strong temporal correlation of high-workload experts between adjacent tokens and uses greedy runtime CPU/GPU expert assignment, residual-based prefetch and workload-aware cache replacement. Hardware: RTX 3090 24 GB + EPYC 7532 + 256 GB DDR4. Models: DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B. Decode speedups 3.97x / 2.16x / 1.48x / 1.32x vs llama.cpp / KTransformers / MoE-Lightning / HybriMoE; reports HybriMoE's cache reaching only 25.3% hit on Mixtral while DALI's reaches ~100% in decode.
findings.note: GPU + host DRAM; the '100% hit' figure reflects DALI's dynamic assignment where misses are computed on CPU, so it is not comparable to a storage-streaming cache.

findings.claim: FlashMoE (Jan 2026) targets SSD-offloaded MoE on a consumer desktop (Ryzen 9 9600X, 16 GB DDR5, RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, SK hynix P51 PCIe 5.0 NVMe 7.4 GB/s) with a lightweight ML cache policy blending recency and frequency; on OLMoE-1B-7B it reports up to 51% higher hit rate than LFU and 21% higher than LRU, on Qwen3-30B-A3B 28%/21% over ARC/LeCaR; token throughput +22% (OLMoE) and +7% (Qwen3-30B-A3B) vs LRU; up to 2.6x vs existing systems and 4x faster model load than llama.cpp.
findings.note: GPU-accelerated, experts stream from SSD. Absolute hit-rate values per cache size were not extracted.

findings.claim: SeqMoE (Sep 2026) reports LRU expert-cache hit rates averaged over Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GPT-OSS-120B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash of 60.02% / 74.24% / 84.49% / 86.37% / 88.50% at 15% / 25% / 35% / 40% / 45% expert residency, vs 84.56% / 91.72% / 95.09% / 96.11% / 96.97% for its seq2seq-predicted, Belady-style cache; top-(k+3) prefetch recall 85.8-90.9%; at 45% residency it reaches 80.22% of full-load throughput (FreeToken 51.5%, others <=28%). Hardware: RTX 4090/5090/PRO 6000 with Xeon hosts, experts in host DRAM.
findings.note: GPU + DRAM; the LRU curve is the most useful cross-model hit-rate-vs-capacity datapoint found for modern 128-expert/top-8 models.

findings.claim: SpecMD (Feb 2026) studies speculative expert prefetching (top-k with overfetch vs score-based, using current gate outputs / future gate functions on current logits) on OLMoE-1B-7B, Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, Phi-3.5-MoE with a single A100 80 GB and software-limited cache of 1% / 5% / 25% of model size; reports >88% hit rate and up to 34.7% TTFT reduction on OLMoE with only 5% (0.6 GB) VRAM cache; measured host->device bandwidth ~5 GB/s.
findings.note: GPU; the high hit rate at 5% capacity is achieved with prediction-driven prefetch, not plain LRU.

findings.claim: MoE-SpeQ uses an INT4 draft model to predict future tokens' experts and prefetch them from host DRAM (90.9% total prediction rate: 44.1% exact + 46.8% partial). A100 40 GB + Xeon Silver 4310 + 256 GB RAM, PCIe 4 x16. Phi-3.5-MoE 163.1 ms/token vs 536.7 ms for Mixtral-Offloading (3.3x); Qwen1.5-MoE 2.5x; DeepSeek-V2-Lite 4.8x vs vanilla Transformers.
findings.note: GPU + DRAM. SP-MoE (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10302) is a related speculative-decoding-aware prefetch system reporting 1.07-3.5x TPOT speedup (hardware/models not in abstract).

findings.claim: MELINOE (Feb 2026) measures that in base OLMoE the top-8 experts by activation within a sequence account for only ~31% of expert activations (weak concentration), then fine-tunes to concentrate routing, achieving a 3.03x reduction in weight transfers over 64 generated tokens; OLMoE on H100 goes 14.2-14.6 -> 22.2-23.3 tok/s with offloading; Phi-3.5-MoE on A100 5.1-5.8 -> 14.3-15.7 tok/s; Mixtral-8x7B 1.2-3x over efficient baselines.
findings.note: Requires fine-tuning; GPU + offload.

findings.claim: MaskCoFT (Sep 2026) reports baseline per-layer cache hit rates with GPU cache B=12 of 64 experts for DeepSeek-V2-Lite: LRU 44.45%, LFU 43.45%, FIFO 43.34%; and B=4 of 8 experts for Mixtral-8x7B: LRU 61.38%, LFU 61.58%, FIFO 60.49%. Its co-adaptive fine-tuning cuts expert fetches/token by 23.7% (Mixtral) and 10.1% (DeepSeek-V2-Lite) and TPOT by up to 16.4% / 5.5% in MoE-Offloading on 2x H200.
findings.note: Clean baseline LRU numbers: ~44% hit at 18.75% capacity for a 64-expert/top-6(+2 shared) model; ~61% hit at 50% capacity for 8-expert/top-2 Mixtral.

findings.claim: ReMoE (May 2026) fine-tunes the router to bias toward recently selected experts, improving expert reuse by 26% with no inference-time cost; gains: +8.4% throughput under vLLM GPU-CPU offload, 43.6-49.8% lower TPOT on Jetson Orin NX, 1.77-1.99x decode speedup in a llama.cpp implementation. Models: DeepSeek and Qwen MoE families.
findings.note: Abstract-level only; cache sizes and baseline hit rates not extracted.

findings.claim: Cache-Aware Joint Router Adaptation (Sep 2026) trains Temporal / Spatio-Temporal routers while preserving native top-K; on Qwen3 it improves adjusted hit rate by 1.15-18.03 points and cuts expert traffic 4.6-53.3% vs the strongest prefetching baseline; GPT-OSS results 'competitive but task-dependent'.
findings.note: Abstract-level; hardware and absolute baseline hit rates not given there.

findings.claim: Qualcomm's 'Mixture of Cache-Conditional Experts' is a CPU-ONLY on-device study (llama.cpp-based, mlock, Snapdragon Android 14 phones with 12 GB / 16 GB RAM, 4-bit / 8-bit models, caches of 30 or 45 experts per layer). Baseline LRU miss rates (Table 10): Qwen1.5-MoE 35%, DeepSeek-V2 28%, Phi-3.5-MoE 22%, Mixtral-8x7B 40%. Cache-prior routing (boost in-cache expert logits, lambda=0.5) cuts misses to 16% / 7% / 9% / 21% with 0.1-3% perplexity increase and <0.1% downstream accuracy drop, yielding over 2x on-device speedup vs plain LRU.
findings.note: Best direct evidence for CPU-only expert caching on edge: LRU alone leaves 22-40% misses even with generous per-layer caches; the 30/45-experts-per-layer configs apply to the 60-64-expert models, so the Mixtral/Phi cache sizes differ (not extracted).

findings.claim: 'Cacheable by Design?' (Aug 2026, pre-registered negative result + systems study) on a commodity desktop (RTX 3070 8 GB, i9-12900, 32 GB DDR4, WD SN530 DRAM-less PCIe 3 NVMe ~2.4 GB/s): Qwen3-235B-A22B Q4_K_M (134 GB) decodes at 0.441 tok/s warm when experts stream from SSD (~12 GB of 4-bit expert reads per token, i.e. exactly the SSD's cold sequential ceiling); batching collapses (B=32 aggregate 0.087 tok/s) from paging thrash. On Qwen3-30B-A3B (48 layers, 128 experts, top-8; layer 24, code domain): P(expert reused at next token) = 0.444 vs 0.223 chance (2.0x); an LRU cache holding 13.4% of experts serves 66% of requests; 95% of traffic flows through 52.5% of experts.
findings.note: Negative result: training routers with locality losses reduced misses up to 60% but every configuration broke the pre-registered <=1% perplexity gate; stacking training-free cache-aware rerouting with trained locality gave ~80% miss reduction at <=3.4% perplexity. Only the 30B routing profile is relevant to the ~25B/3.8B target; the 235B serving numbers show the SSD-bound regime.

findings.claim: 'Not All Models Suit Expert Offloading' (ICLR 2026) defines Segment Routing best Performance (SRP) and Segment Cache best Hit rate (SCH) over 20 MoE LLMs. SRP at segment length 16: LLaMA-MoE-v2 78.16, Yuan2.0 63.48, PowerMoE 55.17, Qwen3 54.14, OLMoE 50.91, Mixtral-8x7B 49.36, LLaMA-MoE-v1 45.29, DeepSeek-V2-Lite 37.92, DeepSeekMoE 36.94, Qwen2 36.74, Qwen1.5-MoE 30.71, Switch 19.3. Findings: shared experts reduce local routing consistency; domain-specialized experts raise it; most models hit the cache knee at roughly 2x the number of active experts (rho=2).
findings.note: Qwen3 (the 128-expert/top-8 shape closest to Gemma 4) and OLMoE are in the high-consistency group; DeepSeek-V2-Lite (with shared experts) is markedly lower. These are oracle (best-case) segment metrics, not online LRU hit rates.

findings.claim: llama.cpp community measurements on Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M (RTX 4070 Ti 12 GB, experts in CPU RAM, 'FATE'/llama-moe-cache): zero-training VRAM expert cache + cross-layer and previous-token prediction gives 99.50% cache hit (75,690 hits / 384 misses) and 33.74 -> 64.45 tok/s (1.91x); Mixtral-8x7B 99.94% hit.
findings.note: Hit rate is for a VRAM cache sized to the per-token working set with experts coming from host RAM (not SSD); README does not state the cache size used, so the 99.5% should not be read as an LRU-vs-capacity result.

findings.claim: llama.cpp PR #27861 (draft, GPU-resident per-layer LRU cache for host-offloaded experts) reports on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (512 experts, 10 routed/token, 28 layers; dual RTX 3090): decode 18.4 -> 24.2 tok/s (+31%) at 48 slots/layer (~4.1 GiB VRAM); LRU-64 ~67% and LRU-128 ~81% hit over a mixed workload, with 85.9%-98.5% depending on slot count; also run on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma4-26B, GLM-5.3-Flash and AMD RDNA3 via Vulkan. Unmerged; decode-only (n_tokens==1).
findings.note: Experts come from host RAM over PCIe, not SSD. Gemma4-26B is listed as tested but no Gemma-specific hit rate was extracted.

findings.claim: llama.cpp Discussion #27149 'Expert-Aware SSD Streaming' is a CPU-ONLY, SSD-streaming prototype on an M1 MacBook Pro/Air with 16 GB RAM: Qwen3-30B-A3B (17.3 GB GGUF, 128 experts, 8 active). Reading only the 8 active experts cuts per-layer I/O from 263 MB to 31 MB (11.4x); expert-contiguous relayout cuts page faults 36x (192 vs 6,912 pages per expert); consecutive tokens share 44.2% of experts; 'Calibrated + LRU = 56%' hit rate on text; prototype 4.7 tok/s; C/BLAS benchmarks 3.81 tok/s at 75% hit and 4.10 tok/s at 88% hit; ~24 MB/layer active buffer, 1-2 GB total footprint; SSD measured 2.97 GB/s sequential / 6.06 GB/s double-buffered.
findings.note: Closest existing analogue to the target scenario (CPU-only, low RAM, experts from storage), but on a ~3-6 GB/s laptop NVMe, i.e. 4-60x faster storage than the 90-800 MB/s cases asked about.

findings.claim: llama.cpp RFC Discussion #24528 (VRAM cache of hot CPU-resident experts, unmerged): Qwen3.5-122B top 10% of experts take ~80% of decode hits (Gini ~0.76; simulated 99% hit at 69% expert budget); DeepSeek-V4-Flash (43 layers x 256 experts) hit rate ~80% at ~31% pool capacity with a near-linear (not early-saturating) curve; 13 models showed +10%..+57% decode gains on 4x RTX 3090 / 48-core EPYC / 256 GB DDR4 (e.g. GLM-5.1 754B 13.96 -> 17.49 tok/s); a GTX 1080 Ti regressed at every cache budget; prefill regresses ~14% (RAM-fit) and -66% when combined with mmap+disk streaming.
findings.note: Experts in host RAM. Shows frequency skew varies strongly by model: very skewed (Qwen3.5-122B) vs nearly flat (DeepSeek-V4-Flash).

findings.claim: FreeToken issue #174: on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (61 MoE layers x 256 experts, RTX 5090 32 GB, 700 cache slots total ~4.5% of experts) LRU achieves only 8-18% decode hit rate while a frequency-pinning oracle at the same size reaches 46% (500 slots 40%, 900 slots 52%); 240-248 of 256 experts per layer are 'live'. Conclusion: for fine-grained MoE 'recency is a poor predictor' and eviction policy, not capacity, drives the gap.
findings.note: Counter-example to the 'temporal locality is strong' narrative: with 256 fine-grained experts and tiny caches, LRU nearly fails.

findings.claim: truespar/paddock issue #8: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_XL (22.4 GB) on an RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB with 18.3 GB of experts in pinned host RAM (PCIe 4 x8, 12.6 GB/s measured) and a 2.75 GB VRAM LRU slot cache decodes at 62 tok/s; LRU hit rates on a 4032-token mixed prose/code prompt: 82% at 64 slots, 90% at 96, 94% at 128 slots per layer.
findings.note: Host-RAM source, not SSD; Qwen3.6-35B expert count not stated in the extract, so the slot fractions cannot be converted to % capacity.

findings.claim: AlexChen31337/gemma4-moe-offload is an in-progress 'LLM in a Flash'-style port for Gemma 4 26B-A4B (ggml-org Q4_K_M ~15.6 GB) on an RTX 3070 8 GB + 16 GB DDR4 + PCIe 3 NVMe (~3 GB/s): attention/embeddings resident (~4.2-4.8 GB), all 128 expert FFNs memory-mapped on NVMe, 9 expert chunks loaded per token (8 routed + shared), a DRAM sliding-window cache of the last k activations claimed to cut NVMe reads ~50-65%, gate/down bundling for contiguous reads. Target >=10 tok/s; predecessor Qwen3.5 project reached 10.20 tok/s; Gemma 4 measurements and hit rates not yet published in the README.
findings.note: The '50-65% read reduction' is a README claim without data and should be treated as unverified. Uses a GPU.

findings.claim: ik_llama.cpp issue #1765: Gemma 4 26B-A4B UD-Q4_K_XL with all 30 MoE layers' experts on CPU (--n-cpu-moe 30) on an RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB + Ryzen 9 7945HX decodes at 30.10 tok/s in upstream llama.cpp vs 6.86 tok/s in ik_llama.cpp (q8_0 KV); experts are read from host RAM.
findings.note: Shows the DRAM-resident (not storage) ceiling for Gemma 4 26B-A4B expert offload on a fast desktop CPU: ~30 tok/s.

findings.claim: llama.cpp's baseline expert-offload mechanism is the --cpu-moe / --n-cpu-moe N flags (PR #15077), which add tensor-buffer overrides so expert tensors stay in host memory (accessed via the mmap'd GGUF / page cache) while attention runs on GPU; a user reports 108 tok/s for gpt-oss-120b on dual RTX 5090 with --n-cpu-moe 3.
findings.note: No expert cache or prefetch: when RAM is smaller than the expert set, each miss is a demand page fault to storage, which is the 'naive mmap' baseline that the 2025-26 caching work compares against.

findings.claim: OD-MoE (Dec 2025) removes the expert cache entirely: experts are loaded on demand in parallel across a ten-node edge testbed using a 99.94%-accurate expert-activation predictor, reaching ~75% of fully-GPU-cached decoding speed with 1/3 the GPU memory, on nodes with <1 GB GPU memory.
findings.note: Distributed, GPU-based; node hardware and tok/s not in abstract.

findings.claim: SMoE (Aug 2025) substitutes low-importance activated experts with functionally similar experts already in GPU cache, reporting >60% expert cache hit rate, 48% lower decoding latency and near-lossless accuracy on consumer-grade edge GPUs.
findings.note: GPU + PCIe; abstract-level.

findings.claim: ZipMoE (ICML'26) applies lossless compression of expert parameters plus cache-affinity scheduling on unified-memory edge platforms, reporting up to 72.77% latency reduction and 6.76x throughput vs state of the art while turning the workload from I/O-bound to compute-centric.
findings.note: Devices and models not named in abstract.

findings.claim: FreeToken (Aug 2026) is an edge-native MoE serving stack (model layout, expert residency, CPU-GPU execution, bandwidth-adaptive runtime) supporting 20+ MoE models and claiming 35B on an 8 GB laptop GPU, 284B on a gaming desktop and 753B GLM-5.2 on a workstation GPU.
findings.note: No tok/s or hit rates in abstract; see FreeToken issue #174 for its own LRU measurement on DSV4-Flash.

findings.claim: MoE-CORE (Oct 2026) targets NPU appliances with an 84 GB memory limit (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A8, GLM-5.2): non-uniform layer-wise cache capacity, domain-informed init, routing-history-aware replacement, cross-layer prefetch; TPOT 38.0-44.8 ms vs 1268.9 ms for vLLM (DeepSeek) and 206.6-220.5 ms vs 5941.5 ms (GLM); 21.5 ms with approximate substitution + MTP.
findings.note: NPU, not CPU/GPU consumer hardware; no hit rates in abstract.

findings.claim: SliceMoE (Dec 2025) caches MSB bit-slices of low-activation experts and full MSB+LSB for critical experts in ~8 GB LPDDR4 (104 Gbps) with UFS 3.1 flash (10 Gbps) on a custom XPU; up to 2.37x decode energy reduction / 1.81x speedup on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and 2.85x / 1.64x on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B; states DRAM access is >50x more energy-efficient than flash.
findings.note: Simulated accelerator; miss rates not reported.

findings.claim: 'SSD Offloading for LLM MoE Weights Considered Harmful in Energy Efficiency' (Aug 2025) finds that offloading MoE expert weights to current SSDs raises per-token decode energy by up to ~12x vs an HBM baseline (DeepSeek-R1 analysis), and that prefetching hides latency but not energy; flash read energy would need ~10x improvement for SSD offload to be energy-competitive.
findings.note: Abstract-level; platform details not given.

findings.claim: 'Who Should Own the Expert Cache?' (Aug 2026) evaluates kernel/page-cache-managed expert tiering on GH200 for 128-896-expert models including a 1.45 TB expert pool: page-cache admission speeds steady decode 1.09-1.10x in a production CUDA engine; an oracle-pinned user-space cache is still 1.09-1.11x faster; perfect one-layer router lookahead gains 5.0% (64.7% measured recall); kernel recency policies were more robust under domain shift than static frequency pinning.
findings.note: Datacenter hardware, but directly relevant to the mmap/page-cache vs application-managed-cache question.

findings.claim: SmallThinker (Jul 2025) co-designs a 21B-A3B / 4B-A0.6B MoE for storage offload: pre-attention router lets the engine prefetch expert weights from storage while attention computes; measured expert skew: 70-80% of experts have activation frequency <0.14 while 20-30% have 0.4-0.6, motivating a DRAM-hot / SSD-cold split. CPU-only results under an 8 GB memory limit (Table 6): PC i9-14900K 20.30 tok/s (vs Qwen3-30B-A3B 10.11), OnePlus 13 15.50 tok/s (vs Qwen3-30B-A3B 0.18 tok/s, i.e. 85x), RK3588 also tested; 4B-A0.6B under 1 GB: 29.99 tok/s on PC.
findings.note: Shows what stock Qwen3-30B-A3B does under an 8 GB cap on a phone with naive offload (0.18 tok/s) vs a model trained for locality/prefetch; storage device/bandwidth not stated.

findings.claim: DynaExq (Nov 2025) Table 1/2: Qwen3-30B-A3B expert activation ratio in decode is 6.3% at batch size 1 (= top-8 of 128) but 62.0% at batch 32; in prefill 46.9% (bs=1) to 96.6% (bs=32); measured on an RTX A6000 48 GB with HF Transformers. The Multi-Layer Scheduling paper (arXiv 2602.21626) separately reports that Qwen3-30B-A3B layers 16, 18, 44, 45, 46 show pronounced expert imbalance over 200 random-dataset requests on 2x A100.
findings.note: Implication: expert caching from storage only pays off for single-stream (batch 1) decode; any batching or long prefill touches most experts per layer. Opportunistic Expert Activation (arXiv 2511.02237) reports 48.8 of 128 experts (~38%) activated per layer at batch 16 for Qwen3-30B-A3B.

findings.claim: 'Accelerating MoE Inference with Adaptive Expert Split Mechanism' (Sep 2025) reports long-tail expert frequency (roughly top 20% of experts ~80% of routing decisions) and consecutive-token reuse (roughly 60-70% of tokens reuse at least one expert from the previous token) for Mixtral 8x7B, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-V2, with its policy reaching ~78-80% hit vs LFU ~65-70% at 30 experts/layer (+12.52% over LRU).
findings.note: Extracted from a PDF via a summarizer that used 'approximately'; exact figures and the per-model breakdown should be re-read from the PDF before citing numerically.

findings.claim: Model configurations (primary config.json): Qwen3-30B-A3B hidden 2048, moe_intermediate 768, 128 experts, top-8, 48 layers (=> 4.72M params per expert, 384 expert visits per token); Gemma 4 26B-A4B hidden 2816, moe_intermediate 704, 128 experts, top_k 8, 30 layers, dense intermediate_size 2112, 20 sliding + 6 full attention layers listed (=> 5.95M params per routed expert, 240 routed-expert visits per token); OLMoE-1B-7B hidden 2048, intermediate 1024, 64 experts, top-8, 16 layers; DeepSeek-V2-Lite hidden 2048, moe_intermediate 1408, 64 routed + 2 shared, top-6, 27 layers (first layer dense).
findings.note: Qwen3: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B/raw/main/config.json ; OLMoE: https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924/raw/main/config.json ; DeepSeek-V2-Lite: https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite/raw/main/config.json . The Gemma 4 config (unsloth mirror) has no explicit shared-expert key; the official model card states '8 active / 128 total and 1 shared' experts, 25.2B total / 3.8B active, 30 layers (https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core/model_card_4). ggml-org GGUF sizes: Q4_0 14.6 GB, Q8_0 26.9 GB, BF16 50.5 GB (https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF).

findings.claim: Raspberry Pi 5 exposes a single-lane PCIe 2.0 interface ('500 MB/s peak transfer rate'); PCIe Gen 3.0 can be enabled but 'The Raspberry Pi 5 is not certified for Gen 3.0 speeds. PCIe Gen 3.0 connections might be unstable.'
findings.note: The task's 800 MB/s 'NVMe Gen3 x1' figure therefore requires the uncertified Gen 3 override; the certified ceiling is ~500 MB/s. The Pi 5 product-brief PDF exceeded the fetch size limit, so microSD (SDR104) and USB 3.0 figures were not re-verified; the 90 MB/s and 350 MB/s figures are taken as the task's assumptions.

findings.claim: Derived (Gemma 4 26B-A4B at ~4.5 bits/weight, Q4_K_M/Q4_0 class): 5.95M params/expert -> ~3.35 MB per routed expert; 240 routed-expert visits per token -> ~0.80 GB of expert bytes per token at 0% hit; total routed-expert pool 3840 experts -> ~12.9 GB (consistent with the 14.6 GB Q4_0 GGUF once ~1.4 GB of dense weights are added). A 2 GB expert cache holds ~15.5% of experts (~20/layer), 3 GB ~23% (~30/layer), 4 GB ~31% (~40/layer). Streamed bytes/token = 0.80 GB x (1 - hit rate): 322 MB at 60% hit, 201 MB at 75%, 121 MB at 85%, 64 MB at 92%.
findings.note: Assumes the ~2.4B dense/active non-expert parameters (~1.35 GB at Q4) are RAM-resident and excluded from the expert cache budget; a Pi with 4 GB total RAM would therefore have well under 2 GB left for experts. At a HOBBIT-style 2-bit cold tier (~2.6 bpw) each miss costs ~1.9 MB instead of 3.35 MB.

findings.claim: Derived I/O-bound decode ceiling for Gemma 4 26B-A4B (bytes/token above divided by storage bandwidth, assuming perfect I/O-compute overlap and expert-contiguous layout): microSD 90 MB/s -> 0.28 tok/s (60% hit) / 0.45 (75%) / 0.74 (85%) / 1.4 (92%); USB3 SSD 350 MB/s -> 1.1 / 1.7 / 2.9 / 5.5 tok/s; NVMe 800 MB/s -> 2.5 / 4.0 / 6.6 / 12.5 tok/s. At the Pi 5's certified PCIe Gen2 ceiling (~500 MB/s): 1.6 / 2.5 / 4.1 / 7.8 tok/s.
findings.note: Realistic LRU hit rates for this 128-expert/top-8 shape from the verified datapoints: ~55-66% with a ~13-15% cache (Cacheable-by-Design 66% at 13.4%; Discussion #27149 56%; SeqMoE LRU 60% at 15%), ~75-85% with a ~31-35% cache (SeqMoE LRU 74% at 25%, 84% at 35%; paddock 82-90%); prediction/frequency-aware policies add ~10-20 points (SeqMoE 84.6% at 15%, 95% at 35%; FlashMoE +21% over LRU; HybriMoE +5-8 pts). So a 2 GB cache lands near 60% (LRU) to ~80% (predictive); 4 GB near 80% (LRU) to ~92% (predictive).

open_questions: No published measurement of Gemma 4 26B-A4B expert-cache hit rates or consecutive-token reuse was found (PR #27861 lists Gemma4-26B as tested but reports no Gemma-specific hit rate; the gemma4-moe-offload README has no data yet); the Qwen3-30B-A3B profile (same 128-expert/top-8 shape, no shared expert) is the closest proxy, but Gemma 4 has a shared expert, which the ICLR'26 paper associates with lower local routing consistency.

The numeric LRU hit-rate-vs-k curve in the Eliseev & Mazur paper (Fig. 2 left) and the exact per-model cache sizes in the Qualcomm Mixtral/Phi runs were not extractable from the pages; both should be read from the PDFs if cited.
The 'Adaptive Expert Split' locality statistics (top-20% -> ~80%, 60-70% reuse) came via a lossy PDF summary and are marked unverified.

The KTransformers SOSP'25 PDF and the Raspberry Pi 5 product brief PDF could not be parsed by the fetch tool; ktransformers numbers come from the GitHub tutorial, Pi 5 PCIe facts from the M.2 HAT+ documentation page, and microSD/USB3 bandwidths are taken from the task prompt, not re-verified.

All CPU-only storage-streaming evidence found (Discussion #27149, Qualcomm phones, SmallThinker, EdgeMoE) used 3-6 GB/s laptop NVMe, UFS, or unspecified storage; nobody has published MoE expert streaming at 90-800 MB/s, so the I/O-bound table is extrapolated and ignores microSD random-read penalties and the Pi 5's ~17 GB/s-class LPDDR4X compute ceiling (not verified here).

Whether a Pi-class CPU can actually consume ~3.35 MB expert chunks at full storage bandwidth while also computing 3.8B active parameters per token (CPU cycles for I/O, page-cache copies, dequantization) is unmeasured; Discussion #27149 on an M1 shows compute and I/O are already comparable at 3-6 GB/s.

Energy: the SSD-offload-considered-harmful result (up to ~12x energy/token vs HBM) suggests storage streaming is costly per token even when latency is acceptable; no edge-device energy numbers were found.
research.summary: Prior art splits into four generations. (1) Dense-sparsity flash streaming: Apple's LLM in a Flash (M1 Max/M2 Ultra CPU and RTX 4090; windowing + row-column bundling; OPT 6.7B per-token 3182 -> 669 ms on CPU, ~4-5x; ~20x on GPU; half the model in DRAM) and PowerInfer-2 (TurboSparse-Mixtral-47B at 11.68 tok/s on a 24 GB OnePlus 12 with CPU+NPU, 2.13 tok/s with 7 GB; 24.6x vs llama.cpp). Both need ReLU-sparsified models, not stock MoEs. (2) GPU + host-DRAM expert offload for Mixtral-class models: Eliseev & Mazur's LRU cache + speculative loading + 2-bit HQQ experts (T4 0.66 -> 2.09 tok/s, ~3x over naive offload), Pre-gated MoE, Fiddler (compute experts on CPU when transfer costs more than compute), MoE-Infinity (request-level activation tracing, 3.1-16.7x), AdapMoE, HOBBIT (low-precision substitutes on miss; 13-19x vs llama.cpp on Jetson Orin), ExpertFlow (91.96% hit with a learned path predictor), ProMoE (84.7%-accurate stride predictor, ~2x), MoE-Lightning (batch throughput), eMoE, HybriMoE and DALI (both on kTransformers), and kTransformers itself (DeepSeek-V3 13.7 tok/s but 382 GB-1 TB DRAM). Every one of these uses a GPU; none streams from storage at edge bandwidths. Hermes is a layer-pipelining paper with no MoE content. (3) Edge/CPU-only work: EdgeMoE (Jetson TX2, Raspberry Pi 4B CPU, Switch Transformers; 1.19-2.77x), Qualcomm's cache-conditional experts (CPU-only llama.cpp on Snapdragon phones: plain LRU still misses 22-40% of expert fetches with 30-45 experts/layer cached; cache-aware re-routing drops that to 7-21% for >2x speedup at 0.1-3% perplexity cost), SmallThinker (model co-designed for prefetch from storage: 15.5 tok/s on a phone under 8 GB vs 0.18 tok/s for stock Qwen3-30B-A3B), and llama.cpp Discussion #27149 (M1, 16 GB, Qwen3-30B-A3B streamed from a ~3-6 GB/s NVMe: 56% calibrated-LRU hit, 44.2% consecutive-token expert overlap, 3.8-4.7 tok/s). (4) 2025-26 cache-policy and router-training work: SeqMoE's cross-model LRU curve (60/74/84/88% hit at 15/25/35/45% residency; predictive 85/92/95/97%), FlashMoE (+21% hit over LRU on SSD-offloaded OLMoE/Qwen3-30B-A3B), MaskCoFT, MELINOE, ReMoE, Cache-Aware Joint Router Adaptation, and the pre-registered negative result 'Cacheable by Design?' (training routers for locality breaks a 1% perplexity gate; Qwen3-30B-A3B shows P(reuse next token)=0.444 vs 0.223 chance, an LRU cache of 13.4% of experts serves 66% of fetches, 95% of traffic goes through 52.5% of experts; Qwen3-235B streamed from a 2.4 GB/s SSD decodes at 0.44 tok/s, exactly SSD-bound). Locality is model-dependent: ICLR'26 SRP ranks Qwen3 (54) and OLMoE (51) high and DeepSeek-V2-Lite (38, shared experts) and Qwen1.5-MoE (31) low; fine-grained 256-expert DeepSeek-V4-Flash gives LRU only 8-18% at 4.5% capacity (oracle 46%), and skew ranges from Gini ~0.76 (Qwen3.5-122B) to nearly flat. Batching destroys the effect (Qwen3-30B-A3B touches 6.3% of experts per layer at batch 1 but 62% at batch 32 and 47-97% in prefill). Critical assessment for a Gemma 4 26B-A4B-class model (128 experts, top-8 + 1 shared, 30 layers; 5.95M params/expert = 3.35 MB at Q4; 240 routed-expert visits = 0.80 GB/token at 0% hit; expert pool 12.9 GB): a 2 GB cache is ~15% of experts and the verified evidence puts plain LRU at ~55-66% hit there, ~80% with a frequency/prediction-aware policy; 4 GB (~31%) gives ~75-85% LRU and ~90-92% predictive. That leaves 320 MB (60%) to 64 MB (92%) of expert reads per token. Dividing by bandwidth: microSD at 90 MB/s caps decode at 0.3-1.4 tok/s even in the best case, so it is not viable; a USB3 SSD at 350 MB/s yields ~1.1-5.5 tok/s (1.7-2.9 at the realistic 75-85% band); NVMe at 800 MB/s yields 2.5-12.5 tok/s (4-6.6 realistic) but on a Pi 5 that bandwidth needs the uncertified Gen 3 override, the certified Gen 2 ceiling of 500 MB/s gives 2.5-4.1 tok/s realistic. These are I/O-only ceilings assuming expert-contiguous layout (36x fewer page faults than interleaved GGUF), perfect prefetch overlap, and RAM for the ~1.35 GB of dense weights outside the expert budget; nobody has measured MoE expert streaming below ~2.4 GB/s, the only sub-GB/s datapoints (EdgeMoE HDD/SD) are for Switch Transformers, and SSD offload costs up to ~12x energy per token versus memory-resident weights. The practical levers with evidence behind them are cache-aware re-routing (Qualcomm, Cacheable-by-Design: 60-80% miss reduction at 1-3.4% perplexity), 2-bit cold-expert tiers (HOBBIT: <=1% accuracy loss, ~43% fewer bytes per miss), and prediction-driven prefetch (SeqMoE/SpecMD/ProMoE: +10-25 hit points over LRU).

checked.claim: LLM in a Flash (Apple) targets dense ReLU-sparse models (OPT 6.7B, Falcon 7B relufied, Persimmon 8B, Phi-2, Llama-2 7B sparsified), not MoE; windowing k=4-5; row-column bundling; M1 Max 1TB / M2 Ultra 2TB SSD CPU runs (>6 GiB/s linear, 2.25 GiB/s random at 32 KiB / 32 threads) + RTX 4090; ~half model in DRAM (52.1% OPT 6.7B); Table 3 OPT 6.7B CPU 3182->669 ms, GPU 2218->84 ms; 13.4 GB -> 0.2 GB per token.
checked.correction: All numbers verified on the arXiv HTML: models and sparsity (OPT 97%, Falcon relufied 95%, Llama-2 FATReLU 90%, Persimmon squared ReLU, Phi-2 2.7B) are dense, none MoE; M1 Max 1TB SSD and M2 Ultra 2TB SSD; 24 GB RTX 4090 Linux box (bf16); '>6 GiB/s for a 1GiB linear read'; 2.25 GiB/s appears in Table 2 as the bundled-read throughput; 32-thread reads; DRAM 52.1% (OPT) and 52.93% (Falcon); Table 3 rows exactly 2196+986=3182 vs 105+58+506=669 (CPU) and 2196+22=2218 vs 30+34+20=84 (GPU); 13.4 GB -> 0.9 GB (predictor+window) -> 0.2 GB (all). Refinements: window is k=4 for OPT/Falcon/Persimmon (OPT reserves DRAM for the past 5 tokens) but k=2 for Llama-2; the paper states both 'up to 4x and 20x' (abstract) and '4-5x / 20-25x' (body). Verified.

checked.claim: PowerInfer-2 runs TurboSparse-Mixtral-47B on OnePlus 12 (24 GB, UFS 4.0, Snapdragon 8 Gen 3) at 11.68 tok/s with ~50% FFN weights offloaded, 2.13 tok/s at 7 GB; 24.6x (up to 27.8x) vs llama.cpp, 3.84x (up to 4.63x) vs LLM-in-a-Flash; CPU+NPU hybrid, GPU avoided; UFS 4.0 4 GB/s seq @512 KB, ~1 GB/s random 4 KB; second device OnePlus Ace 2 (16 GB, UFS 3.1); requires TurboSparse variant.
checked.correction: Numbers verified: OnePlus 12 = 24 GB DRAM (19 GB usable), UFS 4.0, Snapdragon 8 Gen 3; OnePlus Ace 2 = 16 GB (11 GB usable), UFS 3.1, Snapdragon 8+ Gen 1; 11.68 tok/s; 2.13 tok/s at 7 GB; 24.6x (up to 27.8x) over llama.cpp and 3.84x (up to 4.63x) over LLMFlash (Sec. 1 and 7.2.1); UFS 4 GB/s sequential with 512 KB blocks, 1 GB/s 4 KB random; NPU does hot neurons, CPU cold neurons, GPU deliberately not used. One coupling is NOT directly stated: Sec. 7.1 sets the default to 50% of FFN weights offloaded (75% only for Mixtral-47B on the Ace 2), whereas the 11.68 tok/s figure comes from Sec. 7.2.3 / Fig. 10 'at maximum memory utilization (19GB)', where the paper says it is 3.12x LLMFlash and 21.2x llama.cpp; the paper does not state the offload fraction at the 19 GB point. Do not hard-code '11.68 tok/s at exactly 50% offload' as a paper statement. Verified except that pairing (uncertain).

checked.claim: MoE-Infinity (RTX A5000, PCIe 4.0, 32 GB-1 TB host DRAM): request-level Expert Activation Matrix tracing, cosine-matched EAMC (~120 entries suffice), prefetch/eviction with layer-proximity decay; 3.1-16.7x per-token latency vs vLLM/Ollama/DeepSpeed/BrainStorm; at bs=1 <5% of experts repeatedly activated for ~100-expert models, Mixtral ~25%; DeepSeek-V2-Lite TPOT 155 vs 485 (vLLM) vs 737 ms (DeepSpeed); host-DRAM offload only, no SSD.
checked.correction: Verified: 'NVIDIA RTX A5000-24GB', PCIe 4.0 (setup text quotes 24 GB/s measured, 32 GB/s nominal elsewhere), host DRAM 32 GB (DeepSeek) / 64 GB (Switch) / 128 GB (Mixtral) / 256 GB (NLLB) / 1 TB (Arctic); 'increasing the capacity from 1 to 120 allows all MoE models to achieve their lowest average latency'; '3.1-16.7x per-token latency improvements'; 'fewer than 5% of experts are repeatedly activated when decoding tokens for a single request' and 'only 25% activation per request' for Mixtral; TPOT 155/485/737 ms; full model resides in host memory, no SSD streaming. Verified.

checked.claim: Fiddler: experts in host DRAM, computed on CPU for small batches (CPU when cpu_lat(s) < gpu_lat(s) + trans_lat); weight transfer ~2-5x longer than GPU compute; Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB + Xeon Gold 6126 (PCIe 3 x16) and RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB + Xeon 8480+ (PCIe 4); Mixtral-8x7B fp16, 56/256 or 125/256 experts on GPU; 1.26x single-batch, 1.30x long prefill, 11.57x beam search, 1.65x vs Mixtral-offloading long prefill; GPU required; later version validates Phi-3.5-MoE.
checked.correction: Verified: Algorithm 1 runs on GPU iff weights resident or cpu_lat(s) > gpu_lat(s) + transfer_lat(), else CPU (equivalent to the claim); Appendix A: transfer 'about 2-5 times longer than the actual computation time'; Env 1 Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB + Xeon Gold 6126 (48-core) PCIe Gen3 x16 32 GB/s; Env 2 RTX 6000 Ada (paper writes 49 GB) + Xeon Platinum 8480+ (112-core) PCIe Gen4 x16 64 GB/s; 56/256 and 125/256 experts on GPU; 1.26x, 1.30x, 11.57x (beam search vs llama.cpp), 1.65x vs Mixtral-Offloading on long prefill; Phi-3.5-MoE in Appendix E (6.5x vs DeepSpeed-MII). Minor: paper says 49 GB not 48 GB for the Ada card. Verified.

checked.claim: KTransformers: MLA attention/KV/shared expert on one GPU, routed experts in CPU DRAM with AMX kernels + expert deferral; DeepSeek-V3/R1 671B Q4_K_M on dual Xeon Gold 6454S (64 cores) + RTX 4090D: prefill 82.94 (8 exp) / 97.32 (6 exp) tok/s, decode 12.2 / 13.69 vs llama.cpp 10.31 / 4.51 (up to 3.03x decode, 9.44x prefill); 382 GB (single socket) to 1 TB DRAM, >=14 GB VRAM; experts in DRAM not SSD.
checked.correction: Verified against the tutorial's V0.2 table (500-token prompt): dual-socket 6 experts 97.32 prefill / 13.69 decode; 8 experts 82.94 / 12.208 (claim rounds to 12.2); llama.cpp 10.31 / 4.51; 'The highest speedup reaches up to 3.03x in decoding and 9.44x in prefill'; Xeon Gold 6454S 32 cores x 2 sockets = 64 cores; 4090D 24 GB; 382 GB DRAM single socket / 1 TB dual, at least 14 GB VRAM; AMX + cache-friendly layout. Caveats: (a) 'expert deferral' is NOT in the tutorial text (it is a SOSP'25 paper term, unverified here); (b) later tables (V0.2.1: 101 prefill / 13.9 decode at 8K; V0.3-preview: up to 286.55 prefill, 'up to 27.79x vs llama.cpp') give higher numbers, so cite the V0.2 table explicitly. Verified.

checked.claim: Eliseev & Mazur Mixtral offloading: LRU cache k=2 (12 GB) / k=4 (16 GB), speculative expert loading (next layer's gate on current hidden state; Fig. 2 ~60-90% recall preloading 1-2 experts 1-10 layers ahead), HQQ 4-bit attn + 2-bit experts 17.54 GB / 3-bit 21.37 GB / 4-bit 23.99 GB; Table 2 tok/s T4 2.092 / 3060 2.278 / 3080M 2.655 / A100 3.061 vs naive 0.661 / 0.919 / 1.059 / 1.392; without cache & preloading 1.168 / 1.547 / 1.758 / 2.265; README says speculative prefetching not yet implemented.
checked.correction: Verified on ar5iv: 'we use k=2 for 12GB GPUs and k=4 for 16GB ones'; speculative loading applies next layer's gating function to previous layer's hidden states; Table 1 sizes 23.99 / 21.37 / 17.54 GB; Table 2 rows exactly as claimed for all four GPUs and three columns; 'some experts are reused between adjacent tokens'. README (github.com/dvmazur/mixtral-offloading) confirms 'Some techniques described in our technical report are not yet available in this repo' with 'Speculative expert prefetching' listed as upcoming. UNCERTAIN sub-item: the Fig. 2 recall range ('~60-90%') is only a visual reading of a plot; the text gives no numeric recall, and a second reading of the same figure gave ~40-80%. Do not hard-code a recall number from this paper. Everything else verified.

checked.claim: Pre-gated MoE (ISCA 2024): pre-gate at block N emits expert mask for block N+1 for prefetch from CPU DRAM over PCIe; A100 80 GB + EPYC 7V12 (1.8 TB DDR4), PCIe Gen4 32 GB/s; Switch Transformer Base/Large 8-128 experts; 1.7x avg vs on-demand offload, 81% of oracle GPU-only throughput, 4.2x lower peak GPU memory (23% of GPU-only), small accuracy degradation on some tasks; requires fine-tuning.
checked.correction: Verified: ISCA-51 (2024); 'a pre-gate function for the N-th MoE block is trained to generate the activation masks to utilize in the (N+1)-th MoE block'; A100 80 GB HBM, AMD EPYC 7V12 64-core with 1.8 TB DDR4, PCIe gen4 32 GB/s; Switch Base 8/64/128 experts and Large 128 experts (26.4B params, 105.6 GB); '1.7x (max 1.9x)' latency reduction per MoE block vs on-demand, 81% of GPU-only throughput, 4.2x peak memory reduction (23% of GPU-only); fine-tuning required. Nuance: paper's own wording is 'no noticeable degradation in LLM model accuracy' (Table II competitive), slightly stronger than 'small degradation on some tasks'. Verified.

checked.claim: SwapMoE (ACL 2024): dynamically updated compact 'Virtual Experts' set in main memory (importance = sum ||x||*||G(x)_i||*||E_i||), async amortized swapping from storage; Jetson Nano (4 GB) and Jetson AGX Orin; Switch Transformer summarization memory 14.2 GiB -> 4.7 GiB (-67%), 50% lower latency, Rouge-2 -0.041; other setting -37% memory / -18% latency at -0.012 Rouge-2; routes only within in-memory subset.
checked.correction: Verified: importance(E_i,X)=sum_{x in X_i} ||x||*||G(x)_i||*||E_i||; Jetson Nano (4 GB max) and Jetson AGX Orin; 'reduce the memory consumption from 14.2 GiB to 4.7 GiB', 50% latency reduction, Rouge-2 drop 0.041; '37% and 18%' memory/latency reductions with 0.012 Rouge-2 degradation on Jetson AGX; Masked Gating restricts routing to Virtual Experts. Venue: the arXiv HTML does not name the venue, but the ACL Anthology entry 2024.acl-long.363 (ACL 2024 Long Papers, pp. 6710-6720, Bangkok) confirms ACL 2024. Verified.

checked.claim: AdapMoE: sensitivity-based adaptive gating skips ~25% of expert activations vs top-2 without accuracy loss; next-layer prefetching ~90% prediction accuracy on most layers; layer-aware cache allocation (more cache to early layers); Mixtral-8x7B/8x22B at 4-bit and 4+2-bit on RTX 4090 and A6000; 1.35x average latency reduction vs Mixtral-Offloading; GPU + CPU/SSD offload.
checked.correction: Verified: 'reducing the average number of activated experts by 25%' with no accuracy degradation; 'most layers ... achieving rates around 90%'; DP-based layer-aware allocation storing more early-layer experts on GPU; Mixtral-8x7b and 8x22b; '4+2 bit will quantize the attention blocks into 4bit and MoE blocks into 2bit' plus 4-bit; RTX 4090 and A6000; 'average 1.35x vs. Mixtral-Offloading'. Caveat: the paper's experiments do not explicitly state whether inactive experts sit in CPU DRAM or SSD (it only mentions 'CPU memory, SSDs, or Flash storage' generically), so 'CPU/SSD offload' is a generic description, not a measured SSD result. Verified.

checked.claim: HOBBIT (on llama.cpp): token-level low-precision expert substitutes on cache miss, layer-level adaptive prefetch (96% next-layer accuracy), sequence-level multidimensional cache (LRU/LFU/LHU/FLD); Jetson AGX Orin (32 GB unified, 12 CPU cores) and RTX 4090 (24 GB) + 256 GB DRAM, Samsung 980 PRO (7 GB/s); Orin int8: 13.0x (Mixtral-8x7B) / 18.9x (Phi-3.5-MoE) decode vs llama.cpp; 4090 fp16: 3.21x vs Mixtral-Offloading; accuracy drop <=1%.
checked.correction: Verified: built on Llama.cpp (8,000 lines C/C++); next-layer top-1 prediction 'averaging 96% across layers' (~90% for 2-3 layers ahead); cache policies LRU, LFU, LHU, FLD; Orin '32GB of unified memory, shared with its 12 CPU cores'; 4090 24 GB + 256 GB host DRAM + 64 CPU cores; Samsung 980 PRO 'theoretical read speed of 7,000 MB/s (around 3,000 MB/s in practice)'; 13.0x and 18.9x decode speedups on Orin; 3.21x vs MoE-Offloading on 4090; accuracy drop 'no more than 1%'; Orin int8 (int2 substitutes), 4090 fp16 (int4 substitutes). Refinement: cite the SSD as ~3 GB/s measured, not 7 GB/s, if used as an I/O datapoint. Verified.

checked.claim: ExpertFlow (DAC'26): transformer routing-path predictor (~95% in-domain, 5-10 pt cross-domain drop), token scheduling, Predictive Locality-aware Expert Cache; 91.96% hit ratio (up to 61.15 pts better than LRU on Switch-32), up to 93.72% GPU-memory reduction, 2.01x/3.19x/5.86x on Switch-32/64/128 and ~2x on Mixtral-8x7B and Qwen1.5-MoE; A40 48 GB + Xeon Gold 6338.
checked.correction: Verified: DAC '26 (July 26-29, 2026, Long Beach); T5-style encoder-decoder predictor, 'over 90% accuracy in most in-domain cases', 'over 95%' only on Qwen1.5, '5-10%' cross-domain drop; abstract: 'cache hit ratio of 91.96%, outperforming LRU by up to 61.15%' and 'up to 93.72%' memory reduction (Switch-128 15.26 GB -> 1.03 GB); '2.01x, 3.19x, and 5.86x speedups over SE-MoE on Switch-32/64/128' at CS=16, BS=32; Mixtral 1.99x vs Cache-MoE, Qwen1.5 2.12x; A40 48 GB + Xeon Gold 6338. Corrections: the 'on Switch-32' attribution for the 61.15 figure is not in the text (the Switch-32 comparison shown is PLEC 91.90-85.91% vs LRU 76.61-58.37%, a 15-36 pt gap); the abstract gives 61.15% as an 'up to' without naming the model, and it is written as a percent, not explicitly 'points'. '~95%' should be stated as 'over 90% typical, >95% on Qwen1.5'. Cache size for the 91.96% figure is not stated. Verified with those caveats.

checked.claim: ProMoE: learned predictor on intermediate hidden states predicts experts several layers ahead ('stride' prefetch; 84.7% avg accuracy, -5 pts with stride); RTX 4090 24 GB + i9-14900K + 128 GB DRAM, PCIe 4.0 32 GB/s; DeepSeek-MoE 16.4B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite 15.7B, Qwen1.5-MoE 14.3B, Qwen2-MoE 57.4B, Mixtral-8x7B; 2.20x (up to 3.21x) prefill and 2.07x (up to 5.02x) decode vs open-source offloading; 1.78x/1.34x vs hand-crafted caches; predictor runs on CPU.
checked.correction: Verified: small MLP predictor on layer inputs; stride prefetching increases prediction distance and pipelines prediction with prefetch; '84.7%' average accuracy, declines 'by 5%' with stride; RTX 4090 24 GB GDDR6X, i9-14900K, 128 GB host DRAM, PCIe 4.0 32 GB/s unidirectional; model table 16.4B/2.8B, 15.7B/2.7B, 14.3B/2.7B, 57.4B/14.2B, Mixtral 46.7B/12.9B; prefill 2.20x (up to 3.21x), decode 2.07x (up to 5.02x) vs open-source offloading; 1.78x (up to 2.48x) prefill and 1.34x (up to 1.79x) decode vs static/LRU caches; 'ProMoE executes the predictor on the CPU'. Verified.

checked.claim: KEY NUMBERS gemma4_26B_A4B_config: hidden_size 2816, moe_intermediate_size 704, num_experts 128, top_k 8, layers 30, 1 shared expert, total 25.2B, active 3.8B.
checked.correction: config.json (google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it) text_config: hidden_size 2816, intermediate_size 2112 (dense/shared FFN), moe_intermediate_size 704, num_experts 128, top_k_experts 8, num_hidden_layers 30, num_attention_heads 16, num_key_value_heads 8, head_dim 256, vocab_size 262144, sliding_window 1024, enable_moe_block true, model_type gemma4, architectures Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration. Model card table: Total 25.2B, Active 3.8B, Layers 30, Expert Count '8 active / 128 total and 1 shared', vision encoder ~550M. checked.claim: KEY NUMBERS: q4_0_gguf_GB 14.6, q8_0_gguf_GB 26.9 for Gemma 4 26B-A4B-it.
checked.correction: Matches ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF exactly: gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q4_0.gguf 14.6 GB, gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q8_0.gguf 26.9 GB, BF16 50.5 GB (plus mmproj-BF16 1.19 GB, mtp-Q4_0 252 MB, dflash-Q8_0 472 MB). Other repos differ, so hard-code the repo id with the size: bartowski/google_gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF Q4_0 14.76 GB / Q8_0 26.86 GB / Q4_K_M 17.04 GB; google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf ships gemma-4-26B_q4_0-it.gguf at 14.4 GB (official QAT); unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF has NO Q4_0 (Q8_0 26.9 GB, MXFP4_MOE 16.6 GB, UD-IQ4_NL 13.6 GB, UD-Q4_K_M 16.9 GB); unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-GGUF UD-Q4_K_XL 14.2 GB. checked.claim: KEY NUMBERS gemma4_derived_at_4p5_bpw and streamed_MB_per_token / io_bound_tok_per_s tables (5.95M params per routed expert, 3.35 MB, 240 visits/token, 0.8 GB at 0% hit, 12.9 GB pool, 20/40 experts per layer in 2/4 GB; 322/201/121/64 MB at 60/75/85/92% hit; tok/s grids at 90/350/500/800 MB/s).
checked.correction: Inferred (arithmetic from verified config): 3 x 2816 x 704 = 5.947M params per routed expert; x 4.5/8 = 3.35 MB; 30 layers x 8 = 240 visits; 240 x 3.35 MB = 804 MB ~ 0.8 GB; 128 x 30 x 3.35 MB = 12.86 GB; 2 GB / 12.86 = 0.155, 4 GB = 0.31; 2000 MB / 3.35 / 30 = 19.9 -> 20, 40 for 4 GB; 804 x (1-h) = 322/201/121/64 MB; bandwidth / MB-per-token reproduces every tok/s cell (e.g. 90/322 = 0.28, 500/64 = 7.8, 800/64 = 12.5). Assumptions not verified from a primary source: that all 30 layers carry a routed-MoE block (config has a single enable_moe_block true, no per-layer pattern), that each routed expert is exactly gate+up+down of 2816x704, and the 4.5 bpw figure (Q4_0 GGUF at 14.6 GB over 25.2B params is ~4.6 bpw including non-expert tensors). Attention/shared-expert/embedding bytes are excluded from the per-token I/O model by design.
