verify.summary: Adversarial re-check of 12 prior-art claims plus the load-bearing Gemma 4 numbers, all against primary sources (arXiv HTML, ar5iv, ACL Anthology, GitHub, HF config.json / model card / GGUF trees). Result: 12/12 literature claims CONFIRMED on every hard number (per-token latencies, tok/s, GB sizes, speedup factors, expert counts, hardware). No claim refuted. Caveats worth carrying into scripts/prose: (1) PowerInfer-2's 11.68 tok/s is the 19 GB max-memory point of the Fig. 10 sweep (3.12x LLMFlash / 21.2x llama.cpp there); the paper does not state the FFN offload fraction at that point, 50% is the Sec. 7.1 default for the 24.6x/27.8x averages. (2) Mixtral-offloading Fig. 2 recall '60-90%' is a plot reading with no textual number; drop it. (3) ExpertFlow's 61.15 is 'up to 61.15%' in the abstract with no model named; the Switch-32 text shows a 15-36 pt LRU gap; 95% accuracy is Qwen1.5-specific. (4) KTransformers 'expert deferral' is not in the tutorial (SOSP paper term); numbers are the V0.2 table, 12.2 is 12.208. (5) HOBBIT's 980 PRO is ~3 GB/s measured, 7 GB/s theoretical. (6) SwapMoE venue ACL 2024 confirmed via Anthology, not arXiv. Gemma 4 26B-A4B: config confirmed (2816 / 704 / 128 experts / top_k_experts=8 / 30 layers; key name is `top_k_experts`, not `top_k`), model card 25.2B / 3.8B / 1 shared confirmed, GGUF 14.6 GB Q4_0 and 26.9 GB Q8_0 match ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF exactly (bartowski 14.76/26.86, Google QAT q4_0 14.4, unsloth has no Q4_0), and all derived per-token I/O arithmetic reproduces. One datapoint could not be sourced: the 44.2% consecutive-token expert-sharing figure attributed to llama.cpp discussion 27149 is not in that thread (3.81/4.10/4.7 tok/s, 56%, 263->31 MB all are).

research.topic: Prior art for running a dense ~30B LLM with RAM far smaller than the weights, and for the hypothesis "resident cheap base approximation + stream only decision-relevant residual corrections" (nested/progressive precision, residual VQ, low-rank/sparse decompositions, training-free activation sparsity, early exit, CPU/offloaded speculative decoding, logit-margin guarantees)

findings.claim: Matryoshka Quantization (MatQuant, Google, ICML 2025): exploits that int4/int2 are nested in the MSBs of int8; trains one int8 model so MSB slices are usable. Gemma-2 9B (OmniQuant base): int8 74.59%->74.05%, int4 74.33%->73.83%, int2 60.24%->63.35% (+3.11). Naively slicing an int8 OmniQuant baseline gives int4 72.26% and int2 38.11% (collapse). Abstract: int2 extracted by MatQuant beats standard int2 by up to 4% (OmniQuant) / 7% (QAT); layer-wise Mix'n'Match at 2.05 average bits reaches 68.25%.
findings.note: NOT post-training-free: OmniQuant variant learns scales/shifts by gradient descent on 128x2048 calibration samples (~10M tokens, 20M for int2); QAT variant trains end-to-end on 100M C4 tokens. Paper reports no bandwidth/memory-traffic savings, only flexible precision from one artifact.

findings.claim: Any-Precision LLM (2024): post-training (no training, <1 min for 7B). Starts from a 3-bit SqueezeLLM-style non-uniform seed and 'incrementally upscales' one bit at a time (each cluster split in two, parent bits inherited), storing weights as BITPLANES so that 3..n-bit models overlay in the footprint of a single n-bit model. Llama-2-7B WikiText2: 3-bit 6.13, 4-bit 5.62 (vs 5.61 independently quantized), 8-bit 5.47 = FP16 5.47. RTX 4090 mat-vec speedups vs FP16: 3.99x (3-bit), 3.03x (4-bit), 1.56x (8-bit). Paper states that with bitplanes 'any runtime request of reduced bit-width directly translates into proportional speedup, as we can simply load the specified amount of bits'.
findings.note: This is the direct storage-layout prior art for 'base in RAM (MSB planes) + residual (LSB planes) elsewhere'. It selects precision per request, not per token/decision.

findings.claim: AnyBCQ (ICLR 2026): binary-coded quantization storing weights as binary bit-planes plus scale factors; progressive precision expansion refines scale factors while reusing previously assigned binary codes, giving monotonic accuracy as bits are added; kernels give up to 3.0x throughput over half precision and 1.2x over prior multi-precision methods, competitive at 2-bit.
findings.note: Bit-plane layout with per-request precision; abstract does not state training requirement explicitly (PTQ family).

findings.claim: Drop-by-Drop (Jun 2026): multi-bitwidth post-training quantization built on AQLM additive codebooks with Matryoshka-style supervision so codebook PREFIXES give accurate partial reconstructions; precision is lowered at inference by dropping codebooks. Theory: Gaussian sources are successively refinable under a weighted-MSE distortion motivated by LLM loss, i.e. 'successive refinement across distortion levels incurs no rate penalty relative to encoding at each level separately'. Evaluated on Qwen, LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral; lower perplexity than SOTA multi-bitwidth methods.
findings.note: Theoretical support that a 'base codebook + residual codebooks' split need not cost extra bits versus a monolithic 4-bit encoding.

findings.claim: BitStack (ICLR 2025): training-free iterative absolute-value decomposition (W = sign ⊙ |W|; SVD of |W| with small rank, sign packed to 1 bit) producing residual blocks of ~1 bit/parameter that are universally sorted by importance and loaded/offloaded between storage and RAM at megabyte granularity (blocks 0.66-29.13 MB at k=16). Llama-3.1-70B zero-shot avg: ~3-bit 77.0 vs AWQ 77.5; ~4-bit 78.3 vs AWQ 79.1. Triton kernels 3-10x faster than naive PyTorch; latency comparable to GPTQ.
findings.note: Closest published 'residual blocks streamed from storage' design, but blocks are chosen statically by available memory, not per token/decision. The 8B ~3-bit row as read (63.1 vs AWQ 68.8) looks inconsistent with the 2-bit row; re-check Table before quoting.

findings.claim: QuIP# (ICML 2024): weight-only PTQ with randomized Hadamard incoherence + E8P lattice codebook (2-bit), residual VQ (2-bit E8P + 1-bit E8 for 3-bit), then fine-tuning within each block plus layernorms/sign vectors/LM head on 256 RedPajama sequences. WikiText2 (ctx 2048): Llama-2-7B FP16 5.47 -> 2-bit 6.66 / 3-bit 5.79 / 4-bit 5.56; 13B 4.88 -> 5.74 / 5.10 / 4.95; 70B 3.32 -> 4.16 / 3.56 / 3.38. Llama-2-70B 2-bit decodes at 32.74 tok/s (56.84% of peak bandwidth).
findings.note: Post-training with calibration-time fine-tuning of non-quantized parameters (no pretraining). 2-bit costs ~+18-25% perplexity at 13B-70B.

findings.claim: AQLM (ICML 2024): additive multi-codebook quantization (weights = sum of codewords from several learned codebooks), input-adaptive, codebooks jointly optimized per transformer block on calibration data. Llama-2 at 2 bits/parameter on WikiText2: 7B 6.93 (1.81 above FP16), 13B 5.70, 70B 3.94; fast GPU and CPU kernels match/outperform FP16 speed.
findings.note: Post-training (calibration + codebook/block fine-tuning).

findings.claim: VPTQ (EMNLP 2024): post-training vector quantization using channel-independent second-order optimization, with residual and outlier quantization; at 2-bit reduces WikiText2 perplexity vs prior SOTA by 0.01-0.34 (LLaMA-2), 0.38-0.68 (Mistral-7B), 4.41-7.34 (LLaMA-3), QA accuracy +0.79-1.5% / 1% / 11-22%; 1.6-1.8x inference throughput vs SOTA; quantization time 10.4-18.6% of prior algorithms.

GPTVQ (2024): post-training vector quantization (1D/2D/4D codebooks) interleaving column quantization with Hessian-based updates of remaining weights; new SOTA size-vs-accuracy on Llama-v2 and Mistral; 3-11 h on one H100 for Llama-v2-70B; VQ gives better on-device (mobile CPU) latency than 4-bit integer format.

QTIP (NeurIPS 2024 spotlight): trellis-coded quantization with a stateful decoder decoupling codebook size from bitrate/dimension, enabling ultra-high-dimensional PTQ with hardware-efficient bitshift trellis; SOTA quality and inference speed versus VQ methods.
findings.note: Perplexity table not extracted.

findings.claim: SVD-LLM (ICLR 2025): post-training low-rank compression with truncation-aware data whitening and closed-form layer-wise updates; 256 WikiText-2 calibration samples. LLaMA-7B WikiText2: original 5.68 -> 20% compression 7.73, 40% 9.27, 60% 15.00, 80% 31.79 (ASVD at 20%: 11.14; at 40%: 1407). LLaMA-13B 20%: 5.09 -> 6.43; LLaMA-30B 20%: 4.10 -> 5.14. Memory reduction is near-linear in compression ratio.
findings.note: At ~30B scale, a 1.25x traffic reduction (20%) already costs ~+25% perplexity, worse than 2-bit VQ for the same bytes.

findings.claim: ASVD (2023/24): training-free activation-aware SVD that absorbs activation outliers into the weight matrix plus iterative sensitivity-based rank calibration; compresses networks by 10%-30% and KV cache by 50% without performance drop.

SliceGPT (ICLR 2024): post-training structured compression using computational invariance (PCA rotation absorbed into weights, rows/columns sliced, small Q^T Q matrices added on residual); calibration 1024 x 2048 tokens. Llama-2-70B WikiText2: dense 3.32 -> 4.25 (20%), 4.60 (25%), 5.05 (30%). Zero-shot at 25%: 69.75 (91% of dense 76.57) without recovery fine-tuning, 75.62 (99%) with RFT on Alpaca. Throughput 1.55x at 25% on H100.
findings.note: The headline 99% retention requires recovery fine-tuning; training-free is 91%.

findings.claim: LoSparse (ICML 2023): approximates each weight matrix as low-rank + sparse, but it is a TRAINING-TIME method (iterative pruning with importance scores while fine-tuning) evaluated only on DeBERTaV3-base, BERT-base and BART-large (GLUE MNLI-m 81.7% at 20% remaining ratio, 79.7% at 10%); no decoder-only LLM tested.
findings.note: Not applicable post-training to a 30B dense LLM.

findings.claim: TEAL (ICLR 2025 spotlight): training-free magnitude thresholding of the INPUT hidden states of every linear layer (Q,K,V,O, gate, up, down), letting the corresponding weight columns be skipped 'during memory transfer'. Llama-3-8B WikiText2: 0% 5.87 / 25% 5.94 / 40% 6.21 / 50% 6.67 / 65% 9.06; Llama-3-70B: 2.93 / 3.02 / 3.52 / 4.30 / 6.29. Downstream avg Llama-3-70B: 80.41 / 80.22 / 79.29 / 78.26 / 73.07; Llama-3-8B: 68.07 / 67.73 / 66.21 / 63.42 / 52.59. Wall-clock decode speedups up to 1.53x (40%) and 1.8x (50%) on A6000; 1.25-1.45x on A100. Compatible with 8-bit, 4-bit AWQ and 2/3-bit QuIP#; degradation 'compounds somewhat independently'.
findings.note: Best training-free sparsity for SiLU models: ~1.67-2x fewer block-weight bytes at 40-50%, with +20-47% perplexity at 70B; 65% is collapse territory. Does not sparsify the LM head.

findings.claim: CATS (2024): thresholds the SiLU gate output CATS_t(SiLU(x W_gate)) in gated MLPs (threshold = k-th percentile from 500 calibration samples), skipping up/down projection columns/rows for zeroed indices; MLP-only (applying to attention costs 4.3% relative). Zero-shot without fine-tuning: Mistral-7B base 69.94% -> 68.90% at 50% -> 67.09% at 70% (ReLUfication: 32.30%); Llama2-7B 65.89% -> 64.33% (50%) -> 61.43% (70%). ~15% latency gain, 18-21% throughput gain at 50% with custom kernel; optional fine-tuning of ~1% of params.
findings.note: MLP-only sparsity covers ~87% of block weights in Qwen2.5-32B (inferred from config); 70% MLP sparsity costs 4-7 points zero-shot.

findings.claim: R-Sparse (ICLR 2025): training-free, replaces linear layers with rank-aware sparse inference using sparsity of input channels plus singular-value components (no active-channel prediction needed); comparable performance at 50% model-level sparsity on Llama-2/3 and Mistral across ten tasks; 43% end-to-end efficiency improvement with custom kernels.

GRIFFIN (2024): training-free and calibration-free sequence-level selection of FFN 'experts' exploiting 'flocking' activation structure in non-ReLU models; with 50% of FFN parameters, little to no degradation; 1.29x (Gemma 7B) and 1.25x (Llama 2 13B) speedups on an L40.

Deja Vu (ICML 2023): contextual sparsity for OPT-175B (ReLU MLPs): up to 80% of attention heads and 95% of MLP neurons can be skipped per input; small 2-layer MLP predictors per layer are trained on recorded activations and run asynchronously one layer ahead; accuracy maintained to ~75% sparsity; >2x latency vs FasterTransformer, 4.8-6x vs HuggingFace at batch 1. On BLOOM (non-ReLU) MLP sparsity is only ~30% vs 85% for OPT, attributed to the activation function.
findings.note: The 10-20x traffic reductions of Deja Vu/PowerInfer/LLM-in-a-flash rest on ReLU sparsity that dense SiLU/GELU models do not have.

findings.claim: Sirius (NeurIPS 2024): contextual sparsity 'significantly degrades the model performance for reasoning, deduction, and knowledge-based tasks'; sparse and dense models share problem-solving logic and need only a few token corrections; correction mechanism yields ~20% latency reduction for an 8B model on-chip and ~35% for a 70B model with offloading, evaluated on 6 models and 8 reasoning/math/coding tasks.
findings.note: Warns that perplexity-level 'minimal degradation' from sparsity can hide large reasoning losses.

findings.claim: Turbo Sparse (2024): replaces SwiGLU with dReLU and continues pretraining on 150B tokens (<1% of a 15T-token pretraining); FFN sparsity reaches 90%; only 2.5B of Mistral-7B's parameters (4.3B of Mixtral-47B) activated per token; OpenLLM leaderboard avg 63.65 vs Mistral-7B 61.57; 2-5x decoding speedup with PowerInfer; TurboSparse-Mixtral-47B at 11 tok/s on a OnePlus 12 phone.
findings.note: Requires retraining (ReLU-fication + 150B tokens).

findings.claim: ProSparse (2024/25): ReLU substitution plus progressive sparsity regularization (multi-stage sine schedule) and activation threshold shifting; sparsity 89.32% (LLaMA2-7B), 88.80% (LLaMA2-13B), 87.89% (MiniCPM-1B) with performance comparable to the Swish originals; up to 4.52x inference speedup.
findings.note: Requires training.

findings.claim: Q-Sparse (2024): top-K activation sparsification with straight-through estimator; requires training (from scratch, continue-training, or fine-tuning; no training-free setting tested). Continue-trained Mistral-7B: 3.8B activated params scores 63.7 avg vs dense 7.0B at 64.6; 2.9B activated scores 61.7. Inference-optimal sparsity ratio ~45.58% for full-precision models.

LayerSkip (ACL 2024): layer dropout (higher for later layers) + shared early-exit loss during training, then self-speculative decoding (draft from early layers, verify with the remaining layers, shared KV). Training required: continual pretraining 52B tokens for Llama2 7B/13B, 419B tokens for Llama3 8B, 839B tokens for Llama3.2 1B; pretraining-from-scratch runs used 26B tokens. Speedups: 1.86x CNN/DM (Llama2 7B, 12 speculations; abstract: up to 2.16x), 1.83x HumanEval, 2.0x TOPv2. Llama3 models showed a larger drop in last-layer accuracy.
findings.note: Not post-training; verification still reads all layers, so weight traffic is amortized, not eliminated.

findings.claim: CALM (NeurIPS 2022 oral): early exit for T5 (encoder-decoder) with per-token confidence (softmax response, hidden-state saturation, trained classifier) calibrated via Learn-then-Test to give provable 'textual consistency' (bounded expected textual distance from the full model) or 'risk consistency' at a user-specified tolerance; uses one-third to one-half of decoder layers on average, ~50% compute reduction on TPU, up to ~3x speedup.
findings.note: Statistical (distribution-level) guarantee, not a per-token argmax certificate; requires training exit heads/classifier. arXiv PDF 2207.07061 could not be parsed by the fetch tool.

findings.claim: Fast yet Safe: Early-Exiting with Risk Control (NeurIPS 2024): distribution-free, post-hoc risk control that tunes the exit mechanism so 'exits only occur when the output is of sufficient quality', meeting user-specified performance goals on vision and language tasks with substantial compute savings.

FlexEE (Sep 2026): self-speculative, KV-compatible early exiting for offloading-aware inference; needs layer-wise exit supervision (training); speedups 1.27x / 3.16x on Llama2-7B and 1.25x / 2.83x on Llama3-8B under 0% / 50% weight offloading, with minimal accuracy degradation.

SubSpec (NeurIPS 2025): lossless, training-free speculative decoding for offloaded LLMs; the draft shares GPU-resident layers and the KV cache with the target and replaces the offloaded layers with 4-bit (HQQ, group 64) substitute weights. Qwen2.5-32B under a 24 GB VRAM limit (RTX 4090, i7-13700K, PCIe 4.0 x16, 128 GB DDR5): 0.52 -> 6.33 tok/s (12.50x); average acceptance length 27.53 on MT-Bench (greedy); 9.1x for Qwen2.5-7B at 8 GB VRAM. No CPU-only or flash-offload setting is discussed.
findings.note: Shows that a same-model low-bit draft is extremely well aligned (tau ~27), so target-weight traffic is amortized ~27x while remaining exactly lossless. But the 4-bit draft must be RESIDENT in fast memory.

findings.claim: SpecExec (2024): parallel speculative decoding generating up to 20 tokens per target iteration; runs 50B+ LLMs on consumer GPUs with RAM offloading at 4-6 tok/s (4-bit weights) or 2-3 tok/s (16-bit), exploiting the spikiness of token probabilities.

QSpec (2024): speculative decoding pairing a low-precision joint (weight+activation) quantized draft with a high-precision weight-only quantized verifier that share weights and KV cache; up to 1.64x speedup without quality degradation, no retraining or auxiliary models.
Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023): 2x-3x acceleration with identical outputs (exact sampling from the target distribution) and no retraining or architecture change.
findings.note: The only family of techniques here that is exactly lossless w.r.t. the full model while reducing per-token target-weight traffic.

findings.claim: HiRE (2024): cheap low-dimensional/low-precision computation predicts the top-k rows/columns with high recall, then exact computation is restricted to the predicted subset, applied to the softmax LM head and FFN (top ~5% of FFN parameters); on a 1B model it nearly matches pretraining/downstream accuracy and speeds decoding 1.47x on one TPUv5e.
findings.note: Direct precedent for 'cheap approximation first, exact computation only where it can matter', but applied within a layer rather than to streamed weight residuals.

findings.claim: Zhou et al. (Sep 2026, 'The Undetected Damage of Quantization on Retrieval'): a quantized model that keeps classification accuracy still changes 14-46% of top-1 retrieval results; the top-1 is guaranteed to survive quantization only when the gap between the two highest scores exceeds twice the largest rounding error; this gap is measurable without labels and, per input at deployment time, indicates whether the quantized answer matches full precision; proposed fix routes low-gap inputs to full precision.
findings.note: The explicit margin-vs-error argmax criterion the hypothesis needs, but stated for the scoring layer's rounding error, not propagated through 64 transformer layers.

findings.claim: QEBVerif (2022/23): computes guaranteed quantization-error bounds between a DNN and its QNN (weights and activations quantized) via layer-by-layer differential reachability analysis, falling back to an exact MILP encoding.
findings.note: Formal certification exists only for small networks; no LLM-scale propagation of such bounds was found.

findings.claim: MarginGate (May 2026): uses the logit margin between top predictions to trigger exact verification only on low-margin decoding steps (18.56% of steps on Llama-3.1-8B, 15.05% on Qwen2.5-14B), restoring 100% sequence-level deterministic decoding at 2.23x / 1.99x lower latency than constant verification (MATH500, GSM8K, HumanEval, SharedGPT).
findings.note: Empirical evidence that only ~15-19% of tokens are margin-fragile in that (BF16 batch-invariance) setting.

findings.claim: MARS (Jan 2026): training-free, domain-agnostic margin-aware verification for speculative decoding that relaxes exact-match acceptance when the target logit margin shows weak decisiveness, giving consistent speedups while preserving generation quality.

'When Is a Draft Accepted?' (Jun 2026): shows speculative acceptance is governed by local ranking/threshold events; gives exact certificates and sharp margin-based bounds for strict greedy and relaxed (additive/multiplicative) acceptance; rejection regions are lower level sets of the target distribution; relaxed/tree criteria enlarge certified acceptance.

Approximate Speculative Decoding (Aug 2026): accepts selected draft mismatches under a local target-logit regret gate, per-block exception cap and request-level regret budget; training-free, reduces to greedy verification at zero budget; +3.05%-15.26% throughput (avg 7.78%) over strict verification.

MoBiQuant (Feb 2026): token-adaptive any-precision PTQ with a token-aware router choosing each token's weight precision and 'many-in-one recursive residual quantization' to reconstruct higher-precision weights at runtime; up to 1.34x throughput over SOTA any-precision methods while matching single-precision PTQ.
findings.note: Closest published per-token precision selection; residual bits are read for the whole token, not gated by the decision margin.

findings.claim: FlexQuant (2025): post-training dynamic precision switching driven by perplexity entropy and KL divergence; 1.3x end-to-end speedup with negligible accuracy loss. PMPD (2024): phase-aware precision (higher in prefill, progressively lower deeper into the generated sequence); 1.4-12.2x mat-vec speedup over fp16 on Nvidia GPUs, 3.8-8.0x on NPUs, up to 1.54x over uniform quantization.
findings.note: FlexQuant source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12024

findings.claim: GitHub 'precision-escalation' (unpublished): implements the hypothesis almost verbatim — 3-bit resident weights, entropy-gated escalation to higher precision with residual bit-planes to be fetched from RAM/NVMe. On Qwen3-8B/WikiText-2 (RTX 3090 Ti), escalating 22.5% of tokens to bf16 recovers 43% of the 3-bit->bf16 quality gap (27% for random escalation); at 42.7% escalation, 68% (vs 48%). The README states 'No speed or memory measurements: the residual fetch/recompute pipeline is not built'; results are simulated, earlier claims were withdrawn, no paper or peer review.
findings.note: Marked unverified because it is a non-peer-reviewed repo with simulated results; included as the only direct attempt at margin/entropy-gated residual streaming found.

findings.claim: LLM in a flash (Apple, ACL 2024): stores weights in flash and loads on demand; windowing (k=5 recent tokens) plus row-column bundling; relies on ReLU FFN sparsity (OPT 6.7B FFN is 97% sparse) and a low-rank activation predictor, loading only ~2.4% of FFN neurons per token (10% without windowing); DRAM ≈ half the model; M1 Max flash ~6 GiB/s sequential; OPT 6.7B per-token 669 ms on CPU (105 ms I/O) and 84.64 ms on GPU (30.55 ms I/O); runs models up to 2x DRAM with 4-5x (CPU) / 20-25x (GPU) speedups over naive loading. Also tested sparsified Falcon 7B, Persimmon 8B, Phi-2, Llama 2.
findings.note: The per-token I/O savings come from ReLU-level sparsity; for dense SiLU models the same framework would stream nearly all weights.

findings.claim: PowerInfer (2023/24): hot neurons (power-law activation) preloaded on GPU, cold neurons on CPU, adaptive predictors and neuron-aware sparse operators; up to 11.69x over llama.cpp on an RTX 4090; OPT-30B reaches 82% of an A100's generation rate; OPT-175B supported. PowerInfer-2 serves TurboSparse-Mixtral-47B on a smartphone at 11.68 tok/s (up to 27.8x over SOTA frameworks) with negligible accuracy degradation using neuron-cluster scheduling and a segmented neuron cache.
findings.note: PowerInfer-2 source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06282. Both depend on ReLU-sparse (OPT / ReLU-fied / TurboSparse) models.

findings.claim: ActiveFlow (Apr 2025): first DRAM-flash active-weight swapping framework for modern NON-ReLU LLMs on phones: cross-layer active-weight preloading, sparsity-aware self-distillation (adjusts weights to match dense outputs, i.e. a training step), and a DRAM-flash swapping pipeline; claims the performance-cost Pareto frontier (no numbers in abstract). Ripple/Neuralink (arXiv 2410.19274): co-activation-aware neuron placement in flash for smartphones, 1.49x end-to-end latency improvement.
findings.note: Ripple source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19274 (the fetched abstract reports 1.49x end-to-end; the '5.93x I/O latency' figure seen in search snippets was not verified).

findings.claim: llama.cpp: a model larger than RAM 'runs' via mmap page faults, but users report disk at 100% and 'minutes per token' (discussion #638). PR #25294 adds SSD streaming only for MoE routed experts (O_DIRECT, per-layer expert slot cache, 73-79% hit rate, GLM-5.2 ~254 GB on 128 GB unified memory at 1.83-2.20 tok/s decode) and states dense models cannot benefit because every weight is used on every token.
findings.note: Discussion: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/638

findings.claim: Dense ~30B GGUF sizes: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (33B params) Q8_0 34.82 GB, Q6_K 26.89, Q5_K_M 23.26, Q4_K_M 19.85, Q4_K_S 18.78, IQ4_XS 17.69, Q3_K_M 15.94, IQ3_XS 13.71, Q2_K 12.31, IQ2_M 11.26 GB. Google gemma-3-27b-it QAT Q4_0 GGUF is 17.2 GB and the card claims 'similar quality as bfloat16' (no numbers given).
findings.note: Gemma source: https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-3-27b-it-qat-q4_0-gguf. The user's '16-18 GB at 4-bit' corresponds to IQ4_XS/Q4_K_S-class or Gemma-3-27B QAT Q4_0.

findings.claim: Qwen2.5-32B config.json: hidden_size 5120, intermediate_size 27648, 64 layers, 40 attention heads / 8 KV heads, vocab 152064, tie_word_embeddings false, hidden_act silu.

From that config: per layer attention ≈ 62.9M params (q,o 5120x5120; k,v 5120x1024) and MLP ≈ 424.7M (3 x 5120 x 27648) → MLP is ~87% of block weights; 64 blocks ≈ 31.2B; untied LM head 0.78B; so ≈ 32.0B parameters are touched per decoded token (input embedding only one row). Per-token weight traffic ≈ 17.8 GB at 4.46 bpw (IQ4_XS), 19.6 GB at 4.89 bpw (Q4_K_M), ≈ 8.4 GB at ~2.1 bpw (QuIP#/AQLM-class), 12.6 GB at 3.16 bpw (Q2_K).
findings.note: Computed from verified config and llama.cpp bpw figures; ignores KV-cache reads (grows with context) and norm/bias tensors.

findings.claim: At 100-800 MB/s streaming, a dense 4-bit ~32B model (≈17.8 GB/token) takes ≈ 22-178 s per token; 2-bit VQ (≈8.4 GB) ≈ 10.5-84 s; 2-bit + 50% TEAL on block weights (≈4.3 GB incl. 0.2 GB LM head) ≈ 5.4-43 s; a lossless SubSpec-style verifier streaming 17.8 GB once per tau=27.5 accepted tokens would need only ≈ 0.65 GB/token of streamed traffic (≈ 0.8-6.5 s/token) but requires the ~8.4 GB (2-bit) or ~17.8 GB (4-bit) draft to be resident in RAM and tau for a 2-bit draft is unmeasured.
findings.note: Arithmetic from the verified sizes above and SubSpec's tau; SubSpec's tau=27.53 was measured with a 4-bit draft against a bf16 target, so it is an upper bound for a 2-bit draft vs 4-bit target.

findings.claim: Margin-gated residual streaming (the hypothesis) would, if 15-43% of tokens trigger escalation (MarginGate 15-19% of steps; precision-escalation 22.5-42.7%), average ≈ 1.2-3.4 GB/token of residual traffic for a 2-bit residual over 32B params (plus the resident base read from RAM every token) — a 5-15x cut versus streaming all 4-bit weights, but NOT lossless: the only simulation available recovers just 43-68% of the quality gap, and no published layer-wise criterion exists for fetching residuals of only some matrices.
findings.note: Combines verified gate rates with the inferred traffic model; escalation requires the full residual for all layers of that token because the margin is only known after the base forward pass.

findings.claim: Raspberry Pi 5: LPDDR4X-4267 SDRAM (1/2/4/8/16 GB), 'PCIe 2.0 x1 interface for fast peripherals', 'microSD card slot, with support for high-speed SDR104 mode', '2 × USB 3.0 ports, supporting simultaneous 5Gbps operation', Gigabit Ethernet.
findings.note: PCIe 2.0 x1 = 5 GT/s with 8b/10b ≈ 500 MB/s raw and SDR104 ≈ 104 MB/s bus maximum (inferred from the interface names). Secondary reports of ~840-900 MB/s NVMe reads require forcing unsupported Gen 3 and ~90 MB/s for the best microSD cards were seen only in search snippets (Tom's Hardware, Jeff Geerling) and are unverified here. The official product-brief PDF exceeded the fetch size limit.

findings.claim: Bit-serial / digit-serial DNN accelerators already implement 'stop reading bits once the decision is determined': BitFair (12-nm bit-serial CNN accelerator) learns per-layer thresholds that terminate when partial sums reliably predict a zero ReLU output, with adaptive bit ordering (4.0-22.1x effective energy-efficiency gains); MINT computes most-significant-digit-first so computation stops once the desired precision is reached (avg 5.64 bits VGG-16 / 6.04 bits ResNet-18, <2% accuracy loss vs INT8, 26-33% higher throughput). BitSET (ACM TACO) reports 48% fewer bit-level computations and 1.5x speedup with no accuracy loss.
findings.note: MINT: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31514. BitSET page returned HTTP 403 — its numbers come from the search snippet only (unverified). These are CNN/ReLU-output early-termination schemes, not LLM argmax certificates.

research.summary: Prior art splits into five families. (1) Nested/progressive precision — MatQuant (needs OmniQuant/QAT training; int2 slices of Gemma-2 9B 63.35% vs 38.11% for naive slicing), Any-Precision LLM (post-training bitplanes; 4-bit upscaled 5.62 vs 5.61 ppl, 8-bit = FP16; 'load only the bits you need'), AnyBCQ, Drop-by-Drop (AQLM codebook prefixes; successive refinement of Gaussian weights has no rate penalty), BitStack (~1-bit residual blocks streamed from storage, 70B ~4-bit 78.3 vs AWQ 79.1) and MoBiQuant (per-token precision router). These give the exact storage layout the hypothesis needs (MSB/base resident, LSB/residual elsewhere) with little or no bit penalty, but none gates residual fetches on the current decision. (2) Residual/vector PTQ (QuIP#, AQLM, VPTQ, GPTVQ, QTIP): 2 bits/weight is viable at 13B-70B with +18-25% WikiText2 perplexity (Llama-2-70B 3.32→4.16 QuIP#, 3.94 AQLM), i.e. a 2x traffic cut versus 4-bit; all use calibration data and light block fine-tuning but no pretraining. (3) Low-rank/structured (SVD-LLM, ASVD, SliceGPT; LoSparse is training-time and encoder-only): post-training 20-25% parameter cuts already cost +25-39% perplexity at 30B-70B — strictly dominated by 2-bit VQ per byte. (4) Activation sparsity: for dense SiLU/GELU models the training-free ceiling is ~40-50% (TEAL: Llama-3-70B ppl 2.93→3.52 at 40%, →4.30 at 50%, collapse by 65%; CATS/R-Sparse/GRIFFIN ~50% MLP-only); the 90-97% FFN sparsity behind Deja Vu, PowerInfer, LLM-in-a-flash (2.4% of FFN per token) exists only in ReLU models or after ReLU-fication plus ~150B tokens of continued pretraining (Turbo Sparse, ProSparse, Q-Sparse). Sirius shows contextual sparsity hurts reasoning disproportionately. (5) Early exit / speculative: LayerSkip, CALM, FlexEE need training (52B-839B tokens for LayerSkip); SubSpec/QSpec/SpecExec are training-free and exactly lossless — SubSpec's same-model 4-bit draft is accepted ~27.5 tokens per verification for Qwen2.5-32B (0.52→6.33 tok/s, 12.5x), the largest published per-token target-traffic reduction for a dense model, but the draft must be resident. Margin-based guarantees exist only in weak forms: Zhou et al. prove top-1 survives iff the top-2 gap exceeds 2x the maximum rounding error (scoring-layer only); MarginGate finds ~15-19% of steps margin-fragile; MARS/Approximate-SD/acceptance theory give margin bounds for speculative acceptance; CALM/risk-control give distribution-level consistency, QEBVerif certifies only small nets. Critical assessment for a dense ~31B at 4-bit (≈17-19.6 GB read per token; Qwen2.5-32B touches ≈32.0B params/token) at 100-800 MB/s: naive streaming is 22-178 s/token; the best published post-training single techniques each give ≤2x (2-bit VQ ≈8.4 GB/token at ~+20% ppl; TEAL 40-50% ≈1.7-2x with +20-47% ppl at 70B); stacking them reaches ≈4.3 GB/token (~4x) with compounding, un-benchmarked-at-30B loss. No published post-training technique cuts a dense SiLU model's per-token weight traffic by more than ~2x without measurable degradation EXCEPT lossless speculative verification, which moves the cost into a resident low-bit draft (≥8.4 GB at 2-bit) and unmeasured acceptance length for a 2-bit-vs-4-bit pairing. The specific 'margin-gated residual' idea has one unpublished, simulation-only attempt (43% of the 3→16-bit gap recovered at 22.5% escalation) and no layer-wise criterion; the lossless variant of the same idea is SubSpec-style verification with the residual read once per accepted block.

key_numbers.argmax_survival_condition: top-2 gap > 2 x max rounding error (Zhou et al. 2609.24322)
key_numbers.pi5_interfaces: LPDDR4X-4267; PCIe 2.0 x1 (~500 MB/s raw, inferred); microSD SDR104 (~104 MB/s bus, inferred); USB 3.0 5 Gbps

open_questions: Acceptance length (tau) of a 2-bit or 3-bit same-model draft against a 4-bit target is unpublished; SubSpec's tau=27.5 was 4-bit draft vs bf16 target. This single number determines whether lossless speculative verification can beat margin gating in the RAM-starved regime.

No published evaluation of 2-bit VQ (QuIP#/AQLM/VPTQ) stacked with 40-50% TEAL/CATS sparsity at ~30B dense scale; TEAL's paper tests QuIP# 2/3-bit combos on Llama but those tables were not extracted here, and Sirius suggests reasoning tasks degrade more than perplexity shows.

Is there any layer-wise or matrix-wise criterion (rather than token-wise) for deciding which residual blocks to fetch? None found; all margin gates (MarginGate, MARS, precision-escalation, Zhou et al.) operate on final logits after a full base pass, forcing a full-network residual fetch on escalation.

Zhou et al.'s 'gap > 2x max rounding error' certificate is for a single scoring layer; no work propagates a sound error bound through 60+ transformer layers at LLM scale (QEBVerif-style verification is limited to small networks), so a certified-lossless gate would likely trigger on nearly every token.

The precision-escalation repo is simulation-only (no residual fetch pipeline, no bytes/token or tok/s); its 43-68% gap recovery needs independent replication, and the remaining gap sits on tokens where the low-bit base is confidently wrong.

Flash/SD access pattern: TEAL input-channel sparsity skips weight columns; whether a transposed layout plus LLM-in-a-flash-style bundling achieves the predicted traffic reduction on SDR104/PCIe-2.0-x1 storage at 32 KiB+ chunk sizes is unmeasured for dense SiLU models.

Raspberry Pi 5 RAM bandwidth (bus width not stated on the product page) bounds even the resident base read: an 8.4 GB 2-bit base re-read per draft token would cap the draft at a few tokens/s at most; needs measurement.
Gemma-3-27B QAT Q4_0 (17.2 GB) card claims bf16-like quality without numbers; Google's Gemma 3 QAT quality tables should be checked before assuming 4-bit is 'free' for the base model.
BitStack's Llama-3.1-8B ~3-bit row as read (63.1 vs AWQ 68.8) looks inconsistent with its ~2-bit row; verify directly in the paper's Table before citing.
Ripple's '5.93x I/O latency' and the Pi 5 measured NVMe/microSD throughputs (~840-900 MB/s forced Gen 3, ~90 MB/s microSD) were seen only in search snippets and were not verified on primary pages.

checked.claim: MatQuant (Google, ICML 2025): Gemma-2 9B OmniQuant int8 74.59->74.05, int4 74.33->73.83, int2 60.24->63.35; sliced int8 baseline int4 72.26 / int2 38.11; abstract 'up to 4% / 7%'; layer-wise Mix'n'Match at 2.05 average bits reaches 68.25%; OmniQuant 128x2048 C4 (10M tokens, 20M for int2), QAT 100M C4 tokens.
checked.correction: All Table 1 numbers confirmed verbatim from arXiv HTML (verified): bf16 74.38; int8 Baseline 74.59 / MatQuant 74.05; int4 Sliced-int8 72.26 / Baseline 74.33 / MatQuant 73.83; int2 Sliced-int8 38.11 / MatQuant 63.35. Abstract 'up to 4% and 7% with OmniQuant and QAT' confirmed. ICML 2025 confirmed (PMLR v267, proceedings.mlr.press/v267/nair25a.html). Training details confirmed (128 x 2048 C4; 10M tokens, 20M for int2 baseline; QAT 100M C4 tokens). ONE MISLABEL: 68.25% at 2.050 avg bits is NOT 'layer-wise Mix'n'Match' - it is the 'Extra Precision MatQuant' int2 row of Table 7 (Gemma-2 9B, OmniQuant; MatQuant int2 63.35 -> E.P. MatQuant 68.25, log-pplx 3.187 -> 2.823). The Errata (Section 7) explains the extra ~0.05 bit comes from a missing-clamp bug that added an extra bucket (2^r+1 values); with co-distillation ([8,4,2,8->2]) it reaches 70.17 (Table 8). Mix'n'Match (Figure 3) merely uses that 2.050-bit model as its int2 endpoint. Do not hard-code '68.25 = Mix'n'Match'.

checked.claim: Any-Precision LLM (2024): post-training, <1 min for 7B; SqueezeLLM 3-bit seed + incremental upscaling; bitplane storage; Llama-2-7B WikiText2 3-bit 6.13, 4-bit 5.62 (vs 5.61 independent), 8-bit 5.47 = FP16 5.47; RTX 4090 mat-vec speedups 3.99x/3.03x/1.56x; 'proportional speedup' quote.
checked.correction: Verified from arXiv HTML v4 Table 3: Llama-2-7B Wiki FP16 5.47; SqLLM 3-bit 6.13, 4-bit 5.61, 8-bit 5.47; SqLLM+IU (any-precision) 3-bit '-' (the 3-bit seed IS the SqueezeLLM 3-bit model, so 6.13 is correct by construction), 4-bit 5.62, 8-bit 5.47. Table 6 RTX 4090, (1,4096)x(4096,4096): 3-bit 3.99x, 4-bit 3.03x, 8-bit 1.56x (the other two shapes give 4.67x/4.45x at 3-bit etc.). Quote in Section 5.1 verbatim. Table 5 runtime Llama-2-7B total 51.8 s (Seed Gen 36.2 + IU 15.6). Minor: when citing the 3-bit number note it is the SqueezeLLM seed, not a separately listed any-precision cell.

checked.claim: AnyBCQ (ICLR 2026): binary bit-planes + scale factors; progressive precision expansion reuses binary codes; monotonic accuracy; up to 3.0x over half precision and 1.2x over prior multi-precision methods; competitive at 2-bit.
checked.correction: Abstract verbatim confirms every element (bit-planes, scale factors, 'progressive precision expansion mechanism incrementally refines scaling factors while reusing previously assigned binary codes, yielding monotonic improvements', 'up to 3.0x over half precision and 1.2x over state-of-the-art multi-precision methods', 'narrows the accuracy drop in the low-bit regime (e.g. 2-bit)'). Comments line: ICLR 2026. Abstract does not state training/PTQ requirement - the researcher's note is accurate.

checked.claim: Drop-by-Drop (Jun 2026): multi-bitwidth PTQ on AQLM additive codebooks with Matryoshka-style supervision; precision lowered by dropping codebooks; Gaussian sources successively refinable under weighted-MSE, 'no rate penalty'; evaluated on Qwen, LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral.
checked.correction: arXiv 2606.12876 'Multi-Bitwidth Quantization for LLMs Using Additive Codebooks', submitted 11 Jun 2026 (rev. 26 Sep 2026). Abstract confirms the successive-refinability theorem wording verbatim and the four model families. AQLM is not named in the abstract but the body states 'Our method builds on AQLM ... we utilize AQLM as our additive-codebook building block, quantizing weights in 8-dimensional vectors' and 'we dequantize the weights from a prefix of the first k codebooks (k<=M)'; experiments use M in {3,4,5} codebooks of 8 bits each. Also a block-Hadamard rotation is applied (not mentioned in the claim).

checked.claim: BitStack (ICLR 2025): training-free iterative absolute-value decomposition, ~1 bit/parameter residual blocks, blocks 0.66-29.13 MB at k=16; Llama-3.1-70B zero-shot avg ~3-bit 77.0 vs AWQ 77.5, ~4-bit 78.3 vs AWQ 79.1; Triton kernels 3-10x; latency comparable to GPTQ. Note flags 8B ~3-bit 63.1 vs AWQ 68.8 as possibly inconsistent.
checked.correction: ICLR 2025 confirmed (iclr.cc/virtual/2025/poster/28531, openreview lBntjGbyv0). Table 1 (raw HTML) Llama 3.1 70B: 30691 MB (77%) AWQw3g128 77.5 vs BitStack 77.0; 38851 MB (71%) AWQw4g128 79.1 vs BitStack 78.3 - claim correct. Other 70B rows: 79% AWQw3 56.3 vs BitStack 75.5; 73% AWQw4 74.0 vs BitStack 78.4; 83% BitStack 71.1 vs AWQw2g128 29.8. Table 6 (k=16) block sizes 0.66 MB (Llama-3 8B k/v proj) to 29.13 MB (70B MLP) confirmed. '3x to 10x' Triton quote confirmed (Fig. 10b). The 8B 'inconsistency' is a row mix-up: at 69% (g128) AWQw3g128 68.8 vs BitStack 65.7; at 71% (no group) AWQw3 61.0 vs BitStack 63.1; at 75%/76% (2-bit) BitStack 42.4 / 30.8 vs AWQ 28.7 / 29.4. Memory column of Table 1 is in MB (e.g. 70B FP16 134570 MB).

checked.claim: QuIP# (ICML 2024): RHT incoherence + E8P 2-bit codebook, RVQ (2-bit E8P + 1-bit E8) for 3-bit, fine-tuning on 256 RedPajama sequences; WikiText2 ctx 2048 Llama-2 7B 5.47 -> 6.66/5.79/5.56; 13B 4.88 -> 5.74/5.10/4.95; 70B 3.32 -> 4.16/3.56/3.38; Llama-2-70B 2-bit 32.74 tok/s (56.84% peak BW).
checked.correction: All numbers verified in raw HTML Table 2 (context length 2048): FP16 5.47/4.88/3.32; QuIP# 2-bit 6.66/5.74/4.16; 3-bit 5.79/5.10/3.56; 4-bit 5.56/4.95/3.38. Throughput table: 2-70B 32.74 tok/s, 56.84% mem BW (RTX 4090). Section F.4: 'small development dataset of 256 sequences from RedPajama 1T', validated on 128 sequences, 5 epochs. 3-bit = '2 bit E8P codebook and a 1-bit E8 codebook'; 4-bit = E8P applied twice. Caveat for cross-paper comparison: the paper itself notes 'OmniQuant and AWQ use 2048 for Llama 2 while AQLM uses 4096'; QuIP# 2-bit 70B is 4.16 at both 2048 (with FT, Table 2) and 4096 (no FT, Table 1), but the FP16 baseline differs (3.32 @2048 vs 3.12 @4096).

checked.claim: AQLM (ICML 2024): additive multi-codebook, input-adaptive, codebooks jointly optimized per block; Llama-2 2-bit WikiText2 7B 6.93 (1.81 above FP16), 13B 5.70, 70B 3.94; fast GPU and CPU kernels match/outperform FP16 speed.
checked.correction: Numbers are from the v1 abstract (verified, cited URL is v1): 7B 6.93 '1.81 points from FP16', 13B 5.70, 70B 3.94. But the phrases 'input-adaptive', 'joint optimization of codebook parameters across each transformer blocks' and 'fast GPU and CPU implementations ... match or outperform optimized FP16 implementations for speed' appear only in the final abstract (v4, 11 Sep 2024, comments 'ICML, 2024') - cite v4 for those. The final Table 1 (ctx 4096; FP16 5.12/4.57/3.12) also reports BETTER 2-bit numbers than v1: 7B 6.59 @2.02 bits, 13B 5.60 @1.97 bits, 70B 3.94 @2.07 bits; with improved fine-tuning (AQLM*) 7B 6.14, 70B 3.83. AQLM evaluates at Llama-2 native context 4096 ('We used the same context length as models were trained on, for Llama 2 4096'), so its perplexities are not directly comparable to QuIP#'s ctx-2048 table.

checked.claim: VPTQ (EMNLP 2024): 2-bit perplexity reductions vs SOTA 0.01-0.34 (LLaMA-2), 0.38-0.68 (Mistral-7B), 4.41-7.34 (LLaMA-3); QA +0.79-1.5% / 1% / 11-22%; 1.6-1.8x throughput; quantization time 10.4-18.6%.
checked.correction: All ranges match the abstract verbatim; comments line 'EMNLP 2024, Main, Poster'.

checked.claim: GPTVQ (2024): post-training VQ (1D/2D/4D codebooks) interleaving column quantization with Hessian-based updates; SOTA size-vs-accuracy on Llama-v2 and Mistral; 3-11 h on one H100 for Llama-v2-70B; better mobile-CPU latency than 4-bit integer.
checked.correction: Abstract confirms Hessian-based updates, Llama-v2/Mistral, 'between 3 and 11 hours to process a Llamav2-70B model' on a single H100, and mobile-CPU latency advantage over 'a 4-bit integer format'. 1D/2D/4D is not in the abstract but the body reports 'Ours 1D / 2D / 4D' rows (also Mixtral-8x7B is evaluated); the body quantifies the mobile claim as 'a 10% increase in token rate compared to INT4 g128'. No conference venue stated on arXiv (v2, 3 Jun 2025).

checked.claim: QTIP (NeurIPS 2024 spotlight): trellis-coded quantization with stateful decoder decoupling codebook size from bitrate/dimension; hardware-efficient bitshift trellis; SOTA quality and inference speed vs VQ methods.
checked.correction: Abstract verbatim matches ('TCQ uses a stateful decoder that separates the codebook size from the bitrate and effective dimension', 'hardware-efficient bitshift trellis structure', 'state-of-the-art results in both quantization quality and inference speed'); comments: NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight. Perplexity table not checked (not claimed).

checked.claim: SVD-LLM (ICLR 2025): post-training low-rank compression with truncation-aware whitening and closed-form layer-wise updates; 256 WikiText-2 calibration samples. LLaMA-7B WikiText2 5.68 -> 7.73 (20%), 9.27 (40%), 15.00 (60%), 31.79 (80%); ASVD 11.14 / 1407; LLaMA-13B 5.09 -> 6.43; LLaMA-30B 4.10 -> 5.14; memory reduction near-linear.
checked.correction: Numbers exist (arXiv v5 Table 1/Table 3, ICLR 2025 confirmed via iclr.cc/virtual/2025/poster/30003), but the METHOD description is wrong and materially changes what the numbers mean. In the ICLR/v5 version the 'closed-form layer-wise update' of v1 was replaced by 'parameter update with sequential low-rank approximation', which the paper defines as 'a variant of LoRA fine-tuning ... apply LoRA on top of [U] and [V] separately', trained on 'Alpaca dataset with 50K samples for parameter update'. So 7.73/9.27/15.00/31.79, 6.43 and 5.14 are WITH fine-tuning on 50K Alpaca samples, not a 256-sample closed-form PTQ. The fine-tuning-free variant 'SVD-LLM (W)' (whitening only) gives LLaMA-7B 7.94 / 13.11 / 42.30 / 1349 and LLaMA-13B 6.61, LLaMA-30B 5.63 (v5 Tables 1, 3); v1 (closed-form update, no LoRA) reported 7.94 (20%), 13.11 (40%), 53.74 (60%), 13B 6.61, 30B 5.63. The 256 WikiText-2 calibration samples and 'near linear to the compression ratio' (Figure 4 caption) are confirmed. Key number svd_llm_llama30b_20pct_wiki2 '4.10 -> 5.14' should be '4.10 -> 5.63 (training-free) / 5.14 (with Alpaca-50K LoRA-style update)'.

checked.claim: ASVD (2023/24): training-free activation-aware SVD absorbing activation outliers into the weight matrix plus iterative sensitivity-based rank calibration; compresses networks by 10%-30% and KV cache by 50% without performance drop.
checked.correction: Abstract verbatim: 'training-free approach', outliers 'absorbed into the transformed weight matrix', 'efficient iterative calibration process ... varying sensitivity of different LLM layers', 'compress a network by 10%-30%', '50% KV cache reductions without performance drop in a training-free manner'. Note the 'without performance drop' qualifier is attached to the KV-cache claim in the abstract; the 10-30% weight compression is stated without that qualifier (SVD-LLM's Table 1 shows ASVD at 20% = 11.14 ppl vs 5.68 original).

checked.claim: KEY NUMBER matquant_gemma2_9b_int2_matquant_vs_sliced = 63.35% vs 38.11%
checked.correction: Table 1, Gemma-2 9B, OmniQuant: int2 MatQuant 63.35, Sliced int8 38.11 (int2 Baseline 60.24).

checked.claim: KEY NUMBER any_precision_llama2_7b_wiki2_3_4_8bit = 6.13 / 5.62 / 5.47 (FP16 5.47)
checked.correction: Table 3 (v4): 6.13 is the SqueezeLLM 3-bit seed (the any-precision column shows '-' at 3-bit because the seed is that model); 4-bit SqLLM+IU 5.62; 8-bit 5.47; FP16 5.47.

checked.claim: KEY NUMBER quip_sharp_llama2_70b_wiki2_fp16_vs_2bit = 3.32 -> 4.16 and aqlm_llama2_70b_wiki2_2bit = 3.94 (presented side by side)
checked.correction: Both numbers are real, but they are at different context lengths: QuIP# Table 2 is ctx 2048 (FP16 3.32 -> 4.16 with FT); AQLM Table 1 is ctx 4096 (FP16 3.12 -> AQLM 3.94 @2.07 bits; QuIP# listed there as 4.16 @2.01 bits; AQLM* with improved FT 3.83). If used in one table, state the FP16 baseline per row (3.32 vs 3.12) or use AQLM's ctx-4096 table for both.

verify.summary: Checked all 12 prior-art claims against raw arXiv HTML (curl + table extraction, not just the summarizer) plus venue pages. 11 confirmed, 1 refuted-on-method (SVD-LLM), with corrections that matter for hard-coding. (1) MatQuant: every Table 1 number and the training setup verified; venue ICML 2025 confirmed (PMLR v267); but '68.25% at 2.05 bits' is the 'Extra Precision MatQuant' int2 row of Table 7 (an extra quantization bucket from a missing-clamp bug documented in the Errata; 70.17 with co-distillation, Table 8), NOT layer-wise Mix'n'Match. (2) Any-Precision: all perplexities, 4090 speedups (3.99/3.03/1.56 for the 4096x4096 shape), 51.8 s runtime and the quote verified; the 3-bit 6.13 is the SqueezeLLM seed cell. (3) AnyBCQ, (4) Drop-by-Drop (AQLM dependence is in the body, M in {3,4,5} 8-bit codebooks), (8) VPTQ, (9) GPTVQ (1D/2D/4D in body; mobile gain quantified as +10% token rate vs INT4 g128), (10) QTIP, (12) ASVD all confirmed verbatim. (5) BitStack: ICLR 2025 confirmed; 70B rows 77.0 vs AWQw3g128 77.5 (77% compression) and 78.3 vs AWQw4g128 79.1 (71%) are correct; the flagged 8B inconsistency is a row mix-up (65.7 vs 68.8 at g128; 63.1 vs 61.0 no-group); block sizes 0.66-29.13 MB (k=16) confirmed. (6) QuIP#: all nine perplexities, 32.74 tok/s / 56.84%, 256 RedPajama sequences and the E8P + 1-bit E8 RVQ confirmed; table is ctx 2048. (7) AQLM: v1 numbers (6.93/5.70/3.94) confirmed from v1 abstract, but the 'input-adaptive' and GPU/CPU-speed wording is only in the ICML v4 abstract, whose Table 1 reports better 2-bit numbers (7B 6.59, 13B 5.60, 70B 3.94; AQLM* 3.83) at ctx 4096 (FP16 70B 3.12) - so the key-numbers juxtaposition of QuIP# 3.32->4.16 with AQLM 3.94 mixes context lengths. (11) SVD-LLM: numbers 7.73/9.27/15.00/31.79, 6.43, 5.14 exist in v5 (ICLR 2025 confirmed), but they require the paper's LoRA-variant 'sequential low-rank' parameter update trained on 50K Alpaca samples; the training-free whitening-only results are 7.94/13.11/42.30/1349 and LLaMA-30B 5.63, so the key number svd_llm_llama30b_20pct_wiki2 should read 4.10 -> 5.63 (training-free) / 5.14 (fine-tuned), and the 'closed-form layer-wise update' description is v1-only. The remaining KEY NUMBERS (GGUF sizes, llama.cpp bpw, TEAL/CATS/DejaVu, Pi 5 interfaces, etc.) were outside this claim set and were not checked here.

research.topic: Raspberry Pi AI accelerators and LLMs: Hailo-8/8L vs Hailo-10H, AI HAT+ 2 status, other Pi 5 accelerators, and feasibility of a ~25-30B model

findings.claim: Hailo-8 (26 TOPS) and Hailo-8L (13 TOPS) have no external DRAM at all: both product pages state 'Fully Integrated Memory - No External DRAM Required'; typical power 2.5 W (8) and 1.5 W (8L).
findings.note: 8L page: https://hailo.ai/products/ai-accelerators/hailo-8l-ai-accelerator-for-ai-light-applications/

findings.claim: Hailo-8L datasheet Rev 1.9.3 (April 2026) lists an NN core 'Up to 13 TOPs at 8-bit precision', dual Cortex-M4 MCU with '640 KB internal SRAM', 4-lane PCIe Gen3, and no DDR/DRAM interface anywhere in the feature list.
findings.note: PDF read locally with PyMuPDF; the NN-core weight memory size is not stated in the datasheet.

findings.claim: Hailo staff (Klaus Koschinsky, 15 Jun 2024) on running LLMs on Hailo-8/8L: LLMs 'would require 100+ context switches. This would require lot of work and RAM from the host', and 'We therefore have designed a new product called the Hailo-10H. It has a DDR interface and a local DDR memory on the module to free the host from the context switch management.'

Raspberry Pi's official AI HAT+ documentation marks 'Large Language Model (LLM) support: Not supported' for the original AI HAT+ (Hailo-8/8L) and 'Supported' for AI HAT+ 2, and says the AI HAT+ 2 'has its own 8 GB onboard memory, allowing it to run LLMs and VLMs up to ~6 billion parameters.'

Hailo-10H M.2 datasheet Rev 1.0 (June 2025): 40 TOPS INT4 / 20 TOPS INT8, 'equipped with 4GB or 8GB LPDDR4 memory' (part numbers HM22HB2C2FAE = 4 GB, HM22HB1C2FAE = 8 GB), PCIe Gen3 x4, 'consumes up to 8.25W and less than 2.5W under a typical workload', and the characteristic workload table lists 'QWEN2 1.5B @ 11 TPS' at 2.2 W.
findings.note: Product brief confirms 'ON-Module DDR 4|8GB LPDDR4/4X': https://hailo.ai/hailo-files/hailo-10h-m-2-et-product-brief-en/ and https://hailo.ai/products/ai-accelerators/hailo-10h-m-2-ai-acceleration-module/

findings.claim: Hailo staff (omria, 3 Nov 2025): the Hailo-10H memory interface 'runs at speeds up to 4266 MT/s with a 32-bit data bus (using 2 channels in lock-step mode)', giving 'around 17 GB/s as the maximum theoretical bandwidth'.
findings.note: This is the same class of bandwidth as the Pi 5's own LPDDR4X-4267, which is why decode speed on the HAT is not better than the Pi CPU (see CNX review).

findings.claim: Hailo Model Zoo GenAI (main branch = v5.4.0, Sep 2026) supports only: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (7.96 TPS), Llama3.2-1B-Instruct (9.89 TPS), Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct (8.06), Qwen2-1.5B-Function-Calling (6.69), Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (7.35), Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (8.13), Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct (4.78), Qwen2-VL-2B (7.04), Qwen3-VL-2B (4.74), Whisper Tiny/Base/Small. All LLM/VLM entries: context 2048, A8W4 (Qwen3-VL A16W4), TTFT 0.32-1.47 s. Largest text LLM is 1.7B; largest model is 2B.
findings.note: Release tags: v5.0.0 (22 Jul 2025) ... v5.3.0 (31 Mar 2026), v5.4.0 (16 Sep 2026): https://github.com/hailo-ai/hailo_model_zoo_genai/tags . README says the zoo requires a 'Hailo-10H module'.

findings.claim: Hailo's own LLM-on-10H engineering blog (29 Jul 2025): Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct runs at 9.45 TPS, TTFT 289 ms for 96 input tokens, 1.2 GB memory, KV-cache 2048 tokens; weights 'Static, 4-bit symmetric, group-wise', activations and KV-cache 8-bit.

Hailo GA press release (22 Jul 2025) claims 'first-token latency of under 1 second and over 10 Tokens per Second on a variety of 2B language and vision-language models' at 2.5 W typical; no larger models are named.

In April 2024 Hailo claimed the Hailo-10 'can run Llama2-7B with up to 10 tokens per second (TPS) at under 5W' with 8 GB LPDDR4 on module. As of the Sep 2026 model zoo no 7B/8B model has ever been published for the 10H.
findings.note: Claim quoted via CNX (secondary). The 'never shipped' part is inferred from the v5.4.0 MODELS.rst list; a June 2026 write-up also states 'they haven't shipped a downloadable 8B HEF for the chip' (https://mirkobrambilla.github.io/second-shelf/2026/06/25/raspberry-pi-5-hailo-10h-local-llms.html).

findings.claim: Users cannot compile their own LLM for the Hailo-10H. Hailo staff (Klaus Koschinsky, 25 Jun 2026): 'At the moment, it is not possible to compile your own LLM for Hailo. However, we do support LoRA, which allows you to add domain-specific knowledge to a supported model.'
findings.note: Consequence: you cannot bring a GGUF or an arbitrary HF checkpoint; only Hailo-published HEFs run via hailo-ollama.

findings.claim: The only community route to a custom LLM on Hailo-10H is a reverse-engineered DFC flow validated on a 25M-parameter LLaMA2-style toy model (24 Aug 2026); 'Status: experimental but functional' and 'Multi-token generation through the KV-cache path still degrades'.

A ~25-30B model is not feasible on the Hailo-10H: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 GGUF sizes are Q2_K 11.3 GB, Q3_K_S 13.3 GB, Q4_K_M 18.6 GB; Gemma-3-27B QAT Q4_0 GGUF is 17.2 GB. All exceed the 8 GB on-module DRAM even before KV-cache, and there is no supported path to compile such a model anyway.
findings.note: Gemma file size from https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-3-27b-it-qat-q4_0-gguf (page is gated; the 17.2 GB figure was visible in page metadata). Inference: sizes (verified) vs 8 GB (verified) vs no-custom-compile (verified).

findings.claim: Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ 2 announced 15 Jan 2026 at $130: Hailo-10H, '40 TOPS (INT4)', '8GB of dedicated on-board RAM', software = hailo-ollama backend + Open WebUI; named models DeepSeek-R1-Distill 1.5B, Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B, Qwen2.5-Instruct 1.5B, Qwen2 1.5B; Raspberry Pi says such edge LLMs 'typically run at 1-7 billion parameters'.

As of 4 Oct 2026 the raspberrypi.com product page and the product brief ('Published July 2026') list the AI HAT+ 2 at $200, 0-50 C ambient, in production until at least January 2036, 'Runs generative AI models efficiently using 8GB on-board RAM', and say users can 'fine-tune generative AI models using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)'.
findings.note: Brief PDF: https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/1319-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-2/documents/RP-009655-MM-6-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-plus-2-product-brief.pdf . Launch price was $130 (Jan 2026 news post, Jeff Geerling); the $200 figure is what the pages show today.

findings.claim: Raspberry Pi OS setup for AI HAT+ 2 uses a different package than the original HAT ('hailo-h10-all' vs 'hailo-all'; 'These packages can't co-exist'), plus the Hailo Model Zoo GenAI 5.1.1 Debian package and the 'hailo-ollama' server exposing a REST API.

Independent review (CNX Software, 20 Jan 2026, Hailo Ollama Server v5.1.1) measured decode tok/s Hailo-10H vs Pi 5 CPU: DeepSeek-R1 1.5B 6.72 vs 9.04; Qwen2 1.5B 5.89 vs 11.29; Llama3.2 3B 2.60 vs 4.78; Qwen2.5-Instruct 1.5B 6.74 vs 11.73; Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B 8.06 vs 10.26. Power: 7.2-7.6 W (HAT) vs 10.2-10.6 W (CPU). Reviewer: 'feels more like an AI decelerator than an AI accelerator', attributing it to being memory-bandwidth limited.

Jeff Geerling (15 Jan 2026): Hailo-10H max ~3 W vs ~10 W Pi SoC, but the Pi CPU 'trounces the Hailo 10H' on LLM decode, 'The 8 gigs of RAM holds back the LLM use case ... the most'; verdict 'a solution in search of a problem, in all but the most niche of use cases'; recommends a 16 GB Pi 5 instead for LLMs.

Hailo's own positioning: AI HAT+ 2 is 'not designed to be a replacement for cloud inference or large LLMs' (Hailo staff Nadav, 27 Jan 2026) and 'Large LLMs will always run better where compute and memory are effectively unconstrained' (Hailo blog, 19 Feb 2026, which also cites Qwen2.5-1.5B TTFT 320 ms on 10H vs 2039 ms on Pi 5 CPU).
findings.note: Blog: https://hailo.ai/blog/bringing-on-device-generative-ai-to-the-pi-when-and-why-youll-need-the-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-2/

findings.claim: Widely repeated blog claims that the AI HAT+ 2 runs 'Llama 3.2 1B at 30-50 tok/s' or 'Qwen2.5 at 20-35 tok/s' are not supported by any primary source: Hailo's own zoo lists Llama3.2-1B at 9.89 TPS and two independent reviews measured 2.6-8.1 tok/s.
findings.note: Treat these figures as marketing/SEO noise contradicted by the MODELS.rst and CNX measurements above.

findings.claim: llama.cpp has no Hailo, Coral/Edge TPU, or Axera backend; its backend table lists BLAS, BLIS, CANN, CUDA, HIP, Hexagon, IBM zDNN, MUSA, Metal, OpenCL, OpenVINO, RPC, SYCL, VirtGPU, Vulkan, WebGPU, ZenDNN. The RPC backend is described as 'proof-of-concept', 'fragile and insecure'.
findings.note: RPC README: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/tree/master/tools/rpc

findings.claim: Google Coral Edge TPU: '4 trillion (fixed-point) operations per second (4 TOPS), using only 2 watts'; models must be TensorFlow Lite with 8-bit int tensors, 'Tensor sizes are constant at compile-time', 'deep feed-forward neural networks such as convolutional neural networks (CNN)', LSTM 'Unidirectional LSTM only'. No transformer/attention/LLM support is documented. It is useless for LLM inference of any size.
findings.note: coral.ai redirects to this host. FAQ: https://gweb-coral-full.uc.r.appspot.com/docs/edgetpu/faq/ . The Edge TPU on-chip SRAM size was not stated on either page fetched, so it is not reported here.

findings.claim: M5Stack LLM-8850 / AI-8850 (Axera AX8850) M.2 2242 card: '24 TOPS @ INT8', '64-bit LPDDR4x, 4266 Mbps, 8GB capacity', 'PCIe 2.0 x2', '7W @ 3.3V', Raspberry Pi 5 listed as tested host; runs 'CNN, Transformer, CLIP, Whisper, Llama3.2, Qwen3, InternVL3'.
findings.note: CNX (31 Jan 2026): kit ~$215; Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct 15.03 tok/s on Pi 5 vs Hailo-10H 6.74 on the same model: https://www.cnx-software.com/2026/01/31/24-tops-m5stack-ai-8850-llm-accelerator-m-2-kit-offers-an-alternative-to-raspberry-pi-ai-hat-2/

findings.claim: Community GGUF backend for AX8850 on Pi 5 (woolcoxm): Qwen3-0.6B Q4_K_M 24.5 t/s decode, Qwen3.5-0.8B ~27 t/s; only sub-1B models tested; card peak memory ~0.9 GB for the 0.8B model.

A 7B is the practical ceiling on an 8 GB Axera card: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct GPTQ-Int4 on AX650 runs 4.8 tok/s (w4a16) with max context 1024 (Axera HF card); on a Pi 5 + Sipeed Maix4-HAT (24 Feb 2026) Qwen2.5-7B int4 measured 'avg 4.26 token/s' and 'avg 4.30 token/s', TTFT ~930 ms, card CMM 7040 MiB total; another Pi 5 + AX8850 user reports Qwen2.5-7B int4 occupying '4983 / 7040 MiB CMM'.
findings.note: Maix4-HAT write-up: https://nickshek.github.io/article/2026-02-24-Setup-ax650-on-rasiberrypi5.html ; CMM figure: https://github.com/focal55/arlowe-firmware/issues/153 (opened 25 Sep 2026, vendor figures only).

findings.claim: A USB form factor of the Hailo-10H exists (UP Shop 'Hailo-10H USB AI Accelerator [8 GB RAM]', USB 3.1 Gen2 Type-C, $239) but it carries the same 8 GB on-module ceiling and the same Hailo-only model list, so it changes nothing for large models.
findings.note: Pi 5 compatibility of the USB variant was not verified.

findings.claim: No accelerator helps with a 25-30B model on a Pi 5. Every Pi-attachable NPU with LLM support (Hailo-10H, Axera AX8850/AX650) has 8 GB (~7 GB usable) of on-card DRAM; a 30B-class model needs 11-19 GB of weights at Q2-Q4, and llama.cpp cannot use any of these NPUs at all. The only thing that runs a 30B-class model on a Pi 5 is the CPU with 16 GB RAM, and only if the model is a sparse MoE.
findings.note: Derived from: 8 GB on-module (Hailo datasheet, M5Stack docs), GGUF sizes (HF), no llama.cpp backend (llama.cpp README), Hailo no-custom-compile (community #19497).

findings.claim: Pi 5 16 GB CPU-only, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (30.5B total / 3.3B active MoE): Q3_K_S 2.70 bpw reaches 8.03 TPS at 94.18% of BF16 quality (ByteShape, 5 Jan 2026); Jeff Geerling independently measured 7.99 t/s tg128 and 8-10 t/s prompt processing with '-c 4096' to fit in 16 GB, noting it is 'maxing out the CPU for the entire time'.
findings.note: HN comment: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46520373 . Secondary sources; no accelerator involved.

findings.claim: Pooling three Pi 5s (16+16+8 GB) over llama.cpp RPC runs Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M at '~3.4-5.4 tok/s' with 32k context; the attached Axera LLM-8850 NPU in that mesh only serves a separate Qwen3-0.6B 'fast lane' and does not participate in the 30B model.
findings.note: Slower than a single 16 GB Pi running Q3_K_S; the RPC backend is PoC per llama.cpp docs.

findings.claim: A dense ~27B is worse: Gemma 3 27B QAT Q4_0 is 17.2 GB, over the 16 GB Pi 5 maximum; a Pi 5 benchmark blog (Apr/Sep 2026) ran Gemma 3 up to 4B (~3.5-5 tok/s), reported 12B 'doesn't fit' on 8 GB and did not run 27B at all.
findings.note: Gemma size from HF (gated page metadata). Secondary blog; conclusion that dense 27B is infeasible on any Pi 5 is inferred.

findings.claim: Raspberry Pi 5 ships with up to 16 GB LPDDR4X-4267, BCM2712 2.4 GHz quad Cortex-A76, and a single 'PCIe 2.0 x1 interface' for the HAT/M.2; the 16 GB model is listed at $305 on the product page today.
findings.note: Price as displayed 2026-10-04.

open_questions: AI HAT+ 2 price: launched at $130 (Jan 2026 news post, Geerling) but the raspberrypi.com product page and the July-2026 product brief now say $200; no official note on the change was found.

Hailo claimed 'Llama2-7B at up to 10 TPS' in April 2024 and Raspberry Pi docs say 'up to ~6 billion parameters', yet the largest shipped HEF as of v5.4.0 (Sep 2026) is 2B. Whether a 7B/8B HEF will ever be published is unknown.
Llama3.2-3B appears in the hailo-ollama 5.1.1 bundle (CNX review, Brambilla) but not in the v5.4.0 MODELS.rst; its current support status is unclear.
Coral Edge TPU on-chip SRAM size was not stated on the Coral pages fetched; the commonly cited 8 MB figure is therefore not reported as fact.
The Sipeed Maix4-HAT write-up names both AX650N and AX8850; which silicon the board actually carries was not resolved from a primary Sipeed page.
Hailo-10H USB variant: existence and 8 GB spec verified, but no evidence of it being tested with a Pi 5 or exposed via hailo-ollama.
Hailo-10H and Hailo-8/8L chip-level datasheets are Developer-Zone gated; the chip-internal SRAM sizes were not readable from public PDFs.
research.summary: Blunt answers. (1) Hailo-8 and Hailo-8L cannot run LLMs: both are DRAM-less ('No External DRAM Required' on Hailo's pages; the 8L datasheet lists no DDR interface), Hailo staff said in 2024 an LLM would need '100+ context switches' and host RAM, and Raspberry Pi's own docs mark LLM support 'Not supported' on the original AI HAT+. Only the Hailo-10H runs LLMs, because it has 4 or 8 GB of on-module LPDDR4/4X behind a 32-bit, 4266 MT/s interface (~17 GB/s theoretical, per Hailo staff). As of the Sep 2026 Model Zoo GenAI v5.4.0 the entire supported LLM/VLM set is 1-2B parameters (Llama3.2-1B 9.89 TPS, Qwen2.5-1.5B 7.35, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B 7.96, Qwen3-1.7B 4.78, Qwen2/3-VL-2B ~4.7-7.0; context 2048; A8W4). Hailo staff confirmed in June 2026 'it is not possible to compile your own LLM for Hailo' (LoRA on supported models only). The 2024 'Llama2-7B at 10 TPS' claim and Raspberry Pi's '~6B' ceiling have never materialised as a downloadable model. A 25-30B model is categorically infeasible on the 10H: even Q2_K of Qwen3-30B-A3B is 11.3 GB and Gemma-3-27B Q4_0 is 17.2 GB, both over the 8 GB DRAM, and there is no compile path anyway. (2) The Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ 2 (Hailo-10H, 8 GB, 40 TOPS INT4) launched 15 Jan 2026 at $130 (product page/brief now show $200), uses hailo-h10-all + hailo-ollama + Open WebUI. Independent measurements show it is slower than the Pi 5's own CPU for LLM decode on every model (CNX: 2.6-8.1 tok/s on the HAT vs 4.8-11.7 on the CPU; Geerling: the CPU 'trounces' it, 'a solution in search of a problem'); its real benefits are ~3 W power, freeing the Pi's CPU/RAM, and fast TTFT (320 ms vs 2039 ms on Qwen2.5-1.5B). Hailo itself says it is 'not designed to be a replacement for ... large LLMs'. (3) Other accelerators: Coral Edge TPU (4 TOPS, TFLite int8 feed-forward CNNs only) has zero LLM capability. The Axera AX8850 M.2 cards (M5Stack LLM-8850 / Sipeed Maix4-HAT, 24 TOPS INT8, 8 GB LPDDR4x, ~7 GB usable) are the most capable Pi 5 NPUs for LLMs: ~15 tok/s on 1.5B, ~25 tok/s on 0.6B via a community GGUF backend, and a 7B int4 at ~4.3 tok/s with ~5 GB of card memory used; 7B is their hard ceiling. llama.cpp has no backend for Hailo, Coral or Axera. For a ~25-30B model no accelerator helps at all. The only thing that runs a 30B-class model on a Pi 5 is the CPU in a 16 GB board, and only because Qwen3-30B-A3B is a 3.3B-active MoE: Q3_K_S (13.3 GB) gives ~8 tok/s with a 4k context; a 3-Pi llama.cpp RPC mesh is slower (3.4-5.4 tok/s). A dense 27B (Gemma 3 27B, 17.2 GB at Q4_0) does not fit in 16 GB and no one has published it running on a Pi 5.
